• "TO ZEVlTatfa.” 0 Zephyr, let the current of thy wrath. With lightning speed be wafted far away. •Restr .in thy war-like sound, nor let the deep Be lashed to fury 'midst the billow white; Reserve rhy crushing force for winter drear, As wild. in aspect, forth be stands at bay Encased in icy armour sparking bright. Amidst the snowy wreaths that crown him king; The summer sun in all its glory shines, .And sheds a grandeur o'er the landecape fair. But ah the richly verdant scenes around. On whinh the bleating lambkins gasping lie, The leafs, groves, the joyous woodlands wild. The rair;b.rw tinted flowrets on the bank, Are panting 'neath the weight of thy neglect, When all around s ,oald brea`he of love s delight; In langour deep, the pretty songsters droop, With scarce the power to unfold their wings, Yet feebly flut'ring en the outspread branch • With music sweet they call thee to their aid; • Come then sweet Zephyr, let thy balmy breeze, With fragrance laden, flit across the scene, And every tiny bqd shall rise its head To greet thee with a loving smile again. Mark how the joyous fruit upon the bough With ros.ate cheek bends forth to catch one kiss, One fond embrace, as la )ating through the air Like sound of harp wslian thou dost glide, For by thy magic touch new life springs up Within the heart of every tender flower Whr se opening petals court the industrious bee. And bil'him sip the sweets therein concealed. Haste then Zephyrus, haste, and shed abroad The ambrosial influence of thy passing breath, Restrain the sultry rays oppretsive power, And bid the fainting heart again rejoice. MAURICE COBHAM.
Floriston Hall, Wixoe-by-Halstead.

HER DREAM. "Mother, they tell me a dream is true Whenever it comes when dawn Is new, For then, I have heard the gossips say, The mists of the brain are swept away, And clear the eyes of the soul can see The secret things that are yet to be; I dreamed a dream while the dawn was new— Oh, mother, what if my dream is true? 'I saw in my dream a murky sky. And crested billows were leaping high, Leaping and dashing in stormy play On a shattered wreck, their helpless prey; Rolling and breaking in clouds of foam On my love's good ship that sailed from home; The sea-gulls screamed, and the wild wind blew— Oh, mother, what if the dream is true?" • Autumn went by like a story told, And the girlish cheek grew pale and cold; When last year's leaves were faded and shed, A snowdrop rose from its g trden bed; The hoar-frost silvered the cottage pane, When the flower of hope bloomed out again, But skies were bright with a wintry blue ; Could earth rejoice if that dream were true? Days went and came, and the air was sweet In fresh spring fields where the young lambs bleat; When catkins covered the willow trees, Glad tidings came from the far-off seas Of brave lives won from the hungry waves, By Love that watches, and guards, and saves. "Oh. mother," she said, "God only knew My lad was safe, though the dream was true !" —Sunday Magazine. SARAH DOYDNEY.

The corkscrew finds the longest way round the safest way through. Peace is the burden of each man's weary longing and prayer. It is curious—this silent undertone of desire that men have after this certain something which they have not. In every hoashold since time began there have been those 'whose hearts were ransacked, and in a general way it may be said that the broken-hearted have been the richestbearted. No man or woman even of the humblest sort can really be strong, gentle, pure, and good without the world being better for it—without somebody being helped and comforted by the very existence of that goodness. The word " character" comes from a term which means to engrave upon or cut in. Character is that inner, substan- Ca', and essential quality which is wrought into the very soul, and makes a maxi what he actually is. When a member, in the course of a very long speech, called for a glass of water, a member sitting near exclaimed sotto race to his neighbours, "This is all contrary to the laws of meenics—a windogill running by water." It is said that Dr. Johnson once read the Book of Ruth from a rnanueript to a company of fashionable people in London, whereupon their admiration was so excited that they requested to know where he had obtained so exquisite a story. Depend upon it, in the midst of all the science about the world and its ways, and all the ignorance of God and His greatness, the man or woman who can say, 'Thy will be done," with the true heart of giving up, is nearer the secret of things than the geologist and theologian.—George Mac- cloned. Little Paul, clambering on his father's knee: "Pa, what is humbug ?"—Father " Wby-, what do you want to know that for ?"—Paul "I heard you say it to ma a minute ago."—Father: " Yes, my son. Humbug is when your ma pretends she loves me, and there are no buttons on the neck of my shirt." I Creep a shop and sell fancy goods. A gentleman came in to buy something. It was early, and my little boy and I were alone in the hou3e at the time. The gentleman gave me a sovereign, and I had to go upstairs to my cash box. Before doing so I went into the little room next to the shop aid said to the boy, "Watch the gentleman, that he don't sal anything," and I put him on the counter. As soon as I returned, he sang out, " Pa, he didn't steal anything; I watched 'him." You may imagine what a position I was in. TEES LAST Donax OUT.—A man recently in Glasgow

laid a wager that he would won, win' and marry a young lady, who, with hif:, companions, he had just seen arrive at the hotel where he was living. He introduced himself to the damsel, she smiled upon his snit, a minister was called in, and they were married within an hour. The wager, of no inconsiderable amount, was handed over to the bride- groom, who left with his bride the following day. It was afterwards discovered that the couple had long been man and wife, and that they had been travelling about playing the same trick at various hotels.

GENIUS AND ITS ORIGIN.—It was well said of an Indian post, "0! mighty men and great rivers the springs are obscure." The enlarged an purified vision of modern szience may perceive much and guess more of the conditions which make the appearance cif genius possible. But the con- ditions which fix it at the very time and place, the secret Workings of nature which bring it to pass that an rEschylns, a Leonardo, a Faraday, a Kant, or a Spinoza is born upon the earth, are as obscure now as they were a thousand years ago. The power of these men still bears with it the rever- ence and awe that belong to great things unaccountable.— Pollock's Life of Spin6za. MHZ( OF STRAW.—Many years ago men could easily be found to give any evidence, upon oath, that might be re- quired, and some of these persons walked openly in West- minster Hall with a straw in one of their shoes, to signify they wanted employment as witnesses; hence originated the saying, "he is a man of straw." But the custom has high antiquity. A writer in the Quarterly Review (vol. 33, p. 341), says W.-. have all heard of a race of men who used in former days to ply about our own courts of law, and who, from their manner of making known their occupation, were recognised by the name of straw shoes.' An advo- cate or lawyer who wanted a convenient witness, knew by these signs where to find one, and the colloquy between the parties was brief. 'Don't you remember?' said the advo- cate (the play looked at the fee and gave no sign; but the fee increased and the powers of memory .increased with it). To be sure I do.' Then come into court and swear it. And .straw shoes went into the court and swore it." THE MAN WITH THE NOSE! Ileav'ns, what an organ have a care; Of limpid springs and brooks beware. Lest, looking in, thou find the fate That for Narcissus lay in wait, Who saw—and sigh'd away his breath ; They'd say you organised your death. From the Greek.

A sub-committee of a school committee were examining a class in a proprietary school. One of the members under. Look to sharpen up their wits by propounding the following question :—" If I had a mince pia and gave two-twelfths to John two-twelfths to Isaac, two-twelfths to Harry, and should keep half the pie for myself, what would there be left ?" There was a profound study among the boys, but finally one lad held up his hand as a signal that he was ready to answer. "Well, sir, what would there be left? Sdeak up, loud, so that all can hear," said the committee- man. "The plate !" shouted the hopeful fellow. The com- mittee-man turned red in the face, while the other members roared aloud. The boy was excused from answering any more Tiestions.

MAIDENTIO OD AND MARRIAGE.—Let every girl be rather slow than hasty to leave her maidenhood for the married state There is nothing more lowering to womanhood, nething so repulsive to high ideas of female delicacy, tha'n , a young woman making it the one aim and object of her life to be married ; and yet how often do we see this the case in modern English society ! How often do we see a young lady display her intentions in this respect with the most cool, unblushing boldness; how often is the fact made painfully apparent in many of the matrimonial connections contracted in the world around us! Let Christian girls Shun and look down upon this hasty eagerness for marriage as utterly beneath the dignity of their maidenhood. In our day there are, thank God, many beautiful, and useful, and ennobling works which may be undertaken by girls in their maiden years; therefore there is no possible reason why they should want to hurry into marriage. There are schools for our girl zech in—schools of the poor and ignorant; there are Christ's sick and weak to be tended; there are hearts and minds that have never fasted of the blessed Gos- pel fountain waiting for draughts from the water of life; there is knowledge of varied kinds to be won ; there are talents to be cultiv tted ; there is every facility given in our tirne for the intelleetnal improvement of women. Oar girls, then, cannot c npla.in teat marriage is forced upon them a 3 the Only path in life open to woman.—Alice Gray, in the " Own Payer."
SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

The Buddhist tope at Jaggayyapettah, on the Krishna river, Madras, discovered last September, proves to be of grewer importance than was at first supposed. In the opinion of the officers of the Archmelogical Survey who have lately examined it, it is a tope of great antiquity, preceding that at Amraveti by several centuries, and probably belongs to about B.C. 200. It was repaired by one of the early kings of the Andhra dynasty, according to an inscription found on the spot.—Athenceum. Baron :Dancklemann, 'a German meteorologist of repute, has been sent out by the International African Association to join Mr. H. M. Stanley on the Congo. He has taken a very complete outfit of meteorological instruments; and we may hope, therefore, to have before long climatological data. of the highest value. This department of science has un- fortunately hitherto been far too much neglected both on the Congo and in ether 'parts of Africa, and to this un- doubtedly is largely due the loss of so many valuable lives. TRANSPARENCE OF THE Ain.--The result of three years' observations of the air near Upsala, in Sweden, with regard to transparence have been lately published by Herr Ham- berg in the ZeitschrVt ffir Ideteoroloyie. The degree of transparence was estimated by the greater or less distinct- ness with which a wool and houses bounding the view from the Observatory cent' be seen at mid-day. Thus a scale of 6 deg. was formed, from zero (0), representing extremely transparent air, to (5), extremely troubled air. Rainy and snowy weather was excluded. These degrees were found to occur with various frequency in the different months. Ex- treme transparence (0) occurred most frequently in March and April, very frequently also in October, but it was very rare in June and December. The extremely troubled state (5) presented a first maximum of frequency in winter, and another less pronounced in July. No. 4 had a maximum of frequency in July, and a maximum in April, and so on. The transparence was proved to be related to air pressure and direction of wind (in a way we cannot here stop to ex- plain) ; but these two elements do not fully account for the annual variations of transparence. With regard to moisture it appeared that in general the transparence decreased as the moisture increased. In the colder months this relation was very pronounced and regular, but in the warm season, from May to August, the air was very often troubled, though the moisture was not over 30 or 40 per cent., and not in- frequently there was great transparence with a moisture as high as 70 or 80 per cent. Though on an average the air was more transparent on cloudless than on cloudy days, there were great irregularities, and a direct connection be- tween transparence and quantity of clouds could not be affirmed. .0n the whole the cause of differences in the trans- parence of the air seems to be a partial condensation of aqueous vapour. In the warmer months another cause oper- ates, which is probably to be sought in dust and smoke from regions near or distant. This is being investigated by the author. The relation of atmospheric transparence to the amount and frequency of rain was also studied by Herr Hamberg. The tables show that the more troubled the air, the greater is the probability of rain, and the greater the quantity of rain. This does not, however, hold good in the same measure for different seasons. In the months February, March, September, and October the probability of rain with transparent air is very small in comparison with that with troubled air; but in the months April to August, the differ- ence is not nearly so great, evidently because of the dry troubling of the air which then occurs. SOUND SHADOWS IN Waxna.—ln experimenting, long ago, on the velocity of sound in water, Colladon noticed in- aiientally that when the end of the hearing tube plunged in ti e water became screened, by a projecting wall, from the immersed bell the sound was remarkably lessened in in- tensity. These "sound shadows" are known to be much more distinct in water than in air. An interesting contribu- tion to this subject has been lately made by Professor John Le Conte, of Berkeley, California, who got his son, a few years ago, to watch the blasting with 'giant powder," or dynamite, of a sandstone reef 151 t. below, low-water level in the harbour of San Francisco. The suddenness of the shock of each explosion had striking effects. At a distance of 300 ft. two distinct shocks were experienced—one came through the water and was felt (in a boat, or on a wooden pile) as a short concussion or blow before the water sensibly rose over the point of explosion; the other came later by the air (to which it was evidently communicated by the water when the elastic pulse emerged at the place of explosion) and was heard. The gases generated came to the surface much later than this second shock, raising a column of water 25ft. to 301 t. The concussion caused by the explosien killed or stunned fish within a radius of 200 ft. or 300 ft. The "sound Meadow" experiments consisted, first, in lowering in various positions soda-water bottles attached to rigid rods from the tcp of a vertical pile about one foot in diameter and about 4011. from the explosive cartridge, which held about 151 b. of the compound. The bottles were shivered when outside of the geometrical shadow of the pile, but protected when within it; and it was so whether they were filled with water or air. Next, cylindrical glass tubes (Oft. long, liin. in diameter, and half an inch thick) were attached to frames and plunged in a horizontal position behind the pile. In each case the portions projecting beyond the limits of the shadow were shattered, while the middle of the tubs, in the shadow, was saved. A tube being lowered 12ft. beyond the pile, its protected portion was sensibly equal in length to the diameter of the pile; showing that the shadow extended back between sensibly parallel vertical planes. It is noted that the surface of the water just over the explosion ex- hibited numerous jets of water rising about 3in. in the centre of the area. The distinctness of "sound-shadows," like those of light, should depend (according to theory) on short- ness of wave-length, and Professor Le Conte endeavours to show that this must apply to water as well as air (in which acute sounds cast more distinct shadows than grave ones). Where the time of a blow or explosive impulse is exceed- ingly brief, the wave-length must be proportionately short. Now, the efficiency of surface blasting under water with nitro-glycerine compounds depends on the extraordinary suddenness of detonation,' and the wave generated in an elastic medium like water must be very intense and very short, so that an obstacle will give a sharply defined shadow. The author thinks that waves from the less sudden explosion of gunpowder should therefore give less definite shadows. A WELSH MOUNTAIN ON FIRE.—A correspondent writes to the Western Mail, calling attention to a curious pheno- menon, which, although well known in the immediate dis- trict in which it exists, will be new to a large number of people. He says: "I happened to be making a tour a few days ago through the Rhondda Valley, and as I was pass- ing the Cwrn Park Mountain I noticed what at a little dis- tance appeared to be a small bonfire about half-way up its side. Curiosity prompted me to climb the barren hill to see what was being burned. After struggling thtbugh a good deal of mud and over marshy ground I reached the fire, when, to my surprise, I found that the flames were not caused by the burning of rubbish or any other visible sub- et tnce. The fire flamed up through about three square feet of barren earth, which was hot and parched, except where covered with what at first seemed to be boiling water. Upon closer examination I found that only the water near the centre of the fire approached anything like boiling heat, the the rest being in some places lukewarm, and in others quite cold. I was sorely puzzled at first to account for this differ- ence of temperature in the water, for it all boiled and bubbled with equal violence. I drove my walking-stick into the earth two or three inches away from any spot from which fire issued, when, to my astonishment, flames shot up from this newly-made hole at least a foot high. I repeated the experiment two or three times with the same result. It seemed as though a fierce fire existed under this small patch cf ground. The thing that 'puzzled me the most was the non-existence of any cracks or holes in the ground except those which I had myself made. The earth belched forth fire without opening its mouth. I had not been many seconds at this spot before I discovered that I was windward to the flame, for I VMS half suffocated by a sulphurous, grassy stench. I shifted my ground, and after considerable eliberation came to the conclusion that this extraordinary phenomenon was caused by the continuous escape of sub- terranean gas through a deep fissure in the rocks. Subse- quent inquiries in the neighbourhood proved that my con- jecture was right. The inhabitants of the district say that the gas ascends through a fissure in the rocks from a seam of coal several hundred feet below the surface, and that it was set on fire many years ago by some unknown person, and has burned continuously ever since. I also learned that this is not a unique phenomenon in this district. A smaller jet of gas, I was told, has been burning for some years near the head of the Rhondda Valley. To witness the earth on fire is no doubt astonishing, but it can hardly be eompared with the phenomenon which, a fellow' traveller in- formed me, exists near Aberdare. Near that town the gas from a seam of coal forces itself up through a fissure in the rocks, and through the surface of the earth and the waters of a stream. It has been repeatedly lighted, when a large spot on the water through which the gas bubbled seemed to be on firs, just as the ground appeared to me on Cwm Park Mountain. My informant, however, stated that in the former instance the discharge of gas was intermittent, and that consequently the fire went out at intervals, whereas, so far as I could learn, the fire on the mountain has been burn- ing for something like forty or fifty years, and has in that time materially increased in body and force. Indeed, so strong is it now that considerable difficulty, I should imagine, would be experienced in extinguishing it. It cer- tainly forms a notable feature in the landscape at night."

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. The Marchioness of Gueydon, who recently died at Val- abre, has left the sum of £B,OOO, besides extensive and valuable property, for the foundation at that place of a high school of agriculture. JAPANESE FARMING. —The Japanese have more faith in the virtues of town sewage than we have in England. The intensely clever people of that beautiful land utilise the whole of the sewage of their towns and villages for manure. The Japanese farmer, says Professor Kinch, of the Imperial College of Agriculture, at Tokio, treats his Boil as a vehicle in which to grow crops, and does not appear to regard it as a bank from which to draw continual supplies. Thus he manures every crop, and he applies the manure to the crop, and not to the land. It is somewhat difficult to get at the proportion of Japanese soil which is actually cultivated, but It appears to be between a seventh and a tenth of the entire area of the country. The land is naturally remarkably fer- tile, but the Japanese have little faith in soil which has not been lavishly manured. "A new field gives but a small crop," they say, and by the joint aid of manure and the splendid climate they manage to gather two crops off one field in the same year. Sometimes, indeed, the terraced slopes of the heights will produce wheat, rice, and roots all in one season. SELLING CATTLE BY WEIGHT.—A correspondent to the Banffshire Journal expresses regret that Mr. Fowlie now contemplates selling the cattle weighing machine fixed on Tarriff market stance. For this he cannot be blamed, as he has patiently waited, and tried for two and a half years to induce us to use it, but with so little success that it has not been used at all for the last four months. The correspond- ent; who signs himself "Hopeful," says :—" Clearly we, of this-district, do not want to know the exact live weight of our cattle, from which, with a little experience, the dead weight can be calculated as easily as reducing cwts. to stones. Agriculture has not yet taken its- place amongst the exact sciences, and we seem to be so much used to in- exactitude in our operations that to do any business by methodical rules we openly repudiate. We prefer to gauge the weight of the bullocks we sell by the eye or the tape- line in a rude way to a mathematical demonstration of actual weight, and no doubt get so puffed up as to think we can match the dealer of life-long experience. Less than two years ago I heard a dealer telling that he had got seven beasts at £4 per head under value, and another dealer who was presert confirmed this opinion. These cattle were bought on the Hill at Turriff from one of our shrewdest farmers. Slips like this occur more frequently than some of us are aware, yet all the time we credit ourselves with sharpness. At any rate this machine has come a little too soon for us. The schoolmaster must be abroad among us some time longer before we can see through it." Farmers are slow to see their interests in this matter, as in some other things, otherwise the entire traffic in living animals in this country would long ago have been transacted solely by live weight, as determined by weighing machines. Of course, the interests of middle men are strongly opposed to this change. FARMERS AND THEIR Bustsrzss.—An interesting point for agriculturists has been decided by the Court of Appeal. The defendant, who was tenant, under an agreement, of a farm of three hundred acres at Coulsdon, on the chalk hills of Surrey, claimed the right to sell the flint stones upon his farm. The agreement contained the usual stipulations against waste and use of the land for other than agricul- tural purposes, and reserved to the landlord all mines and minerals, sand, quarries of stone, brick-earth, and gravel- pits. But the land was full of flints, which it was necessary to collect and remove. This the farmer did, selling the stones on his own account, urging that he was authorised to do so by the custom of the county. The landlord did not deny the custom, but contended that it could not override his rights in the flints. Mr. Justice Kay thought differ- ently, and the Court ef Appeal affirmed the decision of the Court below. In giving judgment the Master of the Rolls reaffirmed the doctrine that an agricultural custom need not have existed from time immemorial; it was sufficient that it was proved to have existed a reason- able time, and Sir George Jessel went on to say, " the Court ought not to interfere with a well-established custom on the ground that it was unreasonable, without some very strong reasons for doing so. Farmers, like other people, knew their own business a great deal better than lawyers did." There is nothing new in the law as now laid down, .yet who has forgotten the howl that went up when it was first proposed to legislate tenant-right in Ireland? There, too, farmers might be expected to know their own business best—there, too, there was a well-established custom, and had the custom been recognised, as it would have been in England, no legislation would have been necessary. But what is right and just in England is looked upolii by a cer- tain class of politicians as sheer robbery when applied to Ireland. AGRICULTURAL EXPERIBIENTS.—Professor Jamieson is to be congratulated upon the success of the experiments which he carried out last year for the Sussex Association for the Improvement of Agriculture. The season was decidedly an unfavourable one, and the experiments at some of the sta• tions were rendered unsatisfactory by the drought succeeded by floods of rain; but at Hassock's Gate some important re- sults were obtained. There the experiments on turnips and peas were carried out on nearly a barren sand, thus showing the action of the various manures used far more definitely than can be done on land of average fertility, which will grow fair crcps without any manure. One result of the ex- periments on turnips Professor Jamieson declares to be the settlement of the "battle of the phosphates." On different plots, with a duplicate in each case, he tried ground copro- lite, ground bone ash, superphosphate, steamed bone flour, anda mixture of coprolite and steamed bone flour against each other. Two plots got no phosphate, and these yielded less than three ounces each, on an average, of dried produce, while the lowest of the manured plots gave over 79 ounces. Thus the value of undissolved phosphates was strikingly demonstrated. As to the comparative results of the use of dissolved and undissolved phosphates, these were so nearly alike that Mr. Jamieson has no hesitation in declaring that it must be extravagant to go on buying superphosphate when a ton of ground coprolite costs about the same as a ton of superphoqphate, and contains double the amout of phosphate. Still the produce of the superphosphate plots averaged more than that of any other, and as much as five tons per acre more than that of the plot on which the mix- ture of coprolite and steamed bone meal was used. No doubt there is more phosphate left in the soil on these last duplicate plots than on the superphosphate plots; but this can scarcely be as valuable as the extra five tons per acre of turnips. The Professor admits that superphosphate gives turnip plants a better start than undissolved phosphates do, and when he says that steamed bone flour, used with copro- lite, gives nearly as good a start, and that its effects last longer, he does not say enough. A good start often makes all the difference between a good crop and a failure, especially when-turnip fly is prevalent. No doubt a very small quantity of nitrogen, in nitrate of -soda or guano, mixed with the ground phosphate, would afford the rapid start quite as well as superphosphate does, and this may perhaps be recommended. The results of the experiments undoubtedly tend to support the conclusion come to by the Aberdeenshire Association, as one result of their experi- ments; but many people will demur to the statement that the "battle of the phosphates" is over before it has been proved that as good crops can .be grown at a given cost by the use of ground phosphates With or without some stimu- lating addition, as by the use uf superphosphate. But did the applications of manure all cost alike? If not, these re- marks may require modification. A more clear and un- equivocal result of the experiments was the discovery that chloride of potash, often used to supply potash to plants, is absolutely destructive on a soil destitute or nearly destitute of organic matter. As this effect of the manure has not previously been made known, it is certain that some neutra- lising agency has prevented the injurious action. From his own experiments, and from some information given by others, Mr. Jamieson has been able to conclude that a suffi- cient quantity of organic matter neutralises the influence of the chlorine in chloride of potash, and he believes it is the hydrogen in the organic matter which is the neutralising agent. But he has ascertained that the sodium in nitrate of soda also neutralises the chlorine. He concludes that chloride of potash cannot safely be applied, unless with sodium in some combination, to soils which contain less than 10 per cent. of organic matter.—Mark Lane Express. EXPERIMENTS ON POTATO CULTURE.—An account has been published, under the direction of the County Cork Ag- ricultural Society, of the experiments on the Munster farm last year, made under the direction of Mr. T. Carroll, super- intendent of the Agricultural Department under the Com- missioners of National Education. They are a very elabo- rate set of comparative experiments, in which various sorts • were observed as to liability to disease, and in which the Champion potato was subjected to various mannrings. Po- tato growers should procure and read these pages for the information regarding produce which they contain, under the various circumstances in which the crop was grown. The most important lesson of the whole series is the mar- vellous effect of kainit :—"The piece of ground set apart for these experiments was divided inteeas many ridges as there were distinct manures to be experimented upon ; these ridges ran in the direction of the greatest length of the ex- perimental ground. Each ridge being first manured with a particular manure, equal bands were marked out acioss the whole of the ridges, in the direction of the breadth of the experimental ground, giving the whole a chequered appear- ance. Nothing was done to the first band, but each of the other bands was manured with one of the manures used in manuring the ridges. In this way the first band consisted of the ends of the ridges, each manured with a single manure at the rate of two cwt. to the acre; each of the other bands gave combinations of all the manures with each other, the same combination occurring twice in different parts of the series, that is to say, each manure occurring once singly at the rate of two cwt. to the acre, and once with a double quantity, namely, four cwt. to the acre, and twice in com- bination with each of the other manures. Some ridges were also manured with farm-yard dung, at the rate of 30 tons to the acre. Two kinds of dung were used :-1, dung made in the usual way in the open yard; and 2, dung made in covered pits, the object being to ascertain the relative ma- nuring value of manure exposed to the sun and rain, with tkat not so exposed, and from which no liquid manure had escaped." Where no manure was applied the crops appear to have been five tons per acre, and the effect of the addi- tion of sulphate of ammonia or nitrate of soda, bone meal, bone superphosphate, and mineral superphosphate, and other manure is given at two cwt. and four cwt. per acre, both alone and in combination with various auxiliary manures. In every case where kainit was added the produce jumped from six or seven tons to twelve and fifteen tons, and when kainit was applied alone the produce was fourteen tons per acre. Farm-yard manure collected in open yard produced a crop of thirteen tons, and made under cover a crop of six- teen tons. But the following is the principal conclusion to which the es periments led :—" The effect prod aced by

kalnit (potash) is remarkable, being quite comparable with that of good ordinary farm•yard dung, not only as regards gross weight, but also as regards the relative proportion of marketable and small potatoes. Its action is dominant, whichever manure it may be joined with."

less services. He was now Lord Chancellor of Ireland. This position, however, he did not retain long. He soon made way for another rising star, and retired into private life on a handsome pension. When Plunket retired from the stage of politics the cause of religions liberty sustained a heavier loss than any it had suffered tince the death of Fox just twenty years before. Grattan, Mackintosh, Burdett, and Brougham had each and all laid splendid offerings on the shrine, but the shrine was the shrine of party, and they made no particular sacrifice in what they brought. lint Plunket had from first to last little feeling as a party man. An adherent of Lora Gren- yille, he diSmetimes co•operated with the Whigs and some- -times differed from them; but during the fifteen years of his Attorney-Generalship he was alternately brought into antagonism with the followers of Eldon and the admirers of Grey, and neither spared him in the vehemence of their attacks. Without a relative or a connection in Parliament, without a house in London, and without leisure or oppor- tunity to cultivate social intimacies or disarm personal mis- apprehensions, he held his own undauntedly against all odds, and wrung simultaneously from adversaries and allies tributes of homage unlike those paid to other men. Peel, from whom he differed daily, and differed chiefly as to the whole course of his Irish Mministration, stated that the speech for Catholic Emancipation in 1825 was the highest display of reasoning and declamation which he had ever heard. When Mackintosh was asked who had done most for the cause of religious freedom, he answered Plunket, "for all the rest, Grattan, Sydney Smith, O'Connell, spoke what enthusiastic sympathisers already felt, and were eager to applaud, while he wrested with the strongest prejudice in its strongest hold, and by dint of resistless power left it wrecked and prostrate so that it never was the same again." To Plnnket, too, must be awarded the first place among Irish orators. Carran's imagination has been compared to virgin gold crumbling from its own richness. Grattan's mind was pre•eminent for its fertility and force. But neither of them equalled Plunket in the combination of chasteness and purity with splendour, intensity, and power. His loftiest flights and boldest bursts were tempered and re- strained by the severest taste. "He never," says one, "risked an apostrophe, the most dangerous of rhetorical figures, until the audience was thoroughly warmed for its reception. He was never stiltish like Sheridan in the most applauded passages of the Begnm speech, nor melodramatic like Burke in the dagger scenes. He was never gaudy or flowery." In a word, he was wholly free from the faults popularly attributed to the Irish school of eloquence, and this is the reason why some of his greatest triumphs were won in the English House of Commons, in which Flood failed, and Grattan obtained only a qualified success. We need not, therefore, be surprised that O'Connell, speaking of this Illustrious Irishman, should call him "That credit to Ireland, that ornament to the Bar, and that honour to human 'intelligence, William Conyngham Plunket." The luminous career of this boast and ornament of his country was destined to close in darkness and gloom. He shared the fate of Marlborough and Swift. His fine intellect became overclouded, and his fame became, so to speak, a thing of the past before his death. He died in his 90th year on the sth of January, 1854.

No. XVI.—WILLIAM CONYNGHAM PLUNKET. He could plead, &mound, and argue, Fire with wit, with wisdom gedifee—C. Mackay. This Illustrious Irishman was the 'son of a poor Presby- terian minister, in the North of Ireland. In 1768 the family removed to Dublin, where in 1776 the father died, leaving to his offspring little or no fortune beyond a good name— to which, however, the future Chancellor was mainly in- debted for his education. Plunket was only fourteen years of age when his father died, and the Unitarian congregation to. which his father had preached in Dahlia for ten years raised funds to complete his education and to support his mother. The funds thus raised by the paternal congrega- tion were honourably repaid by him in after life with in- terest. One incident of his schooldays is worth recording. His first school was kept by an anti-pugilistic master, and boxing was strictly, prohibited under the severest penalties. The course of education was calculated to awaken rivalry in intellectual conflicts, and obtaining a certain number of good marks entitled the good scholar to a certificate which exempted the possessor from punishment—in effect, an amnesty for any offences whatever. Placket obtained the much coveted certificate, and while its owner had a boyish quarrel with a class-fellow, which, despite the ordnance to the contrary, ended in a fight. Black eyes and bloody lips told their own tale, and the dread fiat was spoken —the offenders should be flogged. Plunket took his punishment like a hero, wincing a little, but not a tear or a moan escaped him, and then the turn of his fellow-combatant came. Plunket pleaded for his antagonist, urged that he alone was in fault; he forced the boy to fight, made him violate the rule, and he alone should suffer the penalty. All was in vain; the offence was too glaring to be overlooked, the guilty should suffer. "Here, then," cried Plunket, handing his late foe the certificate which exempted the holder from any punishment, "I kept this to save you, for now the master can't touch you." "You are a brave, generous lad, Plunket," said the master, "I see you will do us credit some of these days, only keep your temper and mind your lessons." In course of time he entered the Irish University, and there exhibited great scholarship, and highly distinguished himself as a member of the Historic* Society. The mem- bers of this society had the liberty of entering the Irish House of Commons, and it was the privilege of Plunket as a student of Trinity to have heard Henry Bergh, Flood, Yelverton, and Grattan. Charmed by the silvery simple dignity of Burgh, swayed by the powerful diction of Yelver- ton, subdued by the "resistless powers," as he himself calls them, "that waited on the majesty of Grattan's genius," Plunket seems nevertheless to have modelled himself more on Flood than on any orator who appeared during his early youth. Curran, who idolised Grattan, used to say that Flood was immeasurably the greatest man of his time in Ireland, and this seems also to have been the opinion of THE STATE OF IRELAND. Plunket, who respected, admired, adored, loved Grattan as mach as it was in his nature to love any man. div.head: TRIAL OF IWLEAN.
div.p: THE TRIAL OF IWLEAN.

THE ACCUSED FOUND TO BE INSANE. Under a special commission the trial of Roderick lll‘Leatt for the attempt on the life of her Majesty took place on Wednesday at the assize court at Reading, before Lord Cole- ridge (Lord Chief Justice of England) and Baron Huddle- ston. The prisoner was removed early in the morning from Reading Jail to the precincts of the court without observa- tion, but a large crowd assembled around the building as the hoar for commencing the proceedings arrived. There was, however, no pressure in the court itself, adtnission being strictly by ticket. The learned judges entered the court and took their seats at half-past ten o'clock, when the roll of grand jurymen was called over, Sir George Bowyer being the first to answer and consequeutly acting as foreman. It was noticeable that many of the grand jury, as well as these who were seated on the bench on either side of the judges, were wearing bouquets of primroses.—The Lord Chief Justice, in his charge to the grand jurr, explained that as- saults upon the Sovereign were by the law of England high treason, and those who committed them were traitors, and that the Government were in duty bound to treat this case as such cases had been treated for the past five hundred years—namely, as one of high treason.—The grand jury then retired, and were absent about 25 minutes, when they found a true bill against M‘Lean for high treason.—The prisoner was immediately placed in the doek, and looked worn and worried. The indictment, which was a very lengthy document, was read over, and the prisoner, in a clear but low tone, replied "Not guilty."—The Attorney-General, the Solicitor-General, Mr. J. J. Powell, Q.C., Mr. Poland, and Mr. A. L. Smith, appeared for the prosecution; and Mr. Montague Williams and Mr. Yates were for the prisoner. A petty jury having been empanelled without challenge, the Attorney-General opened the case for the prosecution, and said the charge against the prisoner was one of a most aggravated kind, he having directly attempted to compass the life of Her Majesty. He might inform them that if it were established the sentence of the law of the land was that of death. He need not enlarge on the magnitude of the crime. Murder or attempted murder was always horrible, but it was aggravated by the fact that it was in this case aimed at the life of one whose name and character were I known and beloved by millions. The Attorney-General then proceeded to describe the facts of the case' and said he should be able to show the premeditation of the prisoner, but they might have to consider the condition of the pri- soner's mind at the time. That would be a matter of grave consideration for the jury, and although the Crown had made inquiries into the matter, they had no desire whatever to keep back a single fact.---Mr. George Hayes, superinten- dent of the Windsor police, spoke to the arrival of Her Majesty at Windsor Station on the 2nd March, and to her entering a carriage accompanied by the Princess Beatrice, and taking a seat facing the horse. He saw the prisoner pointing a pistol to the carriage. He had just before heard the report of firearms, and saw the smoke proceeding from the pistol. He arrested the prisoner, and took from him a six-barrelled revolver. At the police station he charged the prisoner with shooting at the Queen, and the reply was simply, "Oh, the Queen." The pistol had some of its barrels loaded, and appeared to have been recently dis- charged. The prisoner bad also cartridges upon him. A letter upon him stated the great good a little money could have done, and spoke of the harm which "Mrs. Vic. and a bloated aristocracy" were accomplishing. On examining the spot he found that the shot was almost in a direct line with the carriage.—Mr. Egerton, of Sunderland, said he was at Windsor Station on the 2nd March, when Her Majesty arrived. He heard a shot, and saw the prisoner pointing a pistol at the Queen's carriage. He seized the prisoner, and detained him, assisted by James Burn-ide.— James Burnside, photographer, Windsor, said he was outside the gates of the station on-Her Majesty's arrival. He heard a report, and saw M‘Lean levelling a pistol with a high hand, as though taking aim at the front panel of Her Majesty's coach. He seized the prisoner.—Frank Orchard, one of the Queen's servants, saw the prisoner aiming the pistol at the carriage. Immediately after he heard the shot fired.— George Wilson, a student at Eton College, said he heard a report, and, turning, saw the prisoner with a pistol in his hand. His arm was extended, and the pistol was directed to the centre Of the carriage.—Joseph Tanner, inspector of the Great Western, at Windsor, said he found the bullet the day after the occurrence, on the siding near the waiting-room door.—Evidence was then given as to the puechase of a revolver at a pawnbroker's at Portsea by the prisoner, and also some cartridges at another shop, prisoner saying he was going abroad, and they might be useful, which completed the case for the prosecution, none of the witnesses having been cross-examined.—Mr. Montagu Williams, for the de- fence, said he did not question the facts of the case,-but he should be able to show without doubt that the prisoner was a lunatic, and was not responsible for his actions. He had no doubt whatever that when the evidence for the defence had been heard the jury would be able with pleasure and satisfaction to themselves to say that the prisoner was a man who was not, and who had not for years, been accountable for his actions.—Mr. Towers Smith, of Kensington, deposed to attending the prisoner in 1866 for a wound in the head re- ceived in the streets.—Dr. Goderick, of London, said he was called to attend a man named I.%l‘Lean in 1874, and gave a certificate which stated that he was of unsound mind at the time.—By the Attorney-General : He did not recognise the prisoner, but judging by the terms of the certikate he should say that the man was not likely to recover. He recognised the certificate itself, which was in his handwriting.—Samuel Staseley, an artist at Eavender-hill, London, said he knew the prisonee at Earlscourt-road, and remembered the two last witnesses being calied in to attend him. He was subject to fits and great peculiarities of conduct, and he regarded him as being insane.—Mr. Montagu Williams then put in several letters written by the prisoner shortly before the offence was committed, in which he stated that all the English people were against him, which drove him raving mad; that if they did not cease he should commit murder, and be did not mind if he was hung far it, as he would not be made a fool of.— Lord Chief Justice Coleridge haying summed up, the jury retired at 20 minutes to five, and after five minutes' delibera- tion returned, into court and delivered a verdict of "Not guilty," on tife ground of insanity. The Lord Chief Justice ordered the prisoner to be detained in custody during Her Majesty's pleasure.

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.

It is stated that the Hon. J. C. Dundas will not again con- test Richmond at the next general election. It is expected that the bulk of the Conservative party will support the motion of which Mr. W. H. Smith has given notice relative to the Irish Land Act. _ _

Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote, it is said, will probably visit Glasgow in October next, when there is expected to be a great Conservative "national demonstra- tion." Mr. Edward Shiel, formerly M.P. for Athlone, has been returned for county Meath without opposition. Mr. Shiel was recommended to the electors by the Roman Catholic clergy of the county. Arrangements are being made by the moderate Irish party for taking up the challenge issued by Mr. Gladstone some time since for a formal scheme of Home Rule, and they will arrange to present one in Parliament shortly after the Easter recess. The plan is expected to receive the support of all the Irish members who sit on the Government side of the House.

Major Vaughan Lee, M.P., for West Somerset, on Mon- day informed the Conservative committee of that district that, by the advice of his medical attendants, he has applied for the Chiltern Hundreds. The committee thereupon met and asked Mr. J. Stanley, of Quantock Lodge, near Bridge- water, whether he would come forward, if selected as a candidate, to which Mr. Stanley replied in the affirmative. The Liberal executive meeting have decided not to oppose the return of Mr. Stanley. Amongst the measures of social improvement whose pros- pects are affected by the existing deadlock in the House of Commons is the Bill for amending the Police Superannua- tion Act. The Home Secretary has undertaken to bring this in, but there is at present no prospect of his being able to do so this Session. The necessity for such a measure has been shown afresh by the anomalies descanted upon at several of the Easter Quarter Sessions, and which have operated to he serious disadvantage of members of the palice force. Mr. W. H. Smith has returned from Ireland;having visited that country with the object of gaining information in re- spect of his motion on Irish peasant proprietorship. While in Ireland he had the advantage of talking with a large number of representative men specially requested to meet him, and from them he learnt many particulars of consider- able importance. His observations confirmed rather than altered his previous views, and will probably form the basis of his speech.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIERY ACCIDENT NEAR DURHAM.
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIERY ACCIDENT NEAR DURHAM.
GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

Great excitement was manifested on Tuesday, when it was reported that one of those disasters which unhappily are net rare in the Durham district, had taken place at what is known as the Black Horse Colliery, Tudhoe, a pit in the Brockwell seam, some six miles west of Trimdon Grange Colliery, the scene of a recent disaster. At first the news went forth that by an explosion of gas 100 men had been imprisoned, and of this number it was not known how many would be brought up alive, but as soon as more reliable in- formation could be obtained it was known that a far less number had gone down as a night shift. It was shortly after cne o'clock on Tuesday morning when the explosion took place. At that time 51 men engaged as stonemen and shifters were working below-29 in the Busty seam, and the remainder in the Brockwell seam, 90 fathoms deep. The men in the former seam fortunately succeeded in making their way to Tudhoe Grange Colliery adjoining, which also belongs to the Weardale Iron Company, and with which communication is obtained by a door. As soon as possible after those above had been made aware of the explosion, parties were formed to explore the workings, and then ' attempted the rescue of the men imprisoned in the mine. It was found, however, that such was the force of the ex- plosion that both the east and west shafts had been blocked, and the former had to be cleared before anything more could be done. After an hour and a half hard work this was done, and two parties were quickly lowered. Rapping was heard land voices in the Busty seam, and five men were imme- diately brought up, who reported that after damp was present in small quantities, and also that the rest of the men , in their working had made their way to the Tudhoe Grange, about a mile away, as being a safer exit than the east shaft. div.p: Ihonest politician or an honest man.—This language was ruled to bo unparliamentary, and the member for New Ross I was called upon to withdraw it. In professedly complying with the order of the Speaker, Mr. Redmond slid he regretted that it was not in his power under the rules of the House to make use of the expressisn. This the Speaker considered to be not only offensive to the House, but especially offensive to the right hon. gentleman alluded to, and Mr. Redmond was at once "named" for having dis- regarded the authority of the chair.—On the motion of tit-, Marquis of HARTINGTON the House divided by 207 to 12 that Mr. Redmond be suspended from the service. of the House during the remainder of the sitting.—The lion. mem- ber having left the House, Sir STAFFORD ...S.ORTIICOTE, speaking on the main question, assured th ..e Government that they had the full support of the H. ',use in those mea- sures which they found to be necessary in the critical state of Ireland for the preservation, of law and order. He trusted there would be, no lack of care to protect Mr, Clifford Lloyd, who was acting with great courage. The Marquis. of HARTINGTON remarked that the Chief Sec•Atary was unable to justify on 3 portion of the cimular, but until a complete explanation had been received it would be unfair to dsk the House to pass an opinion upon the conduct of the inspectors of consta- bulary. Mr. J. COWEN, who advised the member for Sligo to adjourn the consideration of the subject until the Chief Secretary was in a position to give -a complete reply, pro- tteded to contend that the Coercion Acts had been a failure, and the Land Act bad not been a success. The Government, he said, bad mistaken a great political and social uprising for an-ordinary agitation, and he hoped that discussion would induce them to regather the lost thread of Irish policy, with a view to a new departure. He hoped, however, that there would be no attempt simply to make a victim of the Chief Secretary, whose, policy had been the policy of the Government, and of the Liberal party. Mr. SEXTON in- timated that he would repeat his question on Monday. The motion for the adjournment of the House was then withdrawn. A discussion on the condition 'of our navy followed.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

- - - Ayoub Khan, the Afghan Pretender, has arrived in Teheran. The appointment of Baron Jomini as Russian Secretary of State is officially reported. The Burmese Embassy has arrived at Calcutta, and will shortly proceed to Simla. The Porte has rejected the proposal of the committee for. the revision of the treaties of commerce between Turkey and foreign countries. On Good Friday, the parish priest of Inbach, near Krems, in Lower Austria, was preaching to his congregation, and had just uttered the words "we must all die," when he sank down and expired. An Imperial Rescript is published summoning the Ger- man Reichstag to meet on the 27th inst. The Emperor William will leave on Tuesday for Wiesbaden, where his Majesty intends staying for one month. It is announced that the coronation of the Emperor Alex- ander 111. of Russia will take place in August next, and that all the dignitaries of the empire will be required to attend the ceremony in Moscow. Reports have reached Rangoon from Mandalay that another Prince, the father-in-law of the King, anct a high official, besides several petty officials, have been killed in prison at that place, on the pretext that they had been en- gaged in a conspiracy. On Sunday night some thieves broke open an iron safe in the Central Post-office in Paris and stole from it 180 registered letters containing money and valuables, which were to have been delivered on Monday morning. The yatue of the pro- perty is estimated at a million of francs. The Foreign Office has issued a return showing the num- ber of foreigners in the service of the Egyptian Govern- ment. It appears from this that 1,324 foreigners are so em- ployed, of whom the English number 295, Italians 338, French 320, Austrians 106, and Greeks 103. The other nations are represented by a small number of officials. The annual salaries paid to foreigners amount to £373,704. The Anglo-Brazalian Times reports that during the night of the 17th ult. two caskets containing jewellery to the 'value of 5200,000, belonging to the Empress of Brazil and the -Princess Imperial, were stolen from the Christovan Palace from a wardrobe in which the person in charge had placed them. Three arrests have been made, but no traceof the jewels have been obtained. On Wednesday, the Porte verbally informed Mr. Foster that it declined absolutely and definitely to authorise the Imperial Ottoman Bank to receive a delegate from the Bank of St. Petersbury to verify the accounts of revenue assigned for payment of the war indemnity, and asked him to com- municate the fact to M. de Novikoff, who has, however, refused to make any change on the conditions on which he had insisted. The Daily News says:---" We hear that the case of Mr. Arthur Evans, the correspondent of the 21Ianchester 'Guar- dian., continues to engage the attention of Sir Henry Elliot, Her Majesty's ambassador at Vienna, who has fol- lowed the proceedings with keen interest. It is hoped Mr. Evans will 'be liberated at the close of the preliminary inquiry." Brigandage as a profession is not without its rewards, at least in Sicily. Commander Notar Bartolo was recently seized by a party of desperadoes in the neighbourhood of Palermo, and his friends have paid fifty thousand francs as the price of his life. The Sicilians recently celebrated with great enthusiasm the anniversary of their deliverance from foreign foe. Suppose they were to turn a little of their enthusiasm against the domestic foes who rob and degrade them The Schiverin theatre has been completely gutted by fire, which broke out during the performance on Monday night, and only the outer walls now remain standing. The clearing of the house was effected without any accident or confusion, the public being informed from the stage of the fire in time to make their escape. The Grand Duke, who was present at the performance, also addressed some re-assuring words to the people. TROUBLES IN TRlPOLl—lntelligence received at Tripoli states that an Italian traveller has been arrested and mal- treated by the Turkish police near Derna, and subjected to insult from the inhabitants on his arrival in that town. Other Europeans in the place have also been insulted, and as the Governor-General of Benghasi has refused to grant any re- dress, the British and foreign 'Consuls at Benghasi have been obliged to charter a vessel to 'bring all Europeans to that town for safety. ANTI-JEWISH RIOTS.—A telegram from Kherson, received by the St. Petersburg Gobs, states that anti-Jewish riots occurred on the 11th and 12th insts , at Beresnegowatoje and Wiesunsk, in the Kherson district. The disturbances were, however, confined to window-breaking. In consequence of further news of a diEquieting character from Beresnegowatoje steps have been taken to despatch troops to the scene of the disorders. On the 13th, slight excesses occurred at Dubassu, whither troops have been sent. One jew who was ill-treated by the populace has since died. A riot has also broken out at Novaja Praja, where a large crowd proceeded on thel6th Inst. to wreck some public-houses, booths, and private dwel- lings. The military stationed there have been reinforced by local troops from Elisabethsgrad. ANOTHER PLOT TO ASSASSINATE THE CZAR. The Vienna Eresse states that trustworthy merchants who have arrived from Moscow bring intelligence that eighty workmen employed on the Uspanski Cathedral there, were arrested on Holy Saturday, in consequence of the discovery of a mine under the edifice, which is thene selected for the coronation of the Czar. A search was being made for a second mine, and no zervice was performed there during Easter. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. DISMISSAL OF EUROPEAN ,OFFICIALS.

Four European officials employed in the Ministry of Finance have been dismissed without .notice, and without any reason being assigned. A circular has been issued by the Ministry of Finance to the contractors requiring all cor- xespondenee to be in,Arabic. The dissention in the army is not confined to the Circas- &ans. Several Arab officers have been arrested, the alleged .conspiracy serving as a good excuse. The court-martial is Ailing daily, and executions are probable. if so retaliation in certain, but Ourabi Pasha urges that a „severe example should be made. Heztates that the prisonerslavour Ismail Pasha. .The final meeting of the English Auxiliary Commission appointed by the BritiahaForeign Office, was held on Mon- day, under the presidency of Sir Edward Malet, British Consul-General, when aresolution was adopted expressing approval of the revision .of the Egyptian codes affected by Mr. Scott, the British member of the Court of _Appeal. In the revised codes, Englich law is only introduced when it ' doec.not clash with the system at present in force ; but, on the other hand, the German and Italian codes are freely utilised when their application is an improvement on the French code now in use. THE INSURRECTION IN THE HERZEGOVINA. The-occupation of Bosnia and the Herzegovina is costing the Austrians dear. The Delgations have been asked for a further sum of nearly 24 million floiins, and the Govern- ment admits that in consequence of the spread of the insur- rection its indispensable to maintain the army of occupa- tion at it:a:present strength. A semi-eicial contradrction in given to a report that the Austrian Alinister Resident at Cettinge has been instructed to confer with the Montenegrin Government with the view of arranging,lor operations against insurgent bawls, who are only accessible from Montenegro. Accounts from Vienna of the .operations in the Herzego- vina and Crivoseie state that the Austrians will very shortlg have 3 complete cordon on the Montenegrin frontier. By this means the ,Carin try, having been far the most part cleared of insurgent banda, will ke kept so. The.task is an arduous . one for the troope. In the Zubci, the border district of the Herzegovina, tovrarde the Montenegrindistrictof Grahovo and the Crivoscie, the troops which have to hold the heights of the Troglava and ,Yardar from which :the insurgents =Jested the canvoya and detachments spassing between Korito, and Gatchko are, according to the correspon- dent of the Pesthcr Lloye, who has just returned from there, encamped in snow a loot deep. They are in excellent spirits, hut exposure, fatigae, and scarcity of water swell the sick list. "People in the Herzegovina," says the same correspondent, "are more and more returning to their homes and resuming work, and the news comes that several of the leaders of the bands about Stolatz and Duraskovics have declared their intention of submitting and of inducing their followers to Ao co likewise and return home."

div.head: EXAMINER, SA.TURDAY, APRIL 22, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA.TURDAY, APRIL 22, 1882.
I'AIISC'ELLANEOUS.

A Gliszow teitgrine Yeeserds the death of the Strathavon "fasting A Chaster correepondent states.that the Irish mail was fired et on Wednesday when passing Aber, and the ball Pas,',ed through the window of a compartment occupied by M.e. Shaw, M.P. for Cork. , An Irish labourer has performed the perilous feat of riding from Holyhead to Chester by clinging to the axle beneath the break-Tan of an express train. For his daring he has been fined 203. and costs by the Chester magistrates. At Birmingham, on Wednesday, George William Long, the local manager of Messrs. Waite, James, and Co., corn I merchants, of Gloucester, Bristol, Birmingham, and other places, was remanded for a week on a charge of embezzling £2,000 belonging to his employers. The prisoner attributes his defalcations mainly to gambling. Though it has not yet been officially announced, it is well understood in Preston that the Prince of Wales will lay the foundation stone of the Free Library and Museum at Preston, during the Guild celebrations, which willl be held in the first week in September next. It is stated that he will be accompanied by their Reyal Highnesses the Duke of Connaught and the Duke of Albany. At the Liverpool Police Court on Wednesday, Joseph Henry Philp was charged with stealing 24 diamond rings, the property of Mr. Bryce Wright, London. The prisoner had written for the rings, which were valued at £6O, on a memorandum form, headed "Miller and Sons, Temple Buildings." He was sentenced to six months' imprison- ment. A memorial to Lord Beaconsfield, including stained-glass windows, peal of bells, and decorations, was dedicated on Wednesday, in Hughenden Church. Her Majesty sent two wreaths for the grave—sue of immortelles, and the other of primroses, his favourite flower. The wearing of primroses in memory of the deceased statesman was largely practised throughout the country, and to a ntticeable extent in Liver- pool. Mr. Bradlaugh told a meeting at Hanley, on Saturday night, that the attempt to make him a bankrupt had resulted in a committee formed at Philadelphia inviting him to deliver a course of lectures in America during the next autumn, for which he would be paid £2,000 in advance. He declined the offer because be would not undertake any fresh engagement till he had fought his battle with Parlia- ment. KILLED AT A. CROSSING.—A terrible sensation was caused at the Midland station at Nottingham, on Wednesday after- noon, by an accident which occurred in full view of many passengers. A gentleman, at present unknown, was passing over the, level crossing, when an engine, travelling from the direction of Lincoln, entered the station. Unheeding the shouts of danger, he went on, and was knocked down and -nearly decapitated. The crossing is used by thousands daily. FEARFUL EXPLOSION OF CHLORATE POTASIL—On Wednesday morning, an explosion occurred at the store of a . colour manufacturer at Castletown, near Rochdale. A cask containing chlorate of potash, striking a wall in course of removal, exploded with terrible force, and the entire build- ing was blown to the ground. William Riley, proprietor, and his sen, were fearfully burned. A boy aged three was killed on the spot. A meeting was held on Monday:'at Chester in aid of the proposed Royal College of Music. There was an influential attendance, though not large in numbers. It was at the out- set suggested by the chairman, Captain Egerton Leigh, that a postponement should take place till the period of the Yeomanry's exercises, when it was likely the Prince of Wales himself would be in Chester. This was agreed to, but an interesting, address was delivered by Mr. Henry At a meeting at Plymouth, on Monday, the proposal to re-erect-Smeaton's Eddystone Lighthouse on Hoe underwent further discussion. A letter was read from Earl Mount Edgcumbe, who gave his adhesion to the original proposal, being chiefly actuated by the wish that the Lighthouse should not be destroyed. There was a strong expression of opinion' however, that the building be re-erected somewhere esle within the limits of the port, where it would serve a ,useful purpose, and a resolution to that effect was adopted. ATTEMPTED MURDER AT LEAMINGTON.—A desperate attempt to murder Rose Hortin, lady's maid to Mrs. Mont- gomery, Lillington Manor, near Leamington, was made' on Wednesday night by Herbert Allen, a discarded sweetheart, who gives an address in Upper Winchester-street, London. About six he called at the manor, asking to see Hortin' and was shown into a sitting-room. Directly !Loftin entered he seized her by her throat, and presented a revolver at her breast. She dashed the weapon upwards as it exploded, and the shot lodged in the ceiling. Five other chambers of the revolver were loaded. THE LIEUTENANT AND THE SOLICITOR'S WIFE —On Wednesday Frank Turner, lieutenant King's Own Borderers, at present stationed with the depot of the regiment at Ber- wick, was brought up charged, on remand, with feloniously stealing or taking away property to the value of -505., belong- ing to Mr. Weddell, solicitor, Berwick. The case arose out of the elopement of the prosecutor's wife with the prisoner, who is a son of General Turner, of the Indian army. Only, a few weeks ago he was presented with a medal for dis- tinguished service in Afghanistan. Evidence as to the elopement and the intimrcy between the parties having been given, the prisoner was committed for trial, which will take place at Newcastle. EXCITING 'SCENE AT A FIRE.—A terrible-scene was wit- nessed at Stockport, on Saturday morning. Shortly after two o'clock a fire broke out in a small house occupied by John Loftus, in a thickly-populated quarter of the town. Nine persons were crowded in the two sleeping rooms, the fire breaking out downstairs. When an alarm was given the flames had obtained a hold upon the staircase, and escape by that means was impossible. A young woman named Loftus threw her baby, four months old, out of the window, and it was caught by some one underneath. The woman then jumped out, but, falling on the pavement, broke her leg. Six of the other persons were rescued from the windows, but the firemen were not able to get into the -house until the flames were extinguished; then a .child four years old, named Mary Ellen Loftus, was found to be dead in bed. TAXATION AND REPRESENTATION.—A parliamentary re- turn has been issued showing the proportions of revenue derived from England, Scotland, and Ireland respectively, for the year ending 31st March, 1880, and the number of members of Parliament which each county would obtain if 658 members were alotted according to the population of each. The total revenue is returned at £66,577,304, of which England contributes £53,223,037, Scotland £7,318,014, and Ireland £6,036,253. The population of the United King- dom stands at 34,930,035, England.having 26,055,406, Scot- land 3,744,679, and Ireland 5,129,950. The members would thus be allotted :—England, 491; Scotland, 70; Ireland, 97. The present division is—England, 493; Scotland, 60; and Ireland, 105. DISAPPOINTED LOVE—At the Durham County Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a prepossessing young woman named Mary Ann Finlay was charged with vagrenclr. The father of the defendant is the hind on the farm at .Ushaw College, and it appeared that some time ago the young woman, who is 22 years of age, was engaged to be married. Her intended husband, however, thought they could make a batter start in life in the New World than at home, and he accordingly took his departure for America, and promised to send for the girl when he got settled. Notting, however, had been heard from him since, and the girl, after drooping daily, took to wandering about the fields and roads, and preferred lying in a hedge-side to her own bed.—The Bench ordered the woman to be imprisoned for 16 days, in order to allow the prison surgeon an opportunity of ascertaining her sanity. 'Newcastle Chronicle. MR. GLADSTONE'S PROTECTION.—A well-attended meet- ing of .IVlintshire ratepayers was held at Bagillt, on Saturday evening, to protest against the action of the Flintshire magistrates in resolving at the last Court of Quarter Ses- sions to demand from the Home Secretary the cost which the-county incurred in specially protecting the Premier when at Hawarden. It was unanimously re,solved, " That this meeting of Flintshire ratepayers disowns and repudiates the resolutions passed at the recent quarter sessions, in which it was affirmed that the cost of providing police protection to the Premier when in the county ought to be paid by the Treasury; and it desires the Chief Constable to take proper precautions to assure the safety of Mr. Gladstone, and that the cost be charged to the rates." It was decided to forward the resolution to the Home Secretary. A resolution was also passed expressing the pride they felt at having the Premier residing amongst them. AN IMPORTANT POINT or LEGITimAcy.—A Crown inquest was held on Tuesday at the Queen's Hotel, Cheltenham, re- specting the illegitimacy of George Perton, formerly a jeweller of Livery-street, Birmingliait and who died at his residence, at Prestbury, in November last, possessed of about £170,000. The Commissioners appointed to hold the in- quest, with the assistance of a jury, were Mr. Dowdeswell, Q,.C., Mr. Cleave, and Mr. Trevor Crisp (solicitor to the Treasury). It appeared that the deceased gentleman was born in Birmingham in 1801, his mother being a Mrs. Clap- perton, whose husband had deserted her. As given in evi- dence, Mr. Pemberton, jeweller, of Livery-street, was taken into the business, became a partner, and afterwards acquired the whole concern. Mr. Pemberton was a bachelor at the time, but afterwards married. He always admitted that Mr. Perton was his illegitimate son, and Perton throughout his life spoke of him as his father. Mr. Perton made several wills, which he destroyed, but in the last be omitted (his solicitor zaid purposely) to name ay residuary legatee. Consequently the bulk of his property would revert to the Crown in the event of. his being found illegitimate. The jury found that he was illegitimate. Therefore the property would go to the Crown. The man Spence was convicted in 1822 of a nnuggling offence, and at the time the peculiar circumstances of the case excited great interest in the neighbourhood. He had been educated as I. gentleman, but somehow got connected with a gang of smugglers.
