It is believes the net proceeds of the recent b,izaar at George's Hill, Liverpool, in aid of the Lancashire Indepen- dent College, will exceed £3,000. At Macclesfield, on Saturday, (John Hill, clogger, of Wel- lingborough, was comthitted for trial at the assizes on the charge of being itn accessory to a burglary committed in
1880: An anonymous letter has been received by the colonel of the 2nd Life Guards, at the Cavalry Barracks, Windsor, threatening to blow up the barracks. Every precaution has
been taken-. A communication has been received by the Mayor of Leicester informing him that the Prince and Princess of Wales will visit that to an on Whit-Monday, and open the

new public park. It is stated that Lord Derby is to be offered the vacant Garter, and that if he declines it will go to, Lsrd Kimberley. The Secretary of State for the Colonies is the only one of the Cabinet Ministers sitting on the front bench in the House

of Lords who is without a decoration. A Central News telegram, dated St. Petersburg,Thursday, states that an imperial order of the day has been promul- gated, declaring the delivery of officers' speeches in public contrary to the spirit of discipline. How many a man has been ruined ley sudden wealth! John Mitchell, butler, "known for some years as a sober steady man," came into a legacy of £3,000. Then he took to drinking, and dropped down dead the other day at the bar of a public-house in London, as the doctor said, from chronic alcoholism. Sir Henry Parkes, K.C.8., the Premier of New South Wales, has been on a visit to Stoneleigh Abbey, Warwick- shire; and as he was born in the village, attended the vil- lage school, and rose to distinction by force of industry and intellect, his arrival at Stoneleigh on Saturday was signalised by a hearty popular demonstration of welcome. , The Home Secretary has directed inquiries to be made in France with the view of clearing up the mystery attending the death of Mr. J. W. Willoughby, whose body was found en the railway between Boulogne and Calais. The case has been placed in the hands of a metropolitan detective inspector, who leaves London on Wednesday for Calais. At a religious service held on Sunday evening in the Charlton-street Mission Hall, Somers Town, an alarm of fire was raised and a panic ensued. The whole of the congrega- tion endeavoured to flee from the building. After the alarm had subsided it was found that two women and a child were severely injured. They were conveyed to theichomes, and the service was ultimately resumed. An Oldham correspondent, writing about the extraordinary and hurried interment of a lady who was said to have com- mitted suicide, without any report of the fact being made to the police, is not likely to result in a prosecution, as the cer- tificate contained the secondary cause of the death, though the primary was not mentioned or suggested. Much consternation has been caused at a village near Coventry by the elopement of a young lady, a governess at a school, with a young college student who was home for a holiday. The pair left by train for the purpose, ostensibly, of visiting a relative, but a letter subsequently received from the lady states that they had sailed for America. The man who on a recent occasion invaded a dinner party of the Premier's at Hawarden, and since then smashed a jeweller's window and stole a ring in Birmingham and was found in possession of a series of extraordinary letters to eeainent public men, has been sent to prison for four months at Birmingham, the prison surgeon not having found in him any trace of insanity. It is officially announced that enrolled members of the volunteer force who may be injured on duty and rendered thereby incapable of resuming their occupations will in future be allowed a gratuity not exceeding 3s. 6d. per day, and for a period not longer than six months. The allow- ance will not be given while the patient may be in a mili- tary hospital. A few days ago a paragraph went the round of the papers to the effect that a portion of Sir Wilfrid Lavvson's estates had been re-let to a tenant upon a ten years' lease at an increased rental of £BO per annum ; and that on Sir Wilfrid learning of the improvements upon the farm that had been made by the tenant he forwarded him a cheque for MO. Sir Wilfrid has been questioned upon the subject by a Bolton gentleman, and he has replied that the story is an entire invention of the newspaper writers. On Sunday morning, at an early hour, the Temple Opera House at Bolton was totally destroyed by fire. The loss is estimated at about £15,000, and the owner of the building is but partially insured. It is supposed that the fire originated through one of the audience having thrown a lighted match through a crevice in the floor, and that this set fire to a 'quantity of waste which had accumulated during the time the place was worked as a cotton mill. On Monday afternoon Cecillie Maclaren, five years of age, went along with some companions to gather flowers near Dysart, Fifeshire. Cdtning to a coal-pit, where a stream of hot water flows down a precipitous cliff from the pit to the sea, the little girl Mclaren stooped to warm her hands, it is supposed. She lost her balance, and was carried down in the hot water to the foot of the cliff, where she lay till scalded to death. Her body was subsequently recovered and taken home. The bronze birthday memorial statue of Mr. Gladstone offered by Mr: Theodore Bryant to the inhabitants of East London is now finished, and will shortly be unveiled by Earl Granville. The sculptor' Mr. Bruce Joy, has been favoured with repeated sittings by Mr. Gladstone, and the result is said to be an excellent likeness of the right hon. gentleman. The statue is nine feet high, and it will be placed on a granite pedestal, the height of which is about twelve feet. A miniature copy .evill •be exhibited at the Royal Academy. The Rev. George Sanger, vicar of Carlton-in-Cleveland, who was apprehended in London last year on a charge of having set fire to his own church, and who was discharged by the"magistrates, has since been charged with certain offences against the ecclesiastical law' and brought before the Archbishop of York for judgment. Mr. Sanger having, in accordance with the Church Discipline Act, consented that sentence should be passed without further proceedings being taken, the Archbishop has suspended him ab officio et bene,ficio for a term of five years. ' THE Porsoareri BUNS.—An Inverness correspondent learns that Dr. Duncan Mackay, medical officerof health for Inver- ness, has examined the contents of the hot cross buns which occasioned so much sickness on Good Friday. Dr. Mackay is not the analyst officially employed, but he found in the buns a salt which exhibits all the appearance of arsenic. Dr. Mackay is satisfied that the poisonous substance is arsenic, as, on comparing the crystals of real arsenic by the aid of a powerful microscope, they were exactly the same. Dr. Mackay leaves it to a chemical expert to give a conclu- sive opinion. CAUTION.—So great has become the popularity of and demand for American " Hop Bitters," because of their won- derful cures and their universal use as a family medicine, some unscrupulous parties are putting up imitations, and others offering for sale formulas and packets of stuff pur- porting to make the Bitters, and using the exact words and form of our advertisements, expecting to make honest, un- suspecting people buy them in place of Hop Bitters. Avoid all such spurious stuff, no matter what its name or pretence be and buy nothing but Genuine American Hop Bitters, which are put up in very INrge square, panelled, amber- coloured bottles, with Dr. Soule's name blown in the glass, with white label on one side, printed in black letters, and green hop cluster; and on the other side yellow label with directions in red letters, in English and German. This is the only form in which Genuine American Hop Bitters arc put up or sold. Hop Bitters Co., London, England ; Rochester, U.S.; TorontoaCanada, and Antwerp, Belgium. —Advt. SEQUEL TO A SCOTCH ROBBERY.—CLEVER CAPTURE AT EGREMOZ4T. Information was received on Tuesday by Chief Superintendent Egerton,of the Cheshire Constabulary, that a man and two women who were "wanted" for an ex- tensive robbery at Stranraer, its plunder being large, were on their way to Cheshire via Liverpool. The city police were communicated with, but the information was received too late to be of service, as it was found at Lime-street Station that the train in which the persons had travelled had reached that terminus some time before. A watch was, however, kept at the Seacombe and Egremont ferries by the Cheshire con- stabulary, and three persons of the description given being seen to enter a house in Egremont, they were apprehended by an officer, and taken to the bridewell in Liscard, where Inspector Roche found about £l2O in their possession, the produce, it is believed, of the robbery in question. Chief Superintendent Egerton at once comalunicated with the police in Stranraer. LIBEL ON A BRITISH MINISTER—A remarkable story of ingratitude is told in some papers just issued from the Foreign Office. Several years ago a German subject named Adolf von Conring presented himself to Sir J. Drummond Hay with a letter of introduction from Mr. Weber, the German Minister at Tangier, who was then absent, and asked to be introduced to the Moorish Minister for Foreign Affairs, saying that he was the agent of Messrs. Krupp, and that the object he had in view was to promote commercial relations between Germany and Morocco. It was not usual with Sir John to present people in Von Conring's position ; but, in consideration of the fact that he had temporarily undertaken the charge of German interests, and of the letter that person brought, he complied with the request, and Von Conring was subsequently invited to the Moorish Court. Since then Von Conring has Pufilished a book, entitled, "Morocco, the country and its inhabitants," in which he accuses Sir John of having received £14,000, when, under the guarantee of the British Government, the loan was made to the Moorish Government, to aid the latter in liqui- dating its debt to Spain, and of other corrupt practices, in- cluding the acceptance of a handsome commission on the value of a number of Armstrong guns purchased by the Moorish Government. The work did not come under Sir John's notice till November last, when lie saw it in the form of a Spanish translation. He at once wrote to consult Earl Granville as to whether it was not his duty on public grounds, as well as for private satisfaction, to prosecute the publishers of the book, both in Germany and Spain, for defamation of character. Earl Granville, having carefully considered the matter, Came to the conclusion that a legal prosecution was not desirable, but, concurring in Sir John's wish to repudiate the slanders in a public manner, instructed Her Majesty's representatives at Berlin and Madrid to bring them to the notice of the German and Spanish Governments, undertook to lay the correspondence on the subject before Parliament, and communicated to the Governments of those countries which have relations with Morocco, In notifying to Sir John his intention of taking this course, his Lordship added with regard to the slanders : "It seems scarcsly necessary for me to say that no one who is acquainted with your high character, or with the position you occupy in the country where you have so long and usefully served the Queen, could attach the slightest importance to them." Acknowledging the lettei, his Excellency has expressea I satisfaction wit, and gratitude for the action received upon. '

The King and Queen of the Netherlands have accepted the invitation given them by the Corporation of Londoji to a tuncheon at the Guildhall on Tuesday week. The Prince of Wales will pay a visit to Lord Carrington at Wycombe Abbey next month, and will inspect the Bucks Militia regiment, of which Lord Carrington is colonel. The Queen has, on the recommendation of Mr. Gladstone, been pleased to approve the appointment of the Rev. G. C. Ommanney, of Totterdown, Bristol, to the living of St. Matthew's, Sheffield. The masters of two of the New Brighton ferry steamers were heavily fined on Tuesday for carrying a larger number of passengers than was allowed by the certificates of the Board of Trade. Thirty bodies have been recovered from the Tudhoe Colliery. The explorers were unable to penetrate No. 6 way through the heavy falls. The injured by the disaster are progressing favourably. At the Cutnberland Assizes, Carlisle, on Wednesday, the grand jury brought in no bill against Maynard James Harrison, who was charged with the wilful murder of Lucy Sands' at Workington, on the Ist December last. On Tuesday a runaway engine on the line from Maryport to Cockermouth ran into a train at the latter station, but in consequence of a telegram from an intermediate station the passengers had all alighted a moment before, and thus averted a serious catastrophe. Mr. Ray Lankester, who was a short time ago appointed by the Crown to the Chair of Natural History at Edin- burgh University, in place of the late Sir Wyville Thomson, has resigned. Mr. Chamberlain has given a denial—which was scarcely needed—to Mr. Marriott's assertion that he had put the machinery of the National Liberal Federation ia motion in order to procure an expression of opinion hostile to the famous amendment on the Closure resolution. At the Stockport Police Court, on Wednesday, the Mayor presented to Annie Loftus. 17 years of age, £lO on behalf of the magistrates, and £5 sent by Baron Albert Grant, in ac- kuowledgment of her bravery in rescuing her sister, seven years of age, from the fire which destroyed a dwelling-house occupied by her parents on Saturday. During the Queen's visit to Mentone a cantata in her honour was written by the chef of the municipal band, and was played on two occasions in her presence. Before leaving Mentone the Queen presented the composer with a handsome diamond breast pin as a souvenir of her visit. The Arethusa and Scotland are to be finished at Chatham Dockyard, where preparations are being made for their re- ception. Both vessels are 3,000 tons, but are provided with engines of 5,000 horse power, as they are intended for fast ocean cruisers in time of war. The tailors of Bolton have sent circulars to the employers asking that the system of sending out work should be dis- continued; that the working hours should be in summer from six to eight, and in winter from seven to eight; that on Saturdays work should cease at four, and that 6id. per hour should be paid for overtime. Thd operatives complain that the work sent to the Jews in Manchester tends to propa- gate disease. On Thursday night, when a passenger train reached the bottom of the steep junction where the Rochdale branch joins the main line, near Bacup Station, the engine and some of the carriages left the metals. No one was injured, but the accident caused great alarm, and the line was blocked, the Rochdale trains being unable to enter the station. Assistance was obtained from Bury, and the line is now clear. At Glossop on Thursday morning, James Downs, a weaver, was sentenced to one month's harhabour, for assaulting his wife. Prior to going to work on the morning of the 18th, he struck her repeatedly, and upon his return struck and kicked her violently. The prisoner had been convicted fourteen times previously, on five occasions for assaulting various individuals, twice for assaulting the police, and once

for using threats to them. An unparalleled event occurred at the Paris Morgue this week. A workman waa, engaged painting the ceiling bf the enclosure when he fell from the ladder on the paving, strik- ing the back of his head with great force. In a few moments he expired. As none of his comrades could give his address, his body was temporarily placed upon one of the flags for the reception of the corpses. Mr. Hibbert, M.P., in reply to a conciliatory resolution from the Oldham Land League, says that should they see a cessation of crime and outrages in Ireland, which of late have eo disgraced the country, they would soon pass from a policy of repression to one of trust and confidence, and give a inner and fairer opportunity of dealing with the difficult Irish problems. He appreciated the conciliatory language of the resolution. At Bolton, on Thursday, James Prescott, a collier, of Aspull, was charged with a breach of the special rules under the Mines Regulation Act. The defendant worked at the Wood Shaw Pit, Aspull, and on the 13th inst. he was refused permission to leave the pit, bat shortly afterwards as the cage was about to ascend he jumped into it. It was stated that had he taken the leap a second later he would have been cut ire halves. He was fined 30s. A shocking occurrence resulting in the death of a youth named Matthew Reynolds took place at the well-known iron works of Messrs. Baldwin and Co., Swindon, on Thursday morning. Alfred Hammond, a workman, was lighting his pipe with the end of a red-hot piece of iron, and the lad Reynolds annoyed him by throwing stones. The man asked him to desist, but the lad continued to throw, and Ham- mond, in his passion, burled at him the bar of iron. The heated end entered the lad's groin, and he bled to death in 15 minutes. At the Mansion House, on Tuesday, Mr. Gasquet made an application to the Lord Mayor in the Marquis of Huntley's case. He said that some observations his lordship had made at the last hearing had induced the Standard Bank to consider the matter, and they had come to the conclusion that under the circumstances it was advisable to withdraw from the charge, The Lord Mayor said he entirely con- curred in the course proposed, as he considered the criminal charge could not be sustained. Mr.. Bowen, a solicitor, made a similar application with regard to a second charge, and both the summonses were then formally dismissed. . A correspondent at Portree sends an account of the open- ing of the "land war" in Skye. The large force of police which had been sent to the island succeeded, on Wednesday, in arresting five of the "ringleaders" among the crofters, who are charged with violent attacks on the officers of the law. A considerable crowd assembled, and the police were attacked. In the result the prisoners were loked in Portree Gaol, after severe skirmishing between the Tolice and the infuriated crowd. The latest news states that the police, apprehending an attack and rescue of the prisoners, barri- caded themselves during the night in Portree Drill Hall. It is doubtful whether a delicate woman injured in Wednes- day's melee will recover. A woman, aged 70, mother of one of the prisoners, is also severely injured. THE HATTON GARDEN ROBBERY.—A. Berlin telegram reteived through Reuter's agency states that Edward Smith and two accomplices were arrested on Tuesday at the Eastern railway station there on the charge of being con- nected with the robbery from the Hatton Garden Post Office. The prisoners, who were on the point of starting for St. Petersburg, offered a violent resistance to their cap- tors. Upwards of £3,000 worth of gold watches, diamonds, and other articles of value were found on them, and the the greater part of their luggage, which had already been forwarded, has been stopped by telegraph. Mr. Francis Macdonough, Q.C., the most eminent mem- ber of the Irish bar since the death of Mr. Butt, died on Tuesday morning at an advanced age, at his residence in Rutland-square. He defended Daniel O'Connell in the State trial of 1844, and Mr. Parnell in the State trial of 1881. He was learned, astute, and of polished manners. His eloquence was not of the first order, but his manner was fascinating and his skill as a nisi prizes lawyer and in criminal cases was unsurpassed at the bar. He had long earned the sobriquet of "Silver tongue." Mr. Macdon- ough represented Sligo in Parliament as a Conservative, but at the general election in 1868 failed to retain the seat, and never sought the suffrages of a constituency after- wards. "Matters," a Scotch correspondent tays, " are assuming a serious aspect in Skye, owing to the continued determina- tion of the tenants of Lord Macdonald to pay no rent." The Inverness Courier says that since the Irish revolt against payment of rent a spirit of discontent has been in- dustriously fomented among the poorest, the most illiterate, and the most dependent of the cotters of the West Coast of Scotland. They have been led to understand that they have only to strike against rent and they will obtain terms pre- ferable to those under which they occupy their crofts. It is further reported that 50 policemen have been drafted from Glasgow to the island to assist the authorities there in preserving order, endangered by the defiant attitude of the cottier tenants. It has been found absolutely necessary to have at hand the means of preventing an outbreak. Reliable information is to hand concerning rioting which took place at the Westminster Colliery' near Wrex- ham, on Wednesday night. It appears that when the police reached the colliery they at once made for the offices, where the manager and' a fireman were taking refuge. On reach- ing the office the stone throwing was renewed by the colliers with greater determination than ever, and large stones were rolled down the hillside on the top of the roof. In a few minutes the building was a complete wreck, and the stones beat the men so badly that it was deemed necessary to change their quarters. A rush was made before their assail- ants recovered themselves' the police were rapidly making the best of their way to Wrexham, but two of the officers sustaised very serious injuries. On the receipt of the disas- trous result of the policemen's visit, the military were at once called out. A strong force of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers' accom- panied by a strong detachment of the 3rd battalion of the local militia, who fortunately are up for their annual training, at once proceeded to the.spot, and outposts were placed all along the road from Wrexham to the Moss. The greatest excitement prevailed, as this is the most serious riot that has occurred within the memory of any in the district. A sad accident occurred during the rioting, by means of which a child, while held in its mother's arms, was killed. Great damage has been done to the different collieries by the rioters. The regulars have had a lot of rough work to do during the night. Great anxiety is felt about the Wrexhim and Acton collieries, where it is feared a riot may take place at any moment. Every precaution is being taken.—A later telegram says :—On the arrival of the military at Moss, the scene of the riots, it was found that most of the rioters had dispersed, but evidence of the desperate nature of the attack upon the Westminster Collliery Offices were abun- dant. Window frames and doors of oak were found literally smashed to matchwood, and the roof nearly demolished. The telegraph instruments, and the gas meter and piping were also shattered. The fumes of the escaping gas were overpowering. The rioters having threatened to blow up or fire the house of Mr. Harrop, the manager, a detachment of Royel Welsh Fusiliers was put in charge, and still remain there. A smaller detachment was also ordered to protect , the house of the manager's brother.

CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. MR. •G. •W. LATHAM ON AGRICULTURAL QUESTIONS. The Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture met on Saturday in the Chester Town Hall, under the presidency of the Duke of Westminster, for the discussion of a paper by Mr. Rigby, the secretary, on the necessity for further legislation in regard to agricultural lands and the direction in which it should operate. Mr. RIGBY expressed in a moderate and conciliatory man- ner the views of the tenant farmers, detailing the various objections to present agricultural restrictions and undesir- able regulations as between landlord and tenant. He con- demned the present application of the law of distress, and also the regulations as to cropping, and advocated the payment in full of compensation for unexhausted improve- ments and an extension of the time for giving notice to 12 months. A long discussiqn ensued, In the course of which Mr. G. W. LATHAM said no one now-a-days ventured to deny that a tenant, whether leaving his farm voluntarily or involuntarily, by giving notice or receiving notice, was entitled to receive compensation for what he had spent on the land, and that no tenant should have his rent raised on money which he had himself spent on the farm he occupied. But though they all agreed, when they spoke of those two doctrines, he was sorry to say that in the first place they found that there were exceptional cases in which those doctrines were not followed; and next there was consider- able difference of opinion as to the way in which those doctrines should be put into law. A noble relative of the chairman, the Duke of Argyll, said the tenant was entitled to receive everything which he had spent on the farm out of his pocket, that was to say, the money value of the im- provements he left, but he denied that the tenant had any right to be paid for his brain work. The Duke of Argyll said, in effect, that a man who by an expenditure of £5OO had effected an improvement the capital value of which would amount to £l,OOO, ought only to be paid for the £5OO, and not for the £l,OOO, whereas the argument on the other side was that he ,should be given credit for his intel- lect and skill, and be paid the whole sum. That, he thought, was really and truly the whole difference between the pro- posed Acts of Parliament on the matter; was the tenant entitled to the money actually spent or to the absolute value of the improvement which, whether by money or brains, he had effected? His idea was that the tenant was entitled to the.whole of the value of.the improvement; and he thought it was infinitely fairer to the landlord that that should be the law, because if the tenant was to be entitled only to the absolute money outlay he would be entitled to recover not only money judiciously but money injudiciously spent, and spent so as not to benefit the land or the landlord. It would be fairest to both landlord and tenant that the latter should receive the saleable value of his improvements. Then came the question of how the value was to be ascertained. How. was the tenant's improvements to be separated from the landlord's interest. He had the honour to be a vice-president of the Farmers' Alliance, the gentlemen connected with which ventared to draft a bill attempting to carry their theory into practice. The bill was sent out to the world in order principally that it might receive the comments and criticism of all practical men; and in consequence of the criticism to which it•had been subjected it had been agreed to alter it. A draft copy of the new copy of the new bill was in his possession, but he had net brought it to the meet- ing because it was hardly public property at present. Speaking generally, however, the proposal of the Alliance was that if either landlord or tenant desired it there should be arbitrators appointed, two years' notice to quit having been given. One arbitrator should be appointed, except the parties could agree, by the court of quarter sessions, and the other by farmers renting at more than £5O, whom the sheriff should summon together. That latter provision was intended to apply simply until a County Government Bill was passed, after which time the governing power of the country would probably appoint the arbitrator. In case neither party should wish to arbitrate, then the tenant should have the power to get. into the open market, and if be could find a man to whom the landlord could offer no reasonable objection, sell him the value of the improve- ments on the farm. The result would be very much this, that in the case of all estates near the landlord's residence, where the landlord would like to choose his own occupiers, arbitration would come into force; but in the case'of properties belonging to colleges and ecclesiastical corporations, where no personal likes or dislikes came in, but it was greatly a question of certainty of rent, the principle of sale, which he confessed he believed to be the right one, would be followed out. Some years ago be carried in that room, he thought by a majority of one, a resolution to the effect that it was expedient that the provi- sions of the Agricultural Holdings Act should be compulsory. He believed that Mr. Chaplain and other gentlemen who at that time opposed the making of the section of the Act com- pulsory were now bringing into Parliament bills to carry out what they then objected to, so much had public opinion changed. He was happy to think that the side he was then on was now admitted to be right. They all agreed that compensation for unexhausted improvements was necessary ; the only thing about which they differed was as to how it could be best done. They knew that on all well-managed estates compensation had been given for years and years, and the only object of legislatioa on the subject was to bring bad landlords into exactly the same position as all good landlords had of their own accord occupied for years. (Ap- plause.) With respect to freedom of cultivation' he believed that the statement of Mr. Roberts that he had never been hampered by any clauses in his lease would be the statement of every tenant on a well-managed estate, but at the same time he was of opinion that the clauses against freedom of cultivation had a bad effect. Agents whom he had asked whether they ever put into force their clauses as to the sale of straw, had told him that they never did, until the last year of a tenants occupation; when he was leaving they looked sharply after him. That, he thought, might work great injustice in some cases. (Hear, hear.) He knew this, that if a man sold more off the farm than he ought to do, he, when he came to leave, turned out to be a man of straw, from whom nothing could be got back. He was afraid that that would always be the case in agricultural, as it was in all other trades. Landlords must sometimes make bad debts and suffer losses, and he believed that what landlords ought to do was to choose the best and most substantial tenants they could find, and trust them thoroughly. (Applause.) The noble PRESIDENT, in replying to a vote of thanks, ex- pressed his belief that the Government would deal with the question in a manner which would be satisfactory both to landlords and tenants. He cautioned the Chamber, how- ever, against expecting that legislation immediately, because the way was very much blocked by other important measures. It was, he added, a matter of congratulation that such ex- treme moderation of tone had pervaded the discussions of the Chamber on measures affecting landlords and tenants— a moderation" which was happily very different from the relations between those classes in another country." Another meeting of the Chamber will be held shortly to consider the subject further.

div.head: ALLEGED " NEXT-OF-KIN " SWINDLE.
div.p: ALLEGED " NEXT-OF-KIN " SWINDLE.

The Furneaux frauds which were recently brought to light are likely to be eclipsed, as regards an extent of credulity and deception, by certain revelations in connection with a sham "Next-of-kin " offilli*, called "The International Law Agency." This agency was avowedly established to discover heirs and next-of-kin, and for recovering vast sums of money at present in Chancery. A suite of offices were engaged in Burlington Chambers, Birmingham, a year ago, and branches were opened in London, Manchester, Glasgow, Sheffield, and St. Neots, with important agencies at New York and Melbourne. Advertisements set forth that heirs were wanted for £25,750,000 worth of property unclaimed, and "all possible claimants" were to address "J. S. Rogers, Esq , 8.A.," at one of the offices. The Birmingham offices, situated in the principal thoroughfare, were handsomely -furnished, and were occupied by a manager and clerk and a Solicitor, and were regularly visited by Mr. Rogers, for whom a private room was set apart, and by ' more than one other person represented to be connected with , the management of the branches. A solicitor, who was con- sulted by a duped client, on Saturday took such prompt measures that the reputation of the agency was destroyed at a stroke, and the stories of the other dapes are told. Women have sold furniture and even clothing to raise the fee demanded by the agency, which they believed would obtain for them in return fortunes varying from a few hundreds to £lO,OOO and more. A tailor's assistant was induced to believe that about £15,000 would be secured for him, and his master lent him £lO5, which was paid over to the agency to establish the claim. A member of the Bir- mingham Town Council is among the victims. The head office has been besieged with dupes from various parts of the country, and bailiffs have unsuccessfully attempted to seize the furniture, which does not seem to have been paid for. On the first inkling that the police had scented the agency the principal absconded. It seems the suspicions of the Glasgow police were aroused a fortnight ago, and they sent Rogers' photograph to Manchester and London, asking. if he was " wanted " there, but no action was taken then. On Monday morning, however, Detective-Inspector Cami- nada, of Manchester, and a policeman were informed by an hotel waiter named Barkley that he had been swindled, and they apprehended a Mr. Arthur McKenzie, said to be Rogers' clerk, and Mr. John Henry Shakespear, a solicitor, who, it is alleged, assisted in the agency, and who, on hearing of McKenzie's arrest, surrendered himself. These two prisoners were remanded in custody at Manchester, on Tuesday, after evidence had been given that persons had been defrauded of sums varying from 10s. to £2OO. The court was nearly filled with people who had been swindled. It is e:rpected that six or seven other arrests will be made. On Wednesday, at the Birmingham Police Court, Mr. Warren, barrister (instructed by Mr. Ratcliffe), who is con- ducting the investigation, applied for warrants for the ap- prehension of J. S. Rogers, the acknowledged principal in the agency, and his manager, Edward Beeton. The warrants i were immediately granted, and were placed n the hands of Detective-Inspector Black, who has already numerous ad- dresses at which the men are likely to be found. It is expected that an application for further warrants, or at least one, will be made in a day or two, one of the " managers " of a Scotch branch having often received money from clients at the Birmingham offices. The Birmingham detectives started off on Thursday afternoon in search of "J. S. Rogers, Esq., 8.A.," and E. Beeton, the "manager "of the liiriningham offices. Thou e 4 the warrants were virtually granted by the stipendiary 'en Wednesday, they were not issued till noon on Thursday, the requisite formalities not having been previously complied with. Mr. Ratcliffe, the solicitor, has now ascertained that the amounts paid to the agency by victims, as already dis- covered, exceeds £2,400. Twelve more persors were on

Thursday morning found to have been duped, notwithstand- ing the publicity given of the case. The letters which have arrived show that many victims in country districts are still ignorant of the frauds. On Thursday evening, Inspector Black apprehended Edward Beeton, at Moseley, near Bir- miugham. The prisoner, when charged, declined to make any statement. Large numbers of persons have been de- frauded in Stockport by Rogers and his confederates in the next-of-kin swindle. The victims are principally known as claimants to the Hallworth estate, a large quantity of pro- perty said to have been left intestate in Australia eighteen months ago. Rogers put himself in communication with the claimants, and meetings, attended by hundreds, were held from time to time, and levies of from 25. to ss. per head were made on each occasion for expenses. Large sums have been advanced to the agency by well-to-do claimants. The frauds are very extensive, and great indignation is ex- pressed by the victims. A Bolton family is amongst the victims.

div.head: ENGINEERING TRADES.
div.p: THE ENGINEERING TRADES.

From sources representing both the employers and the men the reports received continue satisfactory so far as the generally active condition of the engineering branches of trade is concerned. The last month's returns from the vari- ous Lancashire districts connected with the Amalgamated Society of Engineers report generally an improvement in trade, with..a continued reduction in the number of men out of employment, there being at the present time fewer mem- bers.on the beoks in receipt of out-of-work donation than has ban the case for the last seven years. Smiths and pat- tern makers especially are in demand throughout the district, and of the latter the Society at the present time have none on their books as out of work. From the employers' side re- ports also agree that works generally are still well engaged, and that the, men were perhaps never in a better position both as 'regards employment and wages. The number .of new inquiries coining in is, however, stated to be not quite so large as a short time back, and those which have been put upon the market during the last two months have not resulted in the amount of new work expected, but there is nothing in this at present to be taken seriously into consider- ation as affecting the actual condition of trade, the con- tinued lowness of prices being the only real ground upon which makers base any complaints. There is, how ever, one, point in connection with the present activity in the engineer- ing trades which ought to be noticed:and that is the large ex- tent to which it has received its stimulus from the extra- ordinary amount of iron shipbuilding going on througho nt the country, As an indication of the amount of work going on in this direction, it may be mentioned that whilst a nor- mal condition of the iron shipbuilding trade represents about half a million tons under construction in the various ship yards of the country, authoritative returns show that at the present time the amount of iron shipbuilding in hand is not less than a million and a half tons. The wages question is still agitating some districts. In the Liverpool district, where the return to the rate of wages ruling about three years ago, which was recently conceded in Manchester, has only been partial, the men are taking steps to enforce the return to the full extent of tbe 7 per cent reduction.

PERSECUTION OF •I HE JEWS IN • RUSSIA. The Vienna Weiner Allgenteine Zcitung publishes intel- ligence respecting the recent anti-Jewish disturbances in Russia received from Podwoloeyskas, the Russian fron- tier station. It states that on the 10th instant, at Balta, in Podolia, the Jewish inhabitants, some thousands strong, assembled to take measures for their own protection, but the local authorities caused them to be dispersed by the military, promising that they would be responsible for the maintenance of order. The troops, in carrying out their instructions, behaved with great brutality, striking the Jews with the butts of their muskets. The authorires took the part of the rioters, and the action of the soldiers, so far as the restoration of order was concerned, was a mere pre- tence, for they assisted in plundering the houses of the Jews, tic. On the 11th inst. at eight a.m. a body of about 600 peasants from the neighbourhood entered the town, and commenced to rob, murder, burn, and violate. Several hundred persons were ;njured, 40 seriously, some of whom have since died. Fully a thousand houses were completely destroyed, and the goods stclen from the Jews were burned. All the Israelites in the town are reduced to beg- gary and starvation. Bread is sent from Odessa and Kieff for the destitute. The damage to property is estimate' at 4,500,000 roubles. Similar riots are reported from Kodiom,. Krutz, Okno, aud Krybraza. The local authoti t at Balta did not inform the Governor of Podolia, M. Milardovitch, of the disturbances until the 12th inst., but as soon as the fact came to his knowledge, he started at once for the scene of the outrage, and soon re-established tranquility. Two hundred arrests 'e ere made by his orders.

div.head: AN EXTRAORDINARY LOAN SOCIETY SWINDLE AT SOUTHPORT.
div.p: AN EXTRAORDINARY LOAN SOCIETY SWINDLE AT SOUTHPORT.

At the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, on Thursday, an elderly man of respectable appearance, named John Doward Thackeray, was indicted for having, at Southport, obtained £3 by false pretences from Thomas Marshall. Mr. M'Con- nell and Mr. George Cooper prosecuted, and Mr. Segar de- fended. It was stated that the prisoner held himself out as the manager of the "Southport and Buxton Branch Bank," and in that capacity offered to advance money on "easy terms." hams his habit to take in a publication called Stubbs' Weckly Gazette, for the purpose of seeing who had given bills of sale or were otherwise in financial difficulties. In that t.pa- peared the name of Thomas Marshall, and the prisoner see- ing it sent him a circular, saying that the " bank " had branches in "all the counties of England ;" that many peo- ' ple were "ruined by fleecing sharks of the common herd of money-lenders ;" warned the prosecutor against them, and offered to lend him money on easy terms. Negotiations took place. The prisoner asked for £3 35. to be advanced for "costs and expenses," and ultimately agreed to advance the prosecutor £lOO. The £3 35. was sent by the prosecu- tor, but he never could obtain the loan of the £lOO. It was stated that the " bank " was in a private house at South- port, and that the " branch " at Buxton was in a room over a stable.—The prosecutor was cele I, and spoke to sending the £3 3s. and not obta:ning the £lOO loan which the prisoner had agreed to advance.—ln answer to Mr. Segar, the prosecutor said he was a Yorkshire- man.—When you went to Southport, what name .did yon give on going to the prisoner's house? West.—Why did you give that name? Because I thought the place seemed westerly. (Laughter.)!—Have you ever borrowed money as cheaply as the terms he offered ? I have borrowed it for nowt—(laughter)—and I have paid as much as £2O for £loo.—The defence was that there was no false pretence, and that the prisoner had acted as a moneylender, and bad actually advanced money to a number of persons.—The prisoner was found guilty. There were other charges against the prisoner, but they were not proceeded with.—The jury recommended the prisoner to mercy on account of his age and previous good character.—Lord Deiby, in passing sen- tence, said it seemed that the prisoner had pursued a system of plundering, and had practised at the expense of the poor. But for the recommendation to mercy by the jury,. ha should have sentenced the prisoner to a longer term of im- prisonment, As it was he would order him to be imprisoned for twelve months.

A Cabinet Council was held on Thursday aftzrnoon at the Premier's official resicleoce, Downing-street. All the Ministers were present except Sir William Harcourt, the Home Secret.try. The meeting concluded at four o'clock, having occupied two hours: The general belief in political circles is that the Ministers had under discussion the whole subject of the pacification of Ireland. Communications from the American Government respecting the release ef the suspects were also under consideration. THE ROYAL WEDDING.—There has b3en a marked im- provement in the health of the Duke of Albany since his return from l‘lentone. His Royal Highness' who is residing in the Queen's Tower, on the south side of Windsor Castle, drives out diily in the environs of the Palace. The Prince's knee is gradually strengthening; but as his plysicians have, it is understood, deemed it ,desirable that he should not at present try it too much. His Royal Highness is availing himself of some slight mechanical support upon entcring or quitting his carriage or moving about within the precincts of the Castle. The trousseau of Princess Helen is being supplied from Paris; but the costumes of her bridesmaids, 'which have, it is unerstood, been approved by the Queen and Princess Beatrice, are being made by the Court mil- , liners in London. The dresses are of white moire antique; • trimmed with whitosatin, the headdresses being composed of clusters of violets, primroses, and white heather Hoorn. Owing to the serious illness of 1 ord Ccnyngham ,Lady Jane Seymour Conyngham will be unable to act as bridesmaid on the occasion o 2 the forthcoming Royal wedding.

'ridiculous objection to what will without doubt prove a blessing of boundless extent to the 'rising population of Runcorn. There are a few of these grumblers who no doubt consider themselves as lights in the local firmament, but how their present brilliancy would have been increased if, in their youthful days, books had bun as cheap as they are to- day, and access to them as easy as it will be made when the Free Library gets in working order. I observe that the commissioners have agreed to put up the necessary shelves for the library in the present boardroom, so that progress— though of a very slow nature—is being Made. The Library Committee have, notwithstanding the remarks of Dr. Steele, appointed Dr. McDougall vice-chairman—a compliment which the gentleman in question has well earned by a good deal of honest work, and the fact that he has borne a vast amount of unfair insinuations quietly. But I fear that the calm in Di.. McDougall's case only precedes a storm, for it would require almvst a second Job to quietly submit to such a torrent of criticism and condemnation as he has lately suffered.

Your publication of Mr. Thomas Beasley's statement of I claim, in last Saturday's Examiner, has caused quite a fluttel. in what I may, perhaps, be permitted to call the commis- sioners' dovecote. The retaining of Mr. Russell seems to have convinced the most doubtful amongst the body that the tug of war is imminent, and preparations are therefore being made to meet it in the best manner possible. I hear that though the business brought before the Widnes Local Board at their first meeting, on Tuesday, proved to be of a very formal description, there were several divisions upon it. The general opinion appears to be that lively times are in store. The Board have paid a well-deserved compli- ment to Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., in electing him chairman, a position which his father filled with so much distinction in years past. lam of opinion that a batter selection could not have been made and a hone may now be entertained that the reins are in the hands of one who will not suffer the time of business men to be wasted by hours of discussion upon points which can be settled in a much briefer space. I hear that the members belonging to the Ratepayers' Associa- tion intend to move a reduction in the salary of Mr. Allen, clerk to the Board, but the rumour may prove to be unfounded.

At the adjourned meeting of Runcorn ratepayers the other evening, Mr. William Handley made a statement as to the financial position of the Burial Board, which must be highly satisfactory to the ratepayers.

On Thursday, a lawn tennis club was opened at Frodsham, and promises to be fairly successful. The United Kingdom Alliance appear to be determined to make the association well known in Runcorn by holding numerous meetings. These have, however, been poorly attended, and either the friends of the movement mdst ba very weak numerically in Runcorn, or they are resting on their oars. Which is it? FLACCUS.

We would direct the attention of our readers to the announcement which we make in another column. Next Saturday we propose to commemorate the royal marriage, during the week, by presenting to each purchaser of The Examiner beautifully lithographed portraits of Prince Leopold and Princess Helen of Waldeck Pyrmont. The portraits, we may mention, are in Messrs. M‘Clure and M‘Donald's best style, they are faithful and striking, and are in the form of two linked medallions, graced with sprays of orange-blossom. The medallion is further enriched with the crown and arms indicating the nationalities of the bride and bridegroom. The whole, when enclosed in a neat frame, will not only form an interesting sotsvenir of the event, but adorn any room.

RUNCORN AND THE CHURCH ASSOCIATION.—Some time recently, the Church Association offered a prize of twenty guineas for the best essay on the "Rule of Faith." We understand that the prize has been secured by the Rev. W. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, from amongst a large number of competitors. THE IRISH NATIONAL FORESTERS AT RUNCORN.— On Monday night, a concert and dramatic entertainment were given in the Public Hall, Runcorn by the Irish Foresters. The object of the performance was to raise funds in order to pay the expenses of the High Court Meeting, which it is expected will be held in the town during the ensuing summer. There was a good attendance. Two pieces were put on the boards by the St. Edward's Catholic Amateurs, called "Paddy the Piper," and "Paddy Miles:' The members of the Runcorn Orchestral Society were present, and added much to the pleasure of the evening's entertainment.

BEnvicz or SONG AT KINGSLEY.—On Tuesday even- ing the "Basket of Flowers" was rendered in the Primitive Methodist Chapel by the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, assisted by a few friends. The chapel was crowded to excess. The service was gone through in an excellent manner, all the solos, duets, and anthems being given with spirit and precision, showing a thorough famili- arity with the work. The service throughout appeared to give the greatest satisfaction. Mr. E. Billingsley, the com- piler, was the organist and conductor, and this gentleman on rising to respond to a vote of thanks passed to him and the choir, received quite an ovation which he acknowledged in a few well chosen remarks. The Rev. J. Pickwell was the reader.

THE REV. GEORGE HACK, OF RUNCORN, ON PROPEECY.—On Wednesday evening, the Rev.. Geo. Hack (Wesleyan Methodist) lectured under the auspices of the Brunswick Improvement Class, on Gratten Guiness' book, entitled "The end of the age." Mr. W. J. Shore presided. The lecture was a very interesting one to all students of prophecy. Mr. Hack said the popular notion was that the inhabitants of the world would continue to improve until the Millenium, when the advent of Christ would take place. He, however, was of a different opinion, and argued that instead of previous dispensations really improving the world to any very great extent, they had all ended disastrously. He pointed out signs that various parts of Biblical prophecy were now receiving their fulfilment. This he considered to be especially the case with regard to the Papacy, which was symbolised by Daniel's "little horn." Popery, he thought, was now tottering, and in the end, would be totally des- troyed. We were undoubtedly on the eve of great events. On the motion of Mr. Fred Norman, seconded by Mr. J. D. Jones, a vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer. WIDNES PRISONERS AT QUARTER SESSIONS.—At the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the Hundred of West Derby, this week, Ann Turton pleaded guilty to bay- ing obtained several pairs of boots and slippers from Ann Williams, at Widnes, by means of false pretences, and was sentenced to three months' imprisonment.—Daniel Colduck (25), labourer, and Wm. Henry Jones (17), labourer, were each sentenced to four months' imprisonment for having, at Widnes, on the 4th of February, stolen 43 zinc patterns, the property of Bartholomew' Hobson.—Mary Morley was sen- tenced to nine months' imprisonment for stealing 40 yards of plaid cloth, the property of William Miller, at Widnes; and Ann Dalton was acquitted on the charge of receiving the same.—The Grand Jury ignored the bill against Sarah Thornton for stealing Bs. from William Dobb, of Widnes, and the bill against Ephraim Hayes, charged with house- breaking at Huyton.—Patrick Fitzgerald and Ann Griffin were indicted for unlawfully wounding Michael Griffin, the husband of the latter, at Whines. The judge said he was determined to put down the brutal Lancashire custom of kicking. He sentenced Fitzgerald to five years' penal servi- tude and the woman to 18 months' imprisonment. Catherine Brunnor (35), for wounding And M'Cormick, at Widnes, on the 27th March, was sentenced to four months imprisonment with hard labour. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENT.—T concluding entertainment on behalf of the class-room fund was given on Tuesday evening. The vicar occupied the chair, and, in opening the proceedings, expressed a hope that the building of the new schools would be proceeded with forthwith. He also highly complimented Miss Purver on the service she had rendered the congregation, at the numerous entertainments which had taken place. The musical part of the programme opened with the glee, "See our oars," and the glee class during the evening also gave, amongst other pieces, "The pearl divers," and "The bells of St. Michael's." Mrs. Rushton rendered "I dreamt I dwelt in marble halls" in a splendid manner, and was heartily encored. Mr. J. Foster gave a reading; Mr. T. Davies sang "Never too late to mend; " and Mr. Large was applauded in "The Pilgrim of Love." Miss Lord favonred the audience with "The battle march of Delhi ; " and Miss Fairley sang "The miller and the main," and was encored. A like mark of approval was shown to Mrs. Rushton in the song, "The sad sea waves." Mr. Large sang "The bloom is on the rye" in charming style. During the evening Mr. Jonas Forster gave a reading from Douglas Jerrold, which pro- voked much laughter.

ST. BEDE'S, APPLETON : SCHOOL EXTENSION FUND —The last of the concerts of the season, on behalf of this fund, took place on Monday evening, the performance belt g given by the Farnworth Amateur Minstrels, who were received with much enthusiasm. The room was very wei filled. A great number of pieces were given during the ewe lug, and amongst them were several well worthy of com- mendatior. Mr. F. C. Davies was applauded in "Off to Brighten ;" and Mr. A. Whitfield received a similar compli- ment in " forget me, darling." Mr. A. G. Davies caused roars (,f laughter in "Michael Murphy," and was re- called. Mr. A. Whitfield gave "Just down the lane ;" and Mr. A. G. Davies "The yellow girl," in which he was en cored. "Cock Robin," sung by Mr. Dan Lea and joined i by the whole troupe, was beautifully given. In the seconn part, Mr. A. G. Davies delivered a stump speech, whic,h delighted the audience by many of its local hits. A farce entitled "Lawyer Graball and his troublesome servant ' followed. Mr. A. B.tlmer as Graball, and Mr. A. G. Davies as "Ginger," were very good. Mr. F. C. Davies appeared as T. Pop, Esquire, and was loudly cheered. Shortly before the conclusion of the proceedings, the Rev. Father Finegan thanked the troupe for their services.
132£611TIVE METHODInt AT Rocs Siva.—lt is pro- posed to erect a Primitive Methodist chapel at Rock Savage, where services have for some time been held in private houses.

RUNCORN CAMDRN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Oa Sunday the Rev. Henry Valentine, formerly of Runcorn, will preach twice in St. Paul's Wesleyan chapel, on behalf of the Cam- den Sunday school. There will probably be large congrega- tions. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, William Roberts, 6, Irwell-street, Widnes, dropped dead at six o'clock in the evening, whilst working for the Widnes Metal Co. Every assistance was rendered to deceased, but medical assistance was of no avail. Death is supposed to have resulted from heart disease.

FARNWORTH AMATEUR MINSTRELS.—On Saturday evening, these minstrels gave an entertainment in the Boys' Church schoolroom. Messrs. A. G. Davies, A. Whitfield, F. W. Wareing, F. S. Lea, F. C. Davies, W. Brown, W. Haddock. D. Lea, C. D. Hunter, and others took part; and the performers were very well received. IMPORTANT SALE AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday night, Messrs. George Turner and Sons offered for sale several very important lots, at the Runcorn Public Hall. The highest bid for Mr. Pankhnrst's shop, Victoria-road, Widnes, was £BOO, and the lot was withdrawn. £950 was offered for 12 dwelling-houses in Handley-street, Runcorn, at rentals amounting to £125 Os., but this lot was also withdrawn. The "Old Hall" property, occupied by Miss Turnbull, elicited a fair amount of spirited bidding; and the property was knocked down at £750. There N% ere no bidders for the policy on Mr. George Ashton's life, or for that of £B,OOO on the life of Mr. W. H. Linaker. The same may be said of nearly every other lot put up. CHILD DROWNED AT WIDNES.—On Thursday afternoon, a child named David Walsh, aged 2ye irs, son of Michael Walsh, chemical labourer, Market-street, was found drowned Ina pit of water which is situate upon waste land belonging to Messrs. Muspratt and Sons. About half-past three o'clock, the grandmother of the child was told what had happened by a woman named Mrs. Murphy, and they went to the spot, which is about 70 yards from the father's house, and pulled the child out of the water. Dr. Cooper was sent for, but pronounced life to be extinct. Two other persons are stated to have been drowned in the same pit, which on Thursday contained about twenty inches depth of water, and no doubt the matter will be fully inquired into at the inquest, which takes place to-day (Saturday).

MARRIAGE AT Rurrconx.—On the morning of the 18th inst., Miss Catherine Webster, eldest daughter of Mr. Thomas James, confectioner, and proprietor Of the Theatre Royal, was married, very quietly, at the Runcorn Parish Church, by the Rev. T. M. Armson, to Mr. Joseph Acton, fanner, of Sutton. Rumour has it that Mr. Yarwood, livery stable proprietor, received instructions to have a carriage and pair ready at Mr. James's door, at half-past ten the fol- lowing morning. He accordingly attended, and young Mr. Yarwood looked quite expectant, as he held the reins, be- lieving that there was a very pleasant duty before him in driving the happy couple to church. The pair came out of the house, and informed Mr. Yarwood that his destination would not be the church, as the pleasant ceremony was over, and his duty would simply be that of driving to a certain station outside of Runcorn, for the purpose of catch- ing the train for Buxton. Mr. Acton has previously been twice married, and he is evidently a lover of peace and quietness on the marriage day, and understands how to man- age these matters better than some people. May the pair be happy! THE PROPOSED NEW CHURCH AT WIDNES. —Writing in the Liverpool Parish Messenger the Vicar of Widnes, re- ferring to the proposed new church, says :—" We hope soon to have some definite announcement to make in this matter. The building season is now fairly upon us, and although the conveyance is not actually completed, it is only a question of a few more days. The forced and continued delays have, unhappily, to all appearance, operated against us in more ways than one, for several of the promises have, in the course of these severe years, become practically value- less, in consequence of death, insolvency, or removal from the neighbourhood; and the £3,000 calculated upon may suffer to a corresponding amount. Nevertheless, the com- mittee wish to start with the least possible delay, depending upon those among us who have hitherto held back, loyally and liberally to fulfil their obligations, whether of the past, the present, or the future. But the church will cost from £B,OOO to £lO,OOO, and they cannot but feel it a perilous matter, even in our peculiar circumstances, to commence the work with but £3,ooo—and that largely in promises."

RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.—The annual general meeting of the members of this club was held on Saturday evening at Wilson's Hotel. Mr. H. Johnson occupied the chair. The balance sheet showed a small deficit on the year, but it was stated that the outstanding subscriptions would amply meet it. Mr. W. Wright, the secretary read the report, which showed that during the year 16 matches had been played, out of which ll'had been won, one drawn, and four lost. The number of goals obtained by the club was 10. 16 tries, and 51 minor points. Nine tries were ob- tained by Mr. Andrews. The following officers were elected: —Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., president; Messrs. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., G. S. Hazlehurst, F. A. Lake, Lloyd Wiga, Chas. Reynolds, J.P.; Philip Speakman. H. Reynolds, J.P., E. A. Chorlton, W. Bate, J. Ashton, J. R. Frith, Lieutenant- Colonel Ashton; Captain Hazlehurst, J.P., and Lieutenant Jolliffe, vice-presidents. Mr. Hugh Hughes was appointed captain of the first team, and Mr. W. J. Larkin sub-captain of the second. Mr. J. Pownall was elected captain, and Mr. W. Riley sub-captain ; Mr. Charles Pownall secretary; and Mr. R. Hughes and Mr. H. Wright umpires. The following working committee was appointed :—Messrs. W. Wright, W. Mason, F. Joule, T. Roach, W. Brimilow, W. H. Broady, J. Sherlock, H. Andrews, J. Gatley, and T. Gleave. Votes of thanks were passed to the retiring officers, after which the proceedings terminated.

MARRIAGE AT FARNWORTII CHURCH. —Oa Thursday morning, Miss Emily Johnson, eldest daughter of Mr. Thos. Johnson, gentleman farmer, Of Bold Heath House, was mar- ried to Mr. Thomas Glover, manufacturing chemist, St. Helens, and son of the late Mr. Wm. Glover. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. George Bond, the vicar of the parish. The road from Bold to Farnworth was decorated with flags and bunting, and the church was packed with an eager crowd of sightseers, Miss Johnson being well and favourably known by all the congregation. The service was a full choral one. After the ceremony the marriage party adjourned to the residence of the bride's hither, which was richly ornamented with various stove and greenhouse plants, and a beautiful display of flowers. Amongst those present at the breakfast were the Rev. George Bend and the Misses Bond; Mr. W. Johnson, late of Halegate ; Mr. B. Glover; Mrs. and the Misses Glover, of Newton-le-Willows; Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Cliffs, of Whitley Hall, Cheshire; Mr., Mrs., and Miss Fairhurst; Mrs. Glover, of Southport; Mrs. W. Glover, Mr. Joseph Johnson; Mr. and Mrs. Lake; Mr. and Mrs. James Glover, of St. Helens; Mrs. Longton and Mr. H. J. Longton, of Winwick; Mr. Edward Glover, of Southport; Mrs. John Johnson, of Eccleston ; and Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Lowe, of Warrington. The dress of the bride was of brocade primrose satin, trimmed with lace, with tulle fall and wreath of orange blossom; and the bridesmaids- -the Misses Johnson—wore cream silk dress skirts, chintz silk bodices, and hats to match. Miss Cliffs and Miss Glover appeared in sapphire silk dresses and hats to match. The following is a list of the presents :—The parents of the bride, handsome pianoforte, in ebony and gold; from the mother of the bridegroom, timepiece, black, and ornamental, with two side ornaments to match, also handsome hall clock and ornaments; Mr. W. Johnson, late of Hale-gate, hand- some case of silver knives and forks; Mr. J. Johnson, Huy- ton, case of silver knives and forks with ivory handles; Mr. H. Johnson, Widnes, case of two sets of silver-mounted carvers; Mr. and Mrs. Lake, elaborately chiseled dish and cover; Mrs. Longton, Winwick, silver and china biscuit jar; Mr. and Mrs. Lowe, china and gold breakfast service; Miss Emily Johnson (sister of the bride), handsome four o'clock tea service; Miss Annie Johnson, black and beaded embroidered footstool ; Mr. W. Johnson (eldest brother cf the bride), case containing handsome brooch and bracelet; Mr. Johnson, Eccleston, silver dessert spoons and scissors; Mr. H. Johnson, Winwick, copper kettle; Miss M. Johnson, ' work basket; Mr. B. B. Glover, set of dessert service (hand- painted) ; Mrs. W. Glover, St. Helens, silver and cut glass flower stand and cut glass mirror flower glasses ; Mr. James Glover, St. Helens, set of skin hair mats ; Mr. Edward Glover, silver-nsounted cut glass claret jug; Miss Minnie .Glover, Newton, embroidered toilet service; Miss Blanche Glover, set of embroidered table napkin rings ; Masters Robert and Harry Glover, set of brackets ; Master James Glover, painted bracket; Mr. Hammill, silver and stained glass preserve dish; Mrs. W. Fairhurst, elaborate bronze figures; Mrs. Chadwick, handsome cut glass flower stand ; Mr. and Mrs. Armstrong, case of handsome knives and forks with ivory carved handles; • Mr. Mrs. and Miss Cliffs, antique china, silver cruet, and butter cooler; Mr. Walter Swinn, silver and glass biscuit jar ; Mr. Alfred Edgar Davies and Miss Barber, ornamental terracotta and silver breakfast cruet; Mr. Brown, neat four-stand glass and silver cruet ; Mr. W. Atherton, neatly painted china and eilver butter cooler ; Mr. Hill, dozen silver dessert spoons ; Miss Ciara Fairhurst. Warrington, toilet sat; Miss Hepherd, War- rington, china ornaments; Mr. and Mrs. Shaw, hand paint- ing neatly framed, the painting being the work of Miss Shaw; Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co.. bank note; An old vrvant, leather satchel bag ; the scholars at Bold Schools, two cast "Angels."

SOTRFE AT THE WARRINGTON WORKMEN'S CLER.—Fol- lowing the sale of work in aid of the above club, a soirée was held in the club-room on Monday evening, with the object of adding to the funds for the purchase of the build- ing. The soiree was fairly attended, anvil the disciples of Terpsichore found enjoyment for several hours in stepping to the strains of Mr. Stirrup's quadrille band. During the evening refreshments were obtained at a table in charge of Mrs. Ramie, Mrs. Venn, and Mrs. Leeson: Songs were given at intervals by Miss Wycherley, Miss Jones, Messrs. Dean, Be!Ilan, and Stout, to the accompaniment of Miss Morris and Mr. F. Booth. Mr. jHargreaves acted as M. 0., and the arrangements were carried out under the direction of Messrs. Eaude, Potter, Leeson, Proctor Jones and M. Joues.

TEE SUICIDE By HANGING.-At the *Unicorn Hotel, Winwick-street, Warrington. on Saturday, Mr. C. E. coroner, held an inquest on the body of Margaret Tickle, 60 years of age, wife of a flagger and slater, residing at 147, Winwick-street. The deceased committed suicide under circumstances stated in our last issue, and after hear- ing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of "temporary insanity."

The Directors of The International Marine Hydro- pathic Company, &afield House, Liverpool, have secured the services, as manager, of Mr. C. Nan. Mr:. Nan is well known to visitors at the establishment at Moffat, he having been -manager there since its opening, and brings with him much experience to discharge satisfactorily the duties of the more important sphere to which he is now appointed.

The Registrar of Friendly Societies has, on the petition of upwards of 500 members, ordered an inquiry into the affairs of the Scottish Legal Life Assurance Society, which has agencies in the chief towns of England and numbers alto- gether about 400,000 members. The petitioners allege against the officials of the society corrupt practices, mis- appropriation of funds, and the publication of misleading statements. The inquiry, which is to take place in Glas- gow next week, will be the first held under the new Friendly Societies Act.

LANCASHIRE BANKnurrs, &c.—(From Friday night's Ga,oette.) Liquidations by arrangement : T. H. Chatton, Farraworth, near Bolton. ironfounder ; J. Nuttall, Bury, joiner and builder; J. Cocker, Royton, Oldham, joiner and builder; and W. J. Baugh, Scotland-road, Liverpool, boot and shoe dealer. (From Tuesday night's Gizette). Bank- rupt :‘ E. Hornsby, Over Darwen, builder. Liquidations by arrangement: R. and P. Derbyshire, Meadow-street, Ancoats; also of Hendham Vale, Collyhurst, and of Wardle, near Rochdale, firebrick manufacturers and lime merchant; J. Geddes, Blackburn, travelling draper, and W. Barton, Wigan, provision dealer. A LYIII.II ASSAULT CASE.—At Altrincham, on Monday, John Riley was charged with assaulting Sarah Wood, at Lymm, on the 12th April.—Complainant is the wife of a carter living at Lyrom, and on the .day named, about three o'clock, the prisoner came to her house and asked the way to Altrincham. She directed him, and then he got hold of her hand and made use of bad language. She got him out- side, when he kicked her violently on the leg, and she fell down.—P.C. Maddock apprehended the prisoner, whe, he slid, behaved in a most violent manner.—The Chairman said the prisoner had behaved abominably, and he would have to pay 20s. and costs, or go to prison for one month.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.-At this court, Bank- street, on Tuesday, John Broderick was brought before Lient.-Colonel Greenall and Mr. Jas. Marson, charged with b-!ing drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of Wm. Beswick, Walton Superior, on the 17th inst. .He was fined 20s. including costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. The fine was paid.—Yesterday, at the same court, before Mr. James Marson, James Raftery, of Keckwick, was charged with assaulting Wm. Tickle, farmer, Keckwick. On account of his insubordinate conduct, the prisoner, who is a farm labourer, was discharged from the complainant's employ. When being paid the money due to him as wages, he kicked the complainant on the body and thigh. He was remanded to Daresbury Petty Sessions.

CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday evening, a concert of vocal and instrumental music was given in the Public Hall, Runcorn, by the members of the band of the training ship "Indefatigable." The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., and the building was crowded. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, alluded to the fact that the concert was given in aid of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen. He considered that the in- habitants of Runcorn ought to be thankful that such mis- sions had been established in the town. ~ They knew-that England owed its great prosperity and proud prestige to its commerce, and where would that be if it were not for her sailors and watermen. It was the seafaring population which brought the raw material for our spindles arid looms, land where would our people be were it not for the corn which was brought across the ocean to supply the wants which our own production was inadequate to - meet. 'Without commerce the rich man would have to do without his luxuries, and the poor man would he de- prived of many of his absolute necessities. These facts must come home to them with tenfold force in a place like Runcorn, which owed whatever little importance it pos- sessed to the seafaring population, and its pecular position on the banks of the Mersey, at that particular part where a vast canal was connected with the river Mersey, which led to the mighty Atlantic. Therefore, the Mersey missions had a special claim upon their support, and he recommended them to their thoughtful consideration. The musical pro- ceedings were opened by the band giving a selection from Sullivan's "Patience," which was followed by Rimbault's "Dame Durden," which was rendered by Messrs. Fredrick- Fon, Hibbert, Williams, and Wesson. A-lad named Anderton sang the comic song "His name was Joshua," and was re- ceived with loud applause. Fredrickson and Teare gave the duet " Land of sunshine," and Tears followed with 4 comic production called Mrs. Brown's luggage. Godfrey Marks song and chorus "Sailing" was sung by Dennis; and Ibbs and Bonastre danced the sailor's horn- pipe in splendid style. The second part of the concert opened with Auber's " Fra Diavalo," by the band, after which Fredrickson sang "Our Jack's come home to-day." A humorous trio succeeded, entitled "Peter Piper," by members of the hand. The gem of the evening was, how- ever, a recitation from Miss Howett, by a youth named Webster, which was received with enthusiastic applause A comic song called "The three little pigs," sung by Pennine.- ton, was remarkably well done. A laughing trio, by the ban 3, set all the audience in a roar; and the proceedings were brought to a conclusion by the playing of the Bohemian dance by the band. During the evening, the Rev. Mr. Patrick, chaplain to the mission, delivered a brief speech, in. which he highly complimented the Rev. Canon Barclay on having espoused the cause of the missions with so much warmth, as was shown by the fact that at all times he had manifested the greatest willingness to help in any move- ment which had for its object the helping of the committee. He proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the vicar, which was carried with acclamation. A similar compliment was paid to Captain Groom, of the Indefatigable training ship, and his creditable band of lads. We understand that the pro- ceeds of the concert will be about £3O. In concluding our notice, we must not forget to pay a high compliment to Mr. Shaw, the local missionary, who has had the chief responsi- bility in getting up the concert, the great success of which must cause him much gratification. CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT WARRINGTON.—The Bishop of Liverpool held a confirmation service at St. Paul's Church, yesterday afternoon, the church being crowded with candi- dates and their relatives and friends. In addressing the candidates, the Bishop impressed upon them the importance of the step they were about to take, and hoped they would not regard what was being done as a dumb-show. They were sow about to fulfil the vows which were made for them at their baptism, and it was a wise and right thing that they should at that time have been received into the church by infant baptism. It was right they should have their names put down in the list of church members, so that when they came to years of discretion they could put in their claims to the things promised for them at their: baptism. The promise was that they should renounce the earth, the flesh, and the devil; that they should believe in the articles of the Church; that they should keep God's Holy Word and Commandments; and that they should walk in the same all the days of their lives. They had been taught the leading articles of the Christian faith and of the Chris- tian religion. They were no more little children but were ' old enough to understand these things for themselves, and the church now called upon them to come forward and do their duty. He called upon them, as they would have to ' answer at the dreadful day, to live a Christian life, to hold the Christian faith, and to walk in Christian ways. The confirmation was then proceeded with, and amongst the can- didates were the following :—St. Paul's, 42 males, 56 females ; St. Barnabas, 13 males' 9 females; Cot ford, 7 males. 7 females; Grammar School, S males; Parish Church, 10 males 31 females; and Trinity, 23 males, 37 females. At the conclusion of the ceremony, the Bishop addressed a few parting words to those who had been confifmed. He prayed that that day of confirmation might be a day of blessing to them, and that the result of that confirmation might be seen in their conduct and behaviour as long as they lived. They had been confirmed but he wanted them to be more than that —he wanted them to be converted and saved. He hoped they would go home with serious thoughts and desire to live a Christian life from this time forth. He urged them to take a few words of advice from the Bishop in the shape of texts, which he impressed upon them the necessity of adhering to, and concluded by calling upon the friends who had assembled to see the confirmation to help the young people by speaking a kind word in season.

THE CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL, WARRINGTON: NEW INFIRMARY.—The following circular, signed by the Bishops of Chester, Manchester, and Liverpool, has been issued :—" At the annual meeting of the subscribers to the Warrington Institution, in A ugeist, 1880, a resolution was passed that an effort should be made to raise funds to build an infirmary, wholly detached from the present building of the Clergy Daughters' School. As it is a rule of sanitary legislation that every case of infectious disease should be isolated, the committee have felt it binding upon them to, according the best mode of providing a building planned accordin to modern knowledge and requirements. It may be added that the rooms now used in cases of sickness are inadequate, and are sorely needed for the better accommo- dation of the assistant governesses. The committee have had several plans for the infirmary under their considera- tion. After consultation with members of the medical profession and the architect, Mr. Littler, the committee have decided to build according to plans involving a cost of £1,209, exclusive of furniture, which it is estimated cannot be provided for less than £3OO. To this must be added the architect's fee. There is in band a sum of £9Ol 145., of which £367 75. id. may be credited to the present diocese of Chester, £529 Os. 11d, to the diocese of Manchester, and £5 to the diocese of Liverpool. Thus it will be seen that a further sum of about £650 is required. For this the com- mittee now confidently appeal to the three dioceses, that the contract may without delay be signed for a building which is necessary for the welfare of the institution. We earnestly commend this proposal to the hearty support of our respective dioceses —WILLIAM OmEsrErt. J. MANCHES- TER, J. C. LIVERPOOL."
