div.head: SERIOUS AFFRAY AT WIDNES.
div.p: SERIOUS AFFRAY AT WIDNES.

THE DYING DEPOSITIONS OF A MAN TAKEN. During the kast few years the local annals of Widnes have been marked by several murders, and by serious assaults in very large numbers. In some towns a man may get into a street row a a violent cbaracter, and escape with a few bruises, but if he thinks of escaping from such an adventure in Widnes without dire consoquences to life and limb, it is I highly probably he will find himself mistaken. Only this ' week a Mrs. Griffin, from this town, has been sentenced to la months' bard labour, and Patrick Fitzgerald to five years' penal servitude for unlawfully wounding Michael Griffin, the hnsband of the woman just named. Yesterday morning, a marine-store dealer named Kerley, was brought up at the I °cat police court for amusing himself by breaking the left leg of a rag-gatherer named Luke Kelly, who, whilst the former has been suffering a term of imprisonment, had been helping his wife to conduct the business. This is the re- ward of the poor fellow for trying to forward Kerley's interests. _ _ _ _

I About four o'clock yesterday afternoon, it became noised. abroad that a labourer named Wm. Myers, living in Edmund-- street, Widnes, was supposed to be in a dying state,. as the result of an attack made upon him during a street quarrel, by two brothers named John Fitzharris and William Pitztarris, who live in Victor ia-street. The matter had been kept a secret by the police, but on the poor fellow being visited during the afternoon by Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen., and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., the local inspector of police, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, the fact could no longer be concealed that the unfortunate man was in a very critical state indeed—so critical that it had been decided to take his "dying depositions." It is considered scarcely prudent to publish in full the statements made by Myers, but we may briefly summarize the facts as follow : On Saturday last, the injured man had a fight with Wm. Fitzharris., in the S'hip Inn beerhouse, Victoria-street, whilst they were playing at skittles, and during the struggle, his (Fitzharris's) brother came up, and apparently thinking that his relative was getting the worst of the combat, hit Myers a violent blow in the mouth. Wm. Fitzharris and Myers then fell, and, as the latter was getting up, Wm. Fitzharris gave him a violent kick in the right breast, and afterwards absconded. John Fitzharris was taken into custody, and the depositions of the supposed dying nun were taken in his presence. John Fitzharris was afterwards taken to the Widnes Police Office, and brought up before Mr. Gaskell, sen., and Mr. &ashen, jun.. charged with wounding Wm. Myers, of Edmund-street, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Prisoner was remanded until Friday next.

div.head: BLUE RIBBON ARMY.
div.p: THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY.
THE WARRINGTON CAMPAIGN.

For some months past rumours have been prevalent of an intended advance upon Warrington of one of the " armies " of whose doings in other parts of the country much has been heard. It has often been reported that the Salvation Army was about to take up its quarters in the town, but the reports have always proved to be without foundation. How- ever, an assault has at length been made upon the borough, not by the Salvationists, but by the Blue Ribbon Army, whose standard has been set up at the Public Hall. The mission of the army is to enlist recruits to the ranks of teetotalism, and the opening of the carnpaigu in Warrington was eminently successful. Previous to the entry into this town, the Blue Ribbon Army, under the generalship of Mr. Edward Murphy, who is designated "the great 'American apostle of temperance," has made a triumphant progress through most of the towns in north-east Lancashire, and has secured many adherents to the cause. Mr. Murphy's fame as a temperance advocate spread far and near, and about a month ago a meeting was held in the ante-room it the Public Hall to consider the dNirability of inviting him to visit Warrington. Ultimately Mr. Murphy was invited to conduct a "gospel temperance mission," and during the past fortnight a large quantity of mural and other literature has been disseminated announcing that fact, and setting forth the success which has attended his efforts elsewhere. In response to the invitation contained in these announce- ments crowds of persons made their way to the Public Hall on Sunday evening, when the fortnight's campaign was openqd. The service commenced at the unusual hour of 8-15 p.m., but at eight o'clock—fifteen minutes after the doors were opened—the spacious building was packed in every part, and many were unable to gain admission. While awaiting the appearance of the gentleman whose renown had attracted the largest audience we have ever seen in the Public Hall on a Sunday, the choir which occupied the platform sang several hymns from Sankey's collection, under the leadership of the Rev. E. Moore, and to the accompaniment of Mr. W. T. Wilkinson. At the time fixed, Mr. Murphy, accompanied by his brother, the Revs. J. A. Beet, T. Rippon, J. Yonge, and J. Warnock, Messrs. John Hall, F. Dixon, J. H. Goraall, and others, ascended the platform, and took his seat. The hymn "Let us gather up the sunbeams" was then sung, and was followed by a portion of scripture read by the Rev. T. Rippon, and prayer by the Rev. J. A. Beet. It was fitting that Mr. Rippon' who since his advent into Warring- ton has from pulpit and platform repeatedly drawn attention to the intemperance of the townspeople, should be chosen to introduce the gentleman whose efforts it is hoped will effect a reform in this matter. In performing this duty the rev. gentleman remarked that they had heard a great deal about the Gospel Temperance Mission and the Blue Ribbon Army; and answering the question " What is it all about ?" ex- plained that the army was introduced and the mission started in America some years ago by Mr. Francis Murphy, father of the Mr. Murphy who was with them that night. Of the title " goepel temperance" he expressed his high appreciation, and afterwards confessed that there never was so good a cause as that of temperance, in the past so wretchedly advocated. He rejoiced as a Christian minister that the churches were now alive to this question, and that the ministers of these churches were taking a right etand. He quoted statistics to show the proportion of abstaining ministers amongst the various religious bodies, and again adverting to the title of the mission, said an explanation of the origin of the Blue Ribbon Army was to be found in the Book of Numbers, 15 chap. 38 v. The Blue Ribbon Army, he observed, had worked wonders in this country, but he wisely determined not to weary the audience with statistics, contenting himself with quoting the number of pledges (11,000) taken in Burnley, the last place miesioned by Mr. Murphy. Mr. Rippon further stated that the army knew no distinction, whether in politics or religion, mentioned that amongst the clergy Canon Wilberforce was one of its strongest adherents, and that amongst the higher classes Lord Mounttemple and his lady gave it their countenance; while only recently ,Lord Cairns had spoken in its favour. He referred briefly to the position of Nonconformists in the movement, and concluded by urging those present to testify their adheelon to principles which they believed to be God sanctioned and Heaven ordained. This address was listened to very attentively and every word was distinclly heard. Another hymn was sung and then Mr. Murphy rose to speak. A slight cheer was heard, but on a signal from Mr. Rippon it was at once suppressed, Mr. Murphy is a young gentleman of medium height, and well built. His complexion is of the cast peculiar to Americans and his features are regular and well moulded. He has, however, a somewhat prominent nose, and a quick observant eye. But for the peculiarity, as he described it, of "speaking thro' the nose," his voice would be sonorous and agreeable. Conscious, however, of this fault, he speaks deliberately, and thus his words lose none of their intended effect. In speaking, be paces back- wards and forwards upon the platform, and gives force to his utterances by frequent gestures. Mr. Murphy at the on- set expressed his belief that in this the 19th century, men were united more by intelligence than by brute force, and proceeded to state the truism that if there was no one to demand intoxicating liquor there would be no one to sell it, and so, he added, the easiest way to solve the problem was for each one to pass the local option bill in their own houses and become teetotallers, and it would be a very pleasant way of doing away with this intoxicating liquor. He then pro- ceeded to trace the history of some reforms, and point out the analogy between them and temperance reform. He alluded to the achievements of William Tell, whose name was the synonym of liberty, and to the work of Martin ruther, the originator of religious liberty. But he believed the drink traffic was nothing more than an enforced despotism, and exclaimed: God speed the time when the people should have the opportunity of saying whether the Local Option Bill shall be pissed. The abolition of slavery in America next came under notice, and Mr. Murphy pointed out the analogy that all these reforms were advocated for a very long time by a minority, which was the fault the temperance reformation had had to cantend with ever since • the day it was born into existence. They might be, he said, in the minority in Warrington, but they could derive consolation from the fact that the prin- ciple they advocated was right, and right, he declared, would triumph. Allusion was then made to the wearing of the blue ribbon, which Mr. Murphy said afforded a pretext to some persons to chaff those who wore it, a practise which he condemned, and in speaking in favour of the donning of the ribbon he created much laughter by the witty remark that he would "rather wear a blue ribbon than a red nose." In pathetic language he described the misery and poverty of the drunkard's home, and appealed to those present to take the pledge. What they wanted was encouragement by Christian people coming forward to sign the pledge, and to "don the blue," thus demonstrating to those who had fallen in the mud hole and mire of intem- perance, that they were willing to make some sacrifice to assist them to a purer, holier, and more sublime life. In eloquent terms he urged them in conclusion to labour earnestly for the cause. Mr. Murphy spoke for a little over half an hour, and his interesting addrees, which was inter- spersed with several amusing anecdotes, commanded the closest attention of his hearers. The choir then gave the hymn" Hold the fort for lam coming," and Mr. Murphy invited those present to "come and sign to-nieht." ' About 400 persons came forward, and their names were taken by 15 clerks, and after signing their pledges, the blue ribbon was given to them by a number of ladies. The hall has been neatly decorated with numerous texts and flags by Mrs. J. Shaw Green. Miss Emma Pendlebury, and Miss Lillie Toft.

Bouquets of primroses, the favourite flower of the late Earl of Beaconsfield, were worn by many of the Conserva- tives Of Warrington, on Wednesday last, it being the anni- versary of the death of that nobleman. A new book on lAncashire Folk-lore is in prepara- tion. The author is Mr. James Bowlter, whose " Goblin Tales of Lancashire" originally appeared in Brierley's Journal, and are now tl be included in the series of Fairy Tales of all nations, issued by Messrs. Sonnenschieu,
LATEST NEWS.
The Duke and Duchess of Connaught arrived at Windsor Castle, yesterday evening, and remain there until after the Royal wedding.

As young man named Flynn, a printer, was shot at in the streets of Cork early yesterday moraing, but was uninjured. Two arrests were subsequently made. Miss Kirk,. a member of the bublin Ladies Land League, was arrested at Limerick, yesterday morning, on a charge of intimidating, and refusing to find bail she was committed to prison for three months.

At a meeting of the operative cotton spinners of Bolton and district, held in the Co-operative Hall, Bolton, on Thursday night, it was agreed to make a grant of £25 per week in support of the operatives' lock-out and on strike at Chorley. It was stated that Blackburn had decided to make a grant of £4O per week, and that other towns in Lancashire were also contributing. The second round in the public schools racquet matches was played at the Princes Club, yesterday. The first match between Eton and Cheltenham uas decided in favour of the former by four games to love. 'Harrow beat Wellington by the same points, and will therefore meet Eton in the final contest to-day. The Fecenian's Joto•nal of yesterday says a letter has. been received by Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., in Kilmainham, from Mr. Parnell, dated Tuesday. He has recovered from the indisposition under which he was ailing, and expects to be back in Kilmainham Gaol without fail on Monday next. Mr. Parnell expresses the heartfelt pleasure he feels at the release of Mr. William O'Brien.

A party of moonlighters were surprised by the police patrol near Ballybunion on Thursday night. The latter fired 14 rounds at them, wounding, it is stated, several of the marauders. One arrest was made.

At a mass meeting of miners held at Gornal and Rowley, yesterday, it was decided that the miners of the South Staf- fordshire and East Worcestershire districts be urged to play on Mondays with a view of preventing over-production and the consequent lowering of wages. It was also resolved that all necessary steps be taken to form a conciliation board, to be composed of equal numbers of employers and workmen.

The case of Lieutenant Turner, of the King's Own Bor- derers, came up at the Newcastle Assizes„ yesterday. The prisoner eloped with the wife of a Berwick solicitor and was now charged with stealing the luggage, which she took with her. The grand jury threw out the bill and strongly censured the prosecution. The judge also remarked that a more absurd and ridiculous case, to commit a man on, he never knew. He should disallow the costs of the prosecution. Yesterday, John Lamb, sergeant of police at South Shields, was charged with embezzling various sums of money received by him as chief clerk in the police office. The defalcations included £l2 for victualling prisoners; £s Ms. 2d. from the poor-box, entrusted to him until the box was repaired; and 14s. received in payment of penalties. He had not accounted for these moneys. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to six months' imprison- ment.

div.head: AN INHUMAN FATHER.
div.p: AN INHUMAN FATHER.

At Barnsley, yesterday afternoon, the magistrates com- mitted Isaac Midgley, a miner living in Grace-street, for one month without the option of a fine, for cruelty and not pro- viding sufficient food for his wife and six children. The Relieving Officer and Doctor Blackburn, who examined the children, found them in a shocking state, they hating been several days without food, whilst the wife was lying ill on some old boards. The wife and family were removed to the workhouse.

div.head: STOPPAGE OF THE LIVERPOOL DAILY MAIL.
div.p: THE STOPPAGE OF THE LIVERPOOL DAILY MAIL.

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, John Maccabe, late proprietor and publisher of the Liverpool Mail, which collapsed so suddenly some time ago, came up for his public exmnination. On the bankrupt being called Mr. W. L. Jackson, the trustee, said Mr. Morton had made a full disclosure of his affairs, and there was no objection, so far as the trustee was concerned, to his passing his public examination. No creditors opposed, and the bankrupt was allowed to pass. STRANGE BEHAVIOUR OF A NAVAL OFFICER.

The Western Horning News of Thursday has the follow- ing:—The erratic movements of the training brig Pilot, Lieutenant Giles commanding, since she grounded a few days since, has excited considerable surprise. The other training brigs have on every available opportunity made short cruises for the instruction of the lads, but on only three occasions has the Pilot slipped her moorings, and not once has she succeeded in getting clear of thr Sound. Once indeed the brig got as far as the breakwater and returned, but on the two other occasions after proceeding a fov hundred yards she anchored in the stream. This extraoidinary conduct could not be unnoticed, and yesterday the brig was recalled into harbour, and a tug was sent down to the Sound to tow her. As soon as she was berthed, Lieut. Giles went on board the Impregnable, and stated that he had been signalled for by the admiral, and that his intention was to have brought the brig into the harbour under sail. With the wind in the quarter in which it was, that would have been impossible. Last evening:the powder was removed from the brig,and she will remain where she now lies until the intentions of the Admiralty have been made known. CONTINUED RIOTING IN NORTH WALES. THE MOB CHARGED.

A Ruibon correppondent telegraphed yesterday morning: —Last night the most intenee excitement prevailed in the Ruabon district on account of the riotOus conduct of the miners. At nine o'clock two large meetings of miners were held on the outskirts of Ruabon. It was reported that both Masses had arranged to meet together, and besiege the resi- dences of the colliery proprietors and managers. A strong force of military left Wrexham by road at nine o'clock, and at eleven o'clock two companies of the Denbighshire and Merionthshire Militia, accompanied by Colonel Sir Robert Cunliffe, MT., Captain Cowan, Major Leadbetter, and several officers, arrived at Ruabon by special train from Wrexham. The three companies then scouted the neigh- bourhood. On nearing the residence of Mr. Carlington, manager at Wynnstag Colliery, a loud cry from a gang of men was heard, and the military were commanded to fix bayonet. The policemen then endeavoured to surround the mob, who were then throwing stones. Finding them- selves surrounded. the rioters took to flight, some of them running on the point of the bayonet. Two received severe cuts, and were taken to Ruabon to have their wounds dressed. One man also received a violent blow upon the head, and was conveyed to hospital, where he now lies. The military were afterwards marched through the district, the colliers everywhere dispersing before them. The military sur- rounded the residences of the proprietors and managers, but no further disturbances took place. They returned to Wrex- ham this morning. THE NEXT-OF-KIN SWINDLE.
MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS AT BIRMINGHAM.

At the Birmingham Police-court, yesterday, before the Stipendary, Edward Becton, 39, the manager to the Bir- mingham branch of the "International Law and Next-of- kin Agency," who described himself as a draper living at Ladypool Lane, Sparkbrook, was charged on a warrant with conspiring with J. S. Rogers fraudulently to obtain divers sums of money from John Lawrence, Clifford-street, Lozells, by falsely pretending that they had the power of recovering certain property of great value to which, it was alleged, Lawrence was entitled, with intent t) cheat and defraud. A large number of persons who had been duped attended the I court, and. from their appearance and exclamations, were evidently and, at the arrest of the accused. The pri- soner is tall, and of gentlemanly appearance. The learned counsel, in asking the stipendlry to grant a remand, said the 1 evidence in the case was of a very voluminous I character, and it was absolutely necessary to examine the statements of a great number of persons who have been de- frauded. The remand he now asked for was until next i IThursday, by which time t was possible that J. S. Rogers, I Esq., 8.A., would also be in custody. The victim Law- rence who believed himself to be entitled to some valuable estates in America, answered an advertisement which set forth that heirs or next•of-kin were wanted for ,15,750,000, and that application should be made to J. S. Rogers, Esq., 8.A., at the International Law Agency, Burlington Cham- bers, New-street, Birmingham. The application for a re- mand was not opposed by the prisoner, but it was asked that he should be liberated on bail. It was asserted that he simply acted as clerk to Rogers, and was paid by galary id

commission.—The Ftipendary said the prisoner was chzrged with a misdemeanour, and was therefore entitled to bail and he should accept two sureties of £lOO each, the prisoner himself being bound over in £2oo.—The prisoner denied the truth of the allegation made by Rogers to many of the clients, that he (Beeton) had faded to account for meneys received by him when acting as manager at the Birmingham offices. Rogers has not yet been arrested.
FENIAN PLOT TO BLOW UP WOOL-
WICH BARRACKS.

The Central News Woolwich correspondent telegraphs : A letter has been received at the barracks here, addressed to Captain W. F. De F. Curtis, of the Depot Brigade, Royal Horse Artillery, signed "One of the Brotherhood," profess- ing to reveal a Fenian plot to blow up some portion or the whole of Woolwich Barracks duang the present week. The letter is couched in polite terms, and the writer professes to be animated by respect and friendship for Capt. Curtis. He states as the depot quarters are especially in jeopardy he cannot refrain from putting the officer on hisguard. -The- communication is regarded in the garrison as merely one of the empty menaces which the Fenian agencies employ to vex the authorities and excite public attention;: but it has, nevertheless, been deemed advisable to be prepared for possi- 6ilities, and a number of extra sentries have been posted about the barracks and other precautions taken. The writer intimated that the destruction of the garriscrn had been fired for some time between Thursday and Sunday night in the present week, and that the Royal Artillery Barracks is menaced in particular; but the precautions have extended to the whole of the barracks, and will probably be con- tinued for some time to come. After nightfall not only the gates are carefully guarded, but sentries are placed in the- roads and passages, and no one can pass without frrquent challenges and interrogatious. The garrison is well supplied with troops, and the extra duties of watching are conse- quently provided for without much inconvenience. It is considered strange that the warning should have been sent to Captain Curtis, who holds no command or appointment in the district other than that of superintending the Royal Artillery theatre and recreation rooms.

div.head: LIST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LIST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS. The Duke of ALBANY'S Established Vote was passed, and received the &Tel assent. Tha Drainage (Ireland) Provi— sional Order Bill was read a second time. The House ad- journed at 7.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

TIIE Wm-Tax VICALIAGE.—On the motion for the second reading of the Walton Vicarage Bill, Mr. CAINE opposed, and moved its rejection. The Bill proposed the purchasing the advowson and vicarage of Walton in order to increase the stipend of the Bishop of Liverpool and other purposes a proceeding he thought unjust and uncalled for.—The Bill was an ecclesiastical job to save the pockets of the rich churchmen in Liverpool.—Mr. ILLINGWORTH supported the motion for rejection.—After some discussion the House divided when there voted for the second reading 160, against, 76. THE PROPOSED DISFRANCHISEMENT OF GLOUCESTER.— Sir M. IlicKs-BEAcn gave notice that after the second read- ing of the Corrupt Practices Disfranchisement Bill he move it be referred to a select committee to take evidence as far as Gloucester was concerned.

Intsn AFFAIRS.—Mr. FewcErr, replying to Mr. Red- mond, said nothing was known at the General Post Office as to the mutilation of a number of copies of the Irish .Nation containing portraits in passing through the post.—Sir W. HARCOURT, replying to Mr. Redmond, declined to give any information as to whether or not letters addressed to the secretary of the Land League of Great Britain had been opened and detained in passage through the Post Office.— Mr. FORSTER, replying to Mr. •Leamy, s iid the number of arrests under the Protection to Life and Property (Ireland) Act, up to the 18th April, was 918. NOTICE or QUESTION.—Sir H. D. WOOLFF gave notice to. ask the Government what they purposed doing as regarded the suspects claiming foreign nationality. ORDER OF BUSINESS.—Lord HARTINGTON said the Cor- rupt Practices Disfranchisement Bill would be proceeded with after the Budget, on Monday next. _ _ _

COOPERS HILL -COLLEGE.-111r. GIBSON called attention to the educational working of Coopers hill college as re- garded the education of students for civil ergineers' appoint- ments and public works in India. He thought an improve- meut in the present system was required, and therefore moved the appointment of a select committee to inquire and report what change was necessary.—Mr. CAnnurr secondcd the proposal.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON opposed the motion, believing that an inquiry at the present time would be premature and undesirable, especial'y as the new scheme had only been in operation about a year. He declined to enter into a discussion as to the desirability of founding the college.—After a few words from Mr. Onslow, Mr. STAN- HOPE insisted the college bgd been successful up to a certain point, and to have an inqriiry now would be to kill all the good that had bln done by cl anges lately made. He h pc& the new, system would have a fair trial, before it was attempted to break up the college.—Mr. D. PLuNIKETT sup- ported the motion. He believed the general interest of the Civil Service rrquired an inquiry.—Sir G. CAIIIP3ELL op- posed the inquiry at the present time, but he had no objection to it farther on.—Mr. PUGH supported the pro- posal of Mr. Gibson.—The motion for a_ select committee I was rejected by 78 against 27.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL PRODUCE.—Sugar market exhibits no change Molaoses. treacle, and rum dull. Coffee and cocoa nothing to report. Logwood and fustic unaltered. Ashes: Pot dull a inguiry. Little doing in gum. Cutch remains steady; good inquiry. Little doing in gum. Nitrate fairly steady. Lard. 575. Tallow and seed oils generally steady. Turpentine, 5s 6d highest value. Petroleum, 6fd extreme prices. LIVERPOOL, CORN.—Wheat Id lower than yesterday with a limited demand. Flour also easier, and rather slow. Mixed corn steady, at 75 for old. Nothing doing in cargoes, either wheat or maize, and less money would be taken. WAKEFIELD CORN.—The wheat trade is steady thi; morning, and holders insist of an advance of Is to 2s. per quarter over last week's prices. Barley quiet Beans and cats rather dearer Maze Is. to 2s. higher. CLYDE CRUSHED BUG us—Market flat. The small business done shows a further aechne of 31. per cwt. Tne official report states: Quiet market at easier prices. _ _ _ _

Mr. J. G. Illalinnies, the menoter for Warrington, was amongst the members who voted for the suspension of Mr. Redmond in the House of Commons on Thursday evening.

WA.ERINGTON PETTY SESSIONS.—At the Warrington Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Artingstall and Mr. Houghton, Michael Costello, a young fellow living a "Pig Hall," was charged with fighting at Fidlers Ferry on Good Friday, and he was bound over to keep the peace.—W. Wailing, patternmaker, Widnes, for obstructing the footpath on Liverpool-road, by riding a bicycle thereon on the Bth inst., was ordered to pay the costs, 7s. 6J. —John Dean and Wm. Hale were fined ss. and 9s. costs each for drunkenness and disorderly behaviour at Rixton on the 2ad inst.—A boy named J. T. Poole, was charged with stealing four keys of the value of 2s. from an unoccupied house at Penketh, the !property of Mr. Cook, a farmer. Superintendent Williamson said, OR Sunday, the prisoner was seen to enter the house, and also to come out with the keys in his hand. When the constable apprehended him, he had the keys in his posses- -1 slim along with a large number of others —The prisoner was stated to be an unruly character, and he was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.—Ann Jones a married woman, was charged with, stealing at Newton on the 15th Inst., 31 lbs. beef of the value of 2s. 7d., the property of Thomas Nevitt, and also i lbs., worth is., the property of Stephen Holland. Tlic prisoner pleaded guilty and said she had committed the theft in consequence of drinx.—She had been twice convicted of theft, and the Bench sentenced her to two months' hard labour.

WESLEILN ItINISTERIAL ENGAGEMENTS FOR 1882. During the last fortnight the Wesleyan March quarterly meetings have been held, the important specialities of which naturally attract the attention of all who- watch the progress of Methodism in Great Britain. These special features are the annual returns of church membership, the recommendation of young men as candidates for the ministry, and the invitation of ministers for the ensuing connexional year. As far as the numerical returns are at present known, there is likely to be a substantial increase in the membership of the Connexion, probably larger than has been the case for i several years past, circuits in the north especially sharing n this increase. It is generally antici- pated that the supply of candidates for the ministr; will be affected by the action of the Liverpool Conference of last i year n declining en m7sse all who offered for the home work. iAs most of these will be brought forward again this i year, t s not expected that any new candidates will be pro- posed. The ministerial arrangements for another year are now completed in the various circuits. Invitations given and accepted are subject to the authority of the Conference. Provisional engaizements of long standing are on the increase, and many circuits make their engagements two r nearly al and three years befcrehand—invitation committees having now become an established Ilus.easgleiteyiann British Methodism. e Between five and six hundredministers,a n of whom will have been the full term of three years in their present spheres of labour, will change circuits at the ensuing Conference. The following list of engagements between ministers and circuits, which have received the official sanction of the March quarterly meetings will be of interest: —G. A. Bennetts, 8.A., London (Sydenham) ; Thomas Brackenbury, London (Great Queen-street) ; Thomas Brum, well, Northwich ; Ebenezer Cole, Crewe; Richard Crozier, Hampstead ; J. M. STATE OF ARPLEY STREET. Sir,—l live jn Arpley-street (off Sankey-street), and my neighbours and myself have great cause for complaint owing to the very dirty and sometimes filthy state of our street. In ordinary weather there are pools of stagnant water, and in wet weather it is scarcely passable. On Sun- days one's best and clean boots are drenched, and the odour from a common nuisance by the side of the circus is intoler- able in passing. As the property in Arpley-street is tolerably good (including a large school,) I think it is the duty of the authorities, or the nuisance inspector, to see after this mat- ter. Although neglected in this particular we are not neglected in the way of paying rates, for they somehow find their way down the dirty street, and we are bound to pay them. Both in paving and cleansing we must be looked after, as it is our just right. By inserting this plaint in your esteemed paper, you will greatly ob.ige, ONE OF THE DISCONTENTS. Arpley-street, 19th April, 1882.

" GREENALL FOR EVER." Sir,—Out of curiosity I went to the Public Hall las' Friday evening, to the meeting held under the above "motto," and promoted, as any one could see, by "our townsman," " the Seraphic Doctor." I, for one, should be very glad to see the Tories adopt the motto, " Mackie for ever ;': we would give him as good a thrashing his countrymen in Perth gave him. Ile seemed to be very discomforted and unhappy; if it had not been for the strong Liberal element present, the meeting would have been as flat as ditch water. However, I suppose they have to make the best of Sir Gilbert's retirement, and fish About for a candidate who can "stump out," for I believe their funds, &c., are in a very dilapidated state. I happened to go in the hall when Mr. W. J. Burgess was speaking, when the thought suggested itself to me, "What a fit and proper person for the mantle to fall upon." Then again, "No," he would not de, he is too weak; his conduct in withdrawing from our "Local parliament" would stamp him as very weak and one who cannot stand defeat, as certainly a Tory candidate would. The support, I'm afraid, we should get from the chairman, would be in the shape of opposition; but as Liberalism in Warrington does not lack for want of good and true candidates, we may say we are fortunate, and being an united party, as instanced at the recent election of Guardians, are ready and prepared to take the field against all corners, be they "baronets," "doctors," or any others. " McMINNIES FOR EVER." Warrington, April 19th, 1882.

WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Picktnere), Major Cartwright, and Mr. Ziba Armitage. VIOLENT PRISONERS: THE WORST CHARACTER IN WAR- BINGTON.—John Shields, a well known rough, was charged with using malicious threats to P. C. Neill. On the 13th ult., four men, of whom the defendant was one, were com- mitted to gaol for various terms of imprisonment for drunkenness and assaulting the police. Their conduct was so bad after being sentenced that five officers had to escort them to the railway station. A large crowd had assembled, and a woman held up a bottle of spirits. The prisoners rushed among the crowd to seize the bottle and the officers had a hard task to get them on the platform. When in the compartment, Burke, one of the men,produced a bottle, hew he had got it was a mysteey, but P.C. Neill seized it and sent it through the window. Upon this Shields turned to P.C. Neill. and pointing to his clogs said he "would kick his out," and threatened to take his life. Arrived at Liverpool the prisoners agreed to lie on the ground, and it was only with the aid of several Liverpool police that they could be moved along at all. They were three quarters of an hour in travelling the short distance from the Central Station to Lime-street. The prisoners used some outrageous threats, but on arriving at Lime-street, the futility of their conduct appeared to present itself, and he remarked to his fellow prisoners that "We have been fools chaps."— P.C. Neill, Clynes, and Chantler gave evidence bearing out this statement, and they all agreed that they "never had such a day."—The prisoner, who had frequently interrupted the witnesses, now turned on the "pump," and with tears in his eyes, said the police dragged him out of his mind." They might as well send him for seven years or else hang him. He had never been out of gaol four weeks for this last eight years. At the same time he admitted he had "one of the worst characters in the town."—The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for twelve months, himself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO, or, in default, one month. BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT.—John Foden was charged with having on the 9th April, that he being licensed to retail table beer to be consumed off the premises at 17. Gerrard's-row, unlawfully did sell the same at 40, Hine- street, off Church-place, where he was not authorised to sell. George Yates, John PI unapton, and George Fox were charged with aiding and abetting.—From the Chief Constable's statement it appeared that at last Brewster sessions, Foden had hi license to sell table beer at 17, Gerard-street, renewed, but three weeks ago that house was pulled down and be removed to 40, Hine-street. On Sun- day, the 9th instant, about 12 o'clock, P.S. Bowen was in Buttermarket-street, when he met a man named George Fox carrying something bulky under his coat, and "looking as though he had got something he ought not to have." Satisfied there was something wrong the officer stopped Fox, who pulled from his coat a bottle containing a quart of table beer. At the officer's request, Fox went with him to Foden's house, where the three other defendants were drinking. Foden's wife admitted serving the beer, and asked P,6. Bowen to deal lightly with her as "her husband was out, and if he got to know he would kill her,”—P.S. Bowen cor- roborated this etatement.—Foden : Was I in the house ? P.S. Bowen: No—Foden: It appears to me you would summons me if my wife cut the cat's head off. (Laughter.) —P.C. Wheatley having given evidence, Yates admitted he had a pint of some liquor but did not know whether it was table beer or ginger beer. Plumpton denied that he had any beer, stating he had hurt his head and went for some herbs. —The Bench said they were inclined to believe Plumpton's statement, and he would be discharged. Feden was fined 40e. and costs lOse and Yates was fined 103. and costs 7s. A warrant was granted for the apprehension of Fox. Stneacrs FOR THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY.—The follow- ing persons were charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct, and a fine was imposed in each case :—John Glynn, Michael Birmingham, Clara E. Brown (17), Catherine Murphy. DAMAGING CHRIST CHURCH SCHOOL, LATCHFORD.— ; Joseph Barber, Thomas Birch, and John Boardman, boys, were charged with committing damage to Christ Church school, Latchford, on Tuesday last. On that evening there was a dramatic performance taking place in the school, when a noise was heard on the roof. Subsequently the de- fendant's were found there, and the spout had been damaged. Boys were in the habit of congregating about the school, and throwing large stones at the ventilators, defacing the building.—The defendants were each ordered to pay 4s. 61. and 6d. damage. AN ASSAULT CASE—Patrick Collins, of WinNvick-street, was charged with assaulting his wife, Sarah, on the 14th The caseWllS adjourned for a month, to give the de- fendant "arother BREECHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT. --Mr. Riley, the attendance officer, summoned 13 persons for not sending their children regularly to school. There were no special features in the cases, and the usual fine of ss. was inflicted on the following persons::—Michael O'Neil, forgernan Pump-yard; John Towey, tanner, 9, Erwood- street ; qichael McHugh. forgeman, 9, Bennett-street; John rleming, labourer, Flag-yard • James Pagatt, glass bottle maker, Glass Hous:-eew ; Flag-yard; Dagnall, soapery, 9, Baxter-street; Joseph Massey, farmer, Mill-lane; Wm. Barlow, carter, Bostock-street ; George Lamb, forgeman, 14, • Lythgoe's-lane; Thomas Connolly, factory operative, Bowcock-street ; Pat Cordeld, labourer, Vernon's-yard; Martha Gleave, 54, Bostock-street ; John Hardy, labourer, Rose-yard. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks.

RECLAIMED!—Jarnes :41cGinnies, a well-known character, was charged with berng drunk and disorderly, in Butter- market-street, on the previous night. Councillor Monks suggested to the prisoner that he should kut himself 'under the influence of the Blue Ribbon Army, and the prisoner 'promised to go to the prkst at once and sign the pledge. On this promise he was released. WEDNESDAY.—There were no cases for disposal. TitrusneY.—Before. Captain Litton (chairman) and Alderman Webster. THEFT FROM I PCBLIC-HOUSE.—Joseph Battersby, des- cribed as a well known glass and crockery dealer, was charged with stealing a gill glass of the value of blence, from the Crown and Sceptre Inn, Buttermarket-street, occu- pied by John lake. On the previous day the prisoner was seen walking through the streets with bulky pockets, and P.C. Neill stopped him and found three glasses upon him. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge, and he was com- mitted to gaol for one month with hard labour. THE ONLY "CURE" FOR WIFE DESERTERS.—John Robinson, a tanner, last from London, was charged under a warrant with running away from the borough on the 23rd November, leaving his wife and child chargeable to the con-I- ran fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said the prisoner's wife had been chargeable since the above date, having received about £6 in relief. For the last three years the prisoner's wife had been chargeable "on and off," and when he left the town he had a good situation where he was earning 255. per week.--Mr. Hunt said the prisoner was brought from London that morning by P.C. was remarked from the Bench that there was no other way of curing such men as the prisoner than sending them to gaol, and the prisoner was sentenced to three months with hard labour. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Messrs. Z. Armitage, and J. White.

A Row AT THE BULL'S HEAD.—John Duffy, a respect- ably dressed.young man, was charged with assaulting Chas Roddy, landlord of the Bull's Head, Bridge-street, on Sun- day aftetnoon, and there was a cross summons charging Roddy with assaulting Duffy.—ln the first case Roddy said defendant and six other men went into his house about 20 minutes to ten in the evening, and asked for drinks round. One of the party pulled out a pack of cards, but compla'n- ant told him r to pick the cards up as he did not allow 'that sort of worli Co he carried on there." On visiting the room a second time he found them still playing, and told them to pick the cards up or he would empty the content A of the glass on the cards. He left the room, and on returning a third time his wife was in the act of "chastising the men" with her tongue. Duffy then called complainant's wife an opprobious name, and complainant took up a glass, part filled with beer, which he threw in defendant's face. De- fendant took up a glass containing more bar and throw tha glass and its contents at

complainant, whose hand was injured. A disturbance then arose, and as many as half-a-dozen pint pots were broken, according to the witnesses, by Duffy's party.—The case for Duffy, from the statement of Mr. Percy Davies, was that Duffy and a friend met two men in Bridge-street, from whom they purchased a pack of cards for two pints of beer, and they went into tlie Bull's Head and ordered the beer. Whilst there they we counting the cards when Roddy told them to put the cards away. Some words took place and Duffy took up a glass and threw the contents at Roddy. The latter then picked up a glass and with all his force threw it across the counter at Duffy and struck him on the bead.- The glass was smashed to pieces, and a great many pieces of glass were taken out of the wound by Dr. Fox the same night. A jug was also thrown at Duffy by Mrs. Roddy, and he and his party were turned out of the house.—After a hearing lasting an hour and fifty minutes, the Bench said there had been a mood deal of hard swearing, and dismissed the cases, each party to pay their own costs, 4s. A NEGLIGENT APPRENTICE.—Mary Coffey, a girl, was summoned by James Oakes, fustian cutter, for 15s. compen- sation by reason of her being his apprentice, and staying away from her work. An order was made for defendant to return to work and to pay 10s., including costs, at the rate of Is. a week.

Heathside infant school had a most attractive and pleas- ing appearance on Monday afternoon, on the occasion of a sale of work held in aid of a fund to employ a mission woman and for other parochial objects. Muslin curtains hung before the windows, trophies of flags and several mottoes adorned the walls, and flowers and plants heightened the effect of the decorations, which gave a cheerful and comfortable aspect to the room. The work was displayed to full advantage upon some half-dozen tables of various sizes, which were loaded with articles of a very superior description. Many of them were handsomely ornamented, and greatly admired, but them was certainly no lack of serviceable goods. Several wall brackets splendidly exe- cuted in leather and crewel work attracted great attention, besides numerous aprons in crewel work; while therewere any number of antimacassors in as many varieties of style. There were several pairs of wool-worked slippers, artistic cushions and tea cosies wool mats and toilet tidies, a variety i of childreas' frocks, a large array of dolls, some handsome- ' ly-painted china plaques, hand painted menu cards, a casket of scent, including the "Warrington bouquet," and other novelties, photos of the vicar and the Rev. E. St. A. Duke, a drawing of Winwick Church (by Mr. F. Esseahigh), together with an assortment of infantile clothing and wearing apparel. We should not forget to mention the refreshment stall, which was replete with tempting delicacies. Lady members presided at the tables, and the amateur sales- woman found constant employment until late in the evening. The time announced for opening the sale was half-past two ' o'clock, and at that time the room was well filled with a fashionable assembly. Amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs. H. Lyon, the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Bea- mont, Mr. and Mrs. Branker, Mr. and Mrs. Venn' Rev. E. St A. Duke, Mrs. John Pierpoint, Mrs. and Miss Chorley, Mrs. Highley, Mrs. Buckton, Mrs. Smethurst. Mrs. Stewart, Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Murray, Mrs. Sharp, Mrs. Litton, Mr. V. and Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Edward Greenall, Mrs. John White, Mrs. John and the Misses Geddes, Miss Garland, Mr. and Mrs. Norris, Miss Athertoa, Miss Braid, Miss Lawless, Miss Marshall, Miss Pollett, Mrs. Townsend, Miss Townsend, Miss Duke, Mrs. Jervis, Mrs. Wood, Miss M. Wood, Miss Smith Miss B. Wilkinson, Miss Fraser, Miss Westwell, Miss Brundritt, the Misses Greening, the Misses Grange, Miss Atherton, Miss Murphy, Miss Craik, the Misses Fair, 'Miss Ashurst, Miss Burrows, Miss Unsworth, Miss Jolley, Mr. Sutton (churchwarden), ' Mr. Finney, Mr. Jos. Robinson Mr. C. Marson, Mr. and Mrs. Lawless, and others. The Rev. S. Wilkinson briefly introduced Mrs. Lyon, who was to perform the duty of opening the sale. Taking her stand at the top end of the room Mrs. Lyon ably discharged the duty. In doing so she said: It gives me very great pleasure to open this sale of work, which, as you are aware, is for an object we must all have at heart. .That is to help to meet the misery in this large town by establishing a mission woman in one of its most populous and needful districts—the new streets that have sprung up over Bewsey-bridge. It is now, I think, a well established fact, that the poor in sickness and need are best helped by one of their own order, acquainted with their peculiar wants and sympathetic with their daily cares and pleasures, and the report of the Parochial Mission, which this one is intended to resemble in many points, is highly interesting, and shows that were the means forthcoming, many more in our crowded cities might be helped to help themselves—the truest way of assisting our labouring brothers and sisters. I need not urge upon you how many in Warrington stand in need of such help, nor how many there are who can neither read nor write, and who, if they have the will, have not the power pf becoming acquainted with the holy scriptures; and the mission woman's aid may indeed become invaluable in bringing a knowledge of the gospel to those whose age, infirmities, or want of education, might preclude them from this privilege. lam requested to add how much Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson are indebted to the kind ladies who have worked so hard all winter to fur- nish the beautiful useful things I see here, and which I hope will find a ready sale. I will not trespass longer on your time, arid! now pronounce the sale open. (Loud applause.) There was a large attendance during the evening, and the hope expressed by Mrs. Lyon was fully realised, as very few articles remained unsold when the sale was closed at about ten o'clock. For the amusement of the visitors, an " Art " gallery was provided, containing the "treasures " usually gathered together on these occasions, but amongst the more noteworthy were "Jumbo," and the "Remains of Pat," as represented by a dilapidated umbrella and an old hat.

SALVATION ARMY. GENERAL BOOTH'S REPLY. The letter of the Rev. Thomas Rippon, Wesleyan minis- ter, Warrington, which appeared in Friday week's Times, has elicited from General Booth, who writes from "The Salvation Army Head Quarters," the following reply, also published in the Times :—The Rev. Mr. Rippon cannot be congratulated on his watchfulness ov.r the interests of the public, since he comes with his warning only a month be- fore the opening of our National Congress Hall at Clapton, and after we. have acquired the OxLrd-street Rink, an equally large building in Camberwell, and various properties all over the country. I trust his warning will, however, have the effect of leading many intelligent persons to look as closely as he can wish into our affairs and system, as I have no doubt we shall then be relieved from the financial strain which prevents our adding to the numbers of our larger halls more rapidly than we do. Not that we avish to acquire real property, for we always avoid spending strength en the raising of money or on building where we can hire commodious places for our services. We have long been kept from attacking Warrington for want of such a meeting place. If Mr. Rippon or any one else will secure for us the long lease of an empty warehouse or other such edifice that will seat 2,000 or more persons, we shall be saved the trouble of acqairing property in that town for the present. But I wish most emphatically to disdain-o°th for the army and for our orders and regulations, any of the spirit of antago- nism to churches or ministers which Mr. Rippon professes to I,ave discovero and which he endeavours to show from one or two expressions sevaet: from their connection. The purpose of the book is simply to direct persons who are labouring outside all the churches aid systems, in perfect goodwill „to all *men. The order book was published ia 1878, and directed our officers how ,to act in presence of then existing facts, which I could easily detail were I not so far from having any wish to speak disparagingly of any church oc minister. Times are changed, thank God, since then. The careful carrying out of the system inculcated in the order book has raised our corps in those three years and a half from 48 to 286, and the number of officers, who are entirely engaged in the work and supported out of it, from 100 to 623. Our War Cry, with its weekly circulation of 255,000, is surely a proof, not only of the acceptability and value of our system to the freedom-loving people of England, but of our friendly spirit towards all classes and sects. Several occupants of the Episcopal bench, the President and several ex-Presidents of the Wesleyan Methodist Church, and many of the most in- fluential ministers and laymen of all denominations, have expressed their sympathy with us and their sense of our brotherly love towards everybody, Se tint ,aowdays, instead of finding a friendly minister to be a rant (Luis; we find acatcely anyone of any weight who will say or write a word against us. What we have said as to Ole failure of ministers to reach the masses with the Gospel is merely. a repetition of what they themselves are saying continually, the figures of recent religions censuses being only too pain- ful conarmation of the 'worst that can be said as to the separation between the pulpit and the multitude. It is indeed a frank retospitiou of these facts, and of the success of our operations t:mong those who are outside the range of all ordinary relieous influence, that has gained for us so hearty a goodwill of late from clergymen and ministers of all denominations. I enclose a copy of our unoffenAing hand- book, and hope that you will be one of many new readers of it.

An adjournment was then made to the lawn in front of the house, where the company were photographed by Mr. Bowers, from Mr. Webster's, Bridge-street, Warrington. - A cheer was then given for the Queen, and one for Colonel McCorquodale, the trumpeters playing "For he's a jolly good fellow." Subsequently the guests retired to the house, and the procession of carriages started for Wigan. The band of the Liverpool Press Guard, which played a selection of music during the breakfast, headed the proteseion, and on leaving the grounds struck up a lively air. Then followed the Newton Company of the Press Guard, which, under the command of Captain J. L. Wood, acted as a guard of honour. The first carriage contained the Mayor of Wigan, who was in state, and members of the Town Council. Arrived at Wigan railway station, the approaches to which were crowded, the Mayor (Alderman Hopwood) briefly addressed the High Sheriff, speaking of the universal esteem in which he was held; and then, on behalf of the Corpora- tion, presented him with the following address, which was handsomely illuminated and bound in morocco leather :•—• TO COLONEL GEORGE WCORQUODALE, HIGH SHERIFF OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER, AC., AC., AC. The Memorial of the Mayer, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Wigan, in Council assembled, respectfully sheweth —That the Town Counll of Wigan beg to offer to you their warm c mgratulations upon the honour which ha., been bestowed upon you by Her Majesty the Queen in appointing you High Sheriff of the County Palatine of Lancaster. As the enter- prising founder of a large industi tel establishment in the neighbourhood of this borough, as one of the originators and the chairman since its commencement of the Haydock Relief Fund, as a county magistrate for nearly a quarter of a century, as the originator of and for many years Lieut.-Colonel and now Honorary Colonel of the Liverpool Press Gnard, and as first chairman of the Newton Commissioners, which position you occupied for a long period, the Corporation feel that your public services have benefited the County Palatine, and they desire to acknowledge your services by their presentation of this address. The Corporation wish you long life and happi- nesS, and a prosperous career in your public duties. Given under the Common Seal of ties Mayor, Aldermen, and Bur- gesses of Wigan, at Wigan, the 2nd day of April, 1862. The High Sheriff, in reply, said he could hardly express the feeling of gratification he experienced in receiving this high compliment. . He ventured to come among the people of n igan a few years ago-as a stranger, and was sent back because he was not competent to take the situation he ap- plied for—(laughter and "No, no "),—and that he should now be received by all parties in that town with such kind- ness and cordiality was an event that he never dreamt of, and one that he would certainly never forget as long as he lived. (Applause.) To pass along their streets, and to find so vast an assembly of people on every side, and to see their cheerful and happy countenances, and to feel that he in some measure was the cause of bringing them out that day, was very flattering to him, and he most thoroughly appre- ciated all this kindness. When the verdict was pronounced against him in Wigan, a f,w years ago, he accepted it, and he could not feel regret or sorrow at his connection with the town. (Hear, hear.) He felt in passing through the streets that day that he had not made a single enemy, but that on the contrary he had had the good fortune to make many friends. (Loud applause.) He expressed his sincere thanks to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Corporation, and to the in- habitants generally. He would greatly treasure the hand- some address he had received, and would hand it down to his children in the hope that it would encourage them in the discharge of the duties of life. (Applause.) It would encourage him in the duties of the effice which her Majesty had conferred upon him, and give him greater conidence in the work he had to perform. (Loud applause.) The High Sheriff then left the station for Manchester. Although early in the morning the weather was of a threatening character, the clouds dispersed as the day wore on, and the sun lent a cheerful countenance to the festivi- ties which passed off with the greatest success.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The first meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. There were present Revs. T. Chambers, Marsh, Tyrer, Pen- keth, Fisher, Leatherbarrow, Agnew, Sadler, Leigh, Gerrard, Birch, Tuson, Dobell, Paris, Hall, Fidler, Newsome, Lowe, Meadows, Buckley, Eatock, Jackson, Birchall, Swift, Gilbody, P. Longton, Griffiths, Syder, Kenwright. ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. Mr. HALL proposed the re-appointment of Mr. Marsh as chairman of the 'Board. Mr. LEATHERB.AILROW seconded in suitable terms. The motion was unanimously carried. Mr. MARSH thanked them for again electing him chair- man of that Board. He was sorry that through a little ill- ness he was unable to be present at the last meeting, of the Board, when they kindly accorded to him a vote of thanks for his past services. He was, however, much obliged to them, and it would give him the greatest pleasure to preside over their deliberations. He was aware that he was getting older, but he trusted that any shortcomings on his part would Tired with their kindly indulgence. ELECTION OF CO:vIIIITTEES. div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.—The counting of the votes for the election of Guardians for the borough of Wigan was con- cluded on Saturday, the following being the result :—Messrs. E. Smith (C), 2,928; W. Brvham, jun. (C), 2,888; J. Nevill (C), 2,734; James Gerrard (b), 2,731 ' • M. Benson (1..), 2,567; W. Strickland (C), 2,373; James Hilton (Cl, -2,273; S. Meaden (C), 1,976; John Harrison (R.C.), 1,975; William Topping (L), 1,494; James Marsden (L), 1,311; W. B. John- son (L), 1,286; Joseph Hill (L), 1,118; Elias Ranecar (L), 954; Thomas Swarbrick (L), 788; E. W. White (L), 682; Joseph Brown (L), 680. The first eight are elected. Tao only change on the Board is that Mr. Meaden takes the place of Mr. Harrison, having polled one vote more. Politically the Wigan Board of Guardians remains as last year, consisting of seven Conservatives and one Liberal, but the Roman Catholics lose one seat by the defeat of Mr. Harrison.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GRAND CONCERT.—The last concert of the season in con neetion with the Go'borne and District Liberal Association was held in the Congregational School, Golborne, on Wed- nesday evening. The following were the artistes :—Mrs. Moss, Mr. McClure, Mr. Grimes, Mr. Armstrong, all of Wigan; Mr. T. Berwick, Golborne ; Miss Minnie Hayes, Earlestown • Miss Wood, Newton; Mr. Stanfield and Mr. Hayes, Earf2stown. Messrs. Grimes and Hayes officiated at the piano. Mrs. Moss was in excellent voice, and her songs were executed in grand style, gaining repeated encores. Miss Wood, who, we are informed, is only 14 years of age, sang with great taste, and was deservedly encored, Mr. McClure, who was suffering from a severe cold and hoarse- ness, was prevented from singing, as he would have wished. Mr. Armstrong sang in his usual well-known style, and met with deserved encores. Messrs. Hayes and Stanfield, in their duetts on pianoforte and violin, were well deserving of the applause they met with. Mr. Berwick was quite at home in his humorous songs. Mr. Grimes, who was substitute for Mr. Dawber, played with great taste and 5k.11,1, and. well deserved the applause he met with. T attendance was not very good, owing to the long .Sioppage of the mills and collieries at Easter.

The Master reported further that Bridget Ryan and Eliza- ' beth Ryan had returned drunk after hay ing been at the Portico Chapel, on Sunday. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS asked how it was that the Portico Chapel was being used when a chapel had been erected for the special purpose of being used jointly by Protestants and Roman Catholics. It was stated that the new chapel was used as a confessional by the Roman Catholic clergy. Mr. PARIS said it was never intended that the new erec- tion was for a confessional, but for public worship. The MASTERMYRS called in, and he said that he understood Father Henry was busy with the Lent services, so that he had not time to come to some arrangements with regard to the new chapel. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said that was quite a sufficient excuse; but one of the reasons for the erection of the new chapel was because some of the inmates returned from Portico drunk. Might he ask the Master if any other member of the Roman Catholic priesthood visited the chapel ? The MASTER replied that Father Henry's assistant came. Rev. T. CHAMBERS asked if in the meantime the inmates were to be permitted to go out to Portico. He thought it ought to cease. He would move that. The Rev. Father FINEGAN said he should certainly oppose that. He had not been in communication with Father Henry, but until they heard something from him, the Board had no right .to deprive the inmates of the right of Sunday devotions. Mr. MEADOWS: I quite agree that it would be wrong to deprive them of Sunday worship. Mr. PARIS said that Father Henry had plenty of time to make arrangements, and he ought to have made them the same as the other clergymen. Mr. FIDLER was very sorry indeed that his opinion had been confirmed, that the two denominations would not work together. They were only commencing that system, and he hoped there would be no dissention amongst them. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he was the last man in the world to deny Roman Catholics or any body else the right of worshipping as they chose; and he would withdraw what he said with regard to not being allowed to go to the por- tico; and suggested that they be allowed next Sunday to go, or until they heard Father Henry's reply. The suggestion was acted upon.

WIDNES IN ARREAR. It was statei that Widnes was £6,000 in arrear, and Mr. St.DLER asked if the Board could grant an assistant to Mr. Rigby (assistant overseer), to enable him to get the rates

The CLERK said the Local Government Board would have to be communicated with. Mr. MEADOWS said Widnes had been in arrear more than seven years, and as business men they were very much to blame to allow it to go on. In answer to the Rev. J. Barnacle the CLERK said Widnes being in arrear did not affect the amount of rates in other townships. Arrears were taken into consideration when laving the next rate; but the other townships suffered in the balance at the bank being overdrawn, thus losing the in- terest. Rev. FATHER FINEGAN said that as the arrear had been gcing on for some time, he thought there was a certain amount of censure due to the Board. Mr. HALL said at the rate Widnes was going the amount owing would never be paid off. Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Are not the Guardians to blame. The CLERK: I think so. It was decided to apply to the Local Government Board for permission to appoint an assistant. THE APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT OVERSEER. It was the opinion of the Board that Mr. Goff, relieving officer, would be appointed assistant overseer in the place of Mr. Rigby, and Mr. Leatherbarrow gave notice that at the next meeting he would move his appointment.

ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT NEAR ST. HELENS. A case exciting great interest in St. Helens and Bold dis- trict was heard at the St. Helens police court, on Monday, in a full court, before Mr. W. W. Pilkington and . Alderman Harrison. This was a case in which James Pemberton, a young man, farmer at Bold (for whom Mr. Shee, birrister, of Liverpool, instructed by Mr. Riley, appeared), was charged on remand with maliciously wounding Thomas Lowe, farmer, Bold, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of the prosecutor. Mr. Swift briefly related the circumstances of the case. He stated that the road where the assault was committed, Pemberton had not been in the habit of using, and the fact that he was on that road that night—which was not denied—proved that he had gone there with the deliberate intent of injuring Lowe. Words had been used by one of the parties -a short time previously in a public-house but such as were not con- sidered at the time in any way Offensive. Their worships after hearing the case would have no doubt that there was a prima facie case triable at the Assizes where he should ask their worships to send the prisoner. He then called prose- cutor, Thomas Lowe, Maypole Farm, Bold. He appeared with his head bandaged, and deposed: On Saturday night, March 18th, I went to the Wheat Sheaf Hotel, about half- past nine. That is near to the St. Helens Junction railway station. First of all I went into the bar, and stood there, and had a small gin. I drank part of it, and took the rest into the parlour. Pemberton was in, and several others, amongst them Mr. Rimmer, who began to talk about some pigs, and asked the company if they had any to sell. Mr. Rirnmer told me that he had been looking at some pigs, and said they were not worth having. I then said "Did they throw water on them." There was no notice taken of the remark, only the people, in the place laughed. Pemberton took no notice of it. I was in the room with them pretty nearly an hour, and stayed some time after I had made that remark. I left before Pemberton, and said "good night "to the company. Pemberton was there sitting in his place. It would be about half•past ten when I left. When I got out- side I turned to my right to go home. comic tunes. He did not want to outrage tender associa- tions, but he would rather have the plainest old f%lsi..ionul music, with heart, than all the performar « ; I t most educated choir in which the congregation ha Thu heart and no soul. And he extended the same law to the pulpit. He would rather have a plain man go into a pulpit, talking from his heart the truth of Christ, though he had no knowledge of Lindley Murray whatever, though he made continual blunders, and though the floor of the pulpit was literally strewn with the " articles " thrown with reckless profusion under him—(laughter)—than he would listen to some elaborate, highly ished, beautifully wrought out sermon, admirable in conception, faultless in style in every form and part, from which the soul of the preacher was absent and in which Christ was not exhibited as the Saviour of the world (Applause.) Speaking of Congregationalism he said that in many things they were behind. He did not say he was sorry for that, but there were certain points hi which the organisations of other churches might produce an impression which their simple constitution did not produce. There was an outward show of authority about what was called the Holy Catholic Church. Whatever was to be gained by those things Congregationalism must lose. They had no hierarchy, they were ruled by no Senate, but believed there was a greater, • and a mightier strength in the simple ad- herence to the highest ideal of Christian life as it was given in the New Testament; that the Church of Christ must con- sist only of Christians. Mr. R. W. DALE, M.A., of Birmingham, who was received with cheers, said in the course of his address that in some directions there appeared to be an undue craving for religious emotion, and that notwithstanding all the supreme claims of religious truth. He wbuld like to say something of the spiritual claims of religious truths upon Christian men. That celebration in which they were engaged suggested what appeared to him a most interesting impression of his position. That union, which was established in 1831, had grown from very.inconsiderable beginnings to great strength. Now in the meetings which Mr. Rogers and himself were and had been holding in various parts of the country, they were not assaulting other Christian churches. Their single desire was to present as vividly as they could to their fellow con- gregationalists the principles which underlay the congrega- tional polity, and enforce upon them the claims of those principles. Some two or three years after that time was founded a new religious movement, beginning in the Univer- sity of Oxford, that had gradually made its power felt in every part of the kingdom. From time to time that move- ment had directed the attention of the whole nation,and from time :•,o time it had awakened something like a general national solicitude, but it had travelled on unchecked from year to year. The movement to which he referred was the Tractarian or Puseyism, or more recently described as the ritualistic movement; and if it trav4lled in the same degree f the next 25 years as it had done during the last 25 years,the work of the Protestant reformation of this country would be almost undone, and large masses of our fellow countrymen would be on the very point of reconciliation with the Church of Rome. , The reasons for alarm were increased., There was a time when people supposed that if they wanted to confess sin to a priest and receive absolution from priestly lips they must forsake the Established Church and, conform to the Romish Union. They attached much more importance to emotion in religion than their forefathers did 100 years ago. One singular and remarkable proof of that was to be found in the sermons by Nonconformist preachers in the middle and towards the end of the last century, and elaborate appeals were made to the intellect. Preachers were then careful in proving Christian doctrine. But there came a great change in the character of their preaching towards the end of the last and beginning of the present century. The vehemence of that time had passed by, and in many instances honest instruction in the practical duties of the Christian life had taken its place; and in many cases there had been the cultivation of a quiet, devout, thoughtful, religious sentiment, and it seemed from the character of the hymns which had become popular that there had been a delight in a certain gentleness and sweet- ness of the religious sentiment. He did not depreciate sen- timent in religion, for that to be withered and blighted by the keen cold winds of mere intellectualism, was to destroy the beauty of religious life, lesson its joy, and 'impair its strength; but to give sentiment superiority was to under- mine religious faith and pave the way for fanaticism and superstition. And this contention was that the great re- Viva] of Roman tdoctrine and practices which they had witnessed during the last 25 years had been largely owing to the craving of the great masses of the English people for religious sentiment. There might be something very touch- ing and charming to religious sentiment in invoking the in- tercession of the virgin and the saints; but was it true that God himself meant that they should appeal to them instead of appealing directly to Himself? If it was true, then by all means appeal to the virgin; but if God did not mean that, thin their appeal to them instead of Him was enough to make them restless on their thrones, and enough to drown the glory with which God had crowned them. After re- viewing the polity of the Independent Church, he resumed his seat Amid applause. A vote of thanks was passed to Messrs. Rogers and Dale and a similar compliment to the chairman.

div.head: WIDNES FOOTB,UL CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES FOOTB,UL CLUB.

The annual meeting of this club was held on Saturday evening at the Central Hotel, Widnes. Mr. David Forster occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN opened the proceedings by calling upon Mr. Ireland to read the annual report, which was as follows: —" Having arrived at the end of season 1881-2, we now submit to you our annual report. The first team have been fairly successful in their engagem.ents, baying played 17 matches of which they have wen nine, lost three, and drawn five. With regard to the second team, the expectations ex- pressed in last year's report have been fully realised. They have played 14 matches, won 12, and lost two. Two matches have been cancelled owing to our opponents' inability to raise a team. 17 goals, 37 tries, and 74 minor points have been obtained, as against three goals, seven tries, and 29 minor points for their opponents. The result is particularly satisfactory, especially when we consider that one of the games, Chorely, was lost through the shortness of our team, 10 men only' turning up. The subscription list shows a deficiency compared with last season, but this is owing to there being no overdue subscriptions to collect, and several of our largest subscriptions have been withdrawn. Owing to bad weather the " gates " in first team matches have been smaller than last year, but the second team receipts show an increase. Notwithstanding these draw- backs we have not found it necessary to encroach on the fund in bank, but have increased it. As a novelty we met the Northern Clowns on February 11th. The match was a decided success financially. The total receipts were £22 14s. 3d., expenses £9 us. 61, leaving a balance to the club fund of £l3 2s. 9d. On March 18th Mr. D.Foster's amalga- mated team (Widnes, Excelsior, and True Blues) played Mr. Houseman's team, of St. Helens, for the benefit of the Widnes Accident Hospital. The result was highly satis- factory, and it is to be hoped the fixture will be an annual one. The receipts were £l2 17s. 9d., expenses 165., which en- ables us to hand over £l2 Is. 9d. to the Hospital Committee. As a small remuneration to the Star of Temperance brass band for the many voluntary services rendered by them on the club's behalf, a match was played for their benefit, the receipts from which were far from what we anticipated for so deserving an object. Owing to Urmston's inability to raise a team at the last moment the match had to be played between scratch teams. In closing this report we beg to thank our president, members, and supporters, for their kind assistance in enabling us to bring the season to a satisfactory conclusion." The list of committee attendances was as under :—Out of a possible 36 :—A. Brown 36, E. M. Davies 35, W. Smith 35, J. Carlisle 35, H. Cooper 34, J. Williams 33, W. Norris 33. F. C. Davies 31, W. Ireland 27, C. Hill 27, J. P. Kershaw 26, S. H. Kenrick 15, E. Wright (resigned), out of a possible 12,-12; H. Tilley (resigned), out of a pos- sible 13,-11 ; W. Patten, out of a possible 16,-10 ; S. Upward (resigned), out of a possible 11,—P; Dr. G. Brown, out of a possible 16,-6. Place-kicking competition, and 120 yards' handicap for members, November 2nd, 1881 :—First team kicking, H. Cooper (president's prize); second team kicking. W. Smith (club's prize). 120 yards' handle q), three prizes presented by club: Ist, F. Sampson (nine yards' start); 2nd, E. Farrell (two yards' start) ; 3rd, W. Patten (scratch.) Mr. E. M. Dims (the treasurer) read the balance sheet for the 12 months, which showed that the receipts had been £BB 18s. 5d., and the balance in hand at the close of the season £3O Os. 11d. (Applause.) Mr. Davies regrettea to say that owing to his numerous engagements he should not

be able to codinue in office during the next year. Several attempts were made during the evening to cause Mr. Davies to give way and take the treasurership again, but he said he was sorry to have to decline. The following officers were elected :—President, H. Wade- Deacon; vice-presidents, Rev. S. A. Spooner, Mesqrs. C. E. Barlow, T. T. Mathiesen, D. Forster, J. B. Booth, McDwaine, Morrison, and A. Gordon. • Mr. Alfred Brown and Mr. Ireland were nominated for the position of captain of the first team of the club. Both gentlemen were re quested to leave the room, and, oh the votes being taken, it was found that each of them had received 14. The announcement wae received with loud .cheers. The CHAIRMAN: I shall give my vote in favour of Mr. Ireland. (Renewed applause.) Mr. Brown was appointed sub-captain. Several gentlemen's names were put before the meeting for the post of captain of the second team. Mr. Wm. Smith received 16, Mr. John Smith 9, and Mr. Patten 4 Totes. Mr. 'William Smith was therefore declared elected, amidst acclamation. Mr. John Smith was appointed sub-captain of the team. Mr. Joe Kershaw was elected treasurer, 31r. Burgess secre- tary, and Mr. Pickering assistant secretary. Ihe following were appointed the committee :—J. Wil- liams, John Hardman, Joseph Hardman, E. M. Davies, W. Norris, G. Brown, H. Cooper, E. 31. Harrison, H. Mason, and W. Patten. The proceedings terminated shortly afterwards.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Dutton Workhouse. There were present the Res s. Canon Barclay, J. W. N. Tanner, and J. Lockwood; Messrs. Norman, Hazlehui st, Mclntyre, Hall, Pickering-, Davies, Rigby, Andrews Weir, Derbyshire, Challoner, Highfield, Smith, Stokes, R. Ashton, Wallington, Lowe, Knowles, W. Whitlow, G. Whitlow, Pickering, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

_ APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. This being the first meeting of the board after the late election, the CLERK said the preliminary business would be to appoint a chairman. The Rev. Canon Barclay was elected to the post, on the motion of Mr. NIELD, seconded by Mr. LOWE. The CHAIRMAN then took his seat, and read a communi- cation from Mr. Ashton, the vice-chairman, stating that he was confined to his room owing to a severe cold, and, there- fore, unable to attend.

div.head: VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: VICE-CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER said they were all aware that Mr. Ashton had during the past twelve months conducted the bwiness of the Board, when he had occupied the post of vice-chairman, with every satisfaction to the members. He therefore proposed that gentleman should be elected vice- hairman. Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, Mr. HIGHFIELD sup- ported it, and it was passed unanimously. The CHAIRMAN said that, personally, he was exceedingly pleased at the selection the Board had made.

div.head: 'WORKHOUSE CHILDREN.
div.p: THE 'WORKHOUSE CHILDREN.

At this part of the proceedings the children of the Work- house were paraded in the front of the Board-room, previous to attending the concert which was being held at Runcorn, on behalf of the Mersey Mission to Seamen. The children looked remarkably well, and on the mption of Mr. CHAL- LONER, seconded by Mr. RIGBY, a hearty complimentary vote was passed to the master and matron of the house, and the schoolmaster and schoolmistress.
