RIINCOIIN LEVI OUT IN TliE COLD.

Mr. lionatex brought under the notice of The Guardians the fact that owing to the work of nominating not having been attended to, Runcorn was short of three representatives to which it was legally entitled. He was very sorry that the late representatives of the Board had been left out in the cold—(langhter)—and he proposed that a resolution should be forwarded to t:-.e Local Government Board asking them to send down an order for the election of three Guar- dians. _

Mr. LOWE : But ought not that apdlication to come from the ratepayers of Runcorn? (Laughter.) What is to be done if they do not even feel sufficient interest in the matter to make the application? I think the number of representa- tives which you have for Runcorn is already sufficient. (Loud laughter.) The CHAIR-max said the present mode of electing Guar- dians was a most absurd one. He had thought of nomina- ting several gentlemen, but he was afraid that if he did so it would involve the township in a contest. Mr. LOWE : I think they should have looked to it. After the Deputy-Clerk had read the section of the Act relating to the matter, Mr. NORMAN made some ebservations to the effect that the Board would be quite justified in applying to the Local Government Board for an order such as he had mentioned. A similar course was pursued in the case of Newton and Helsby. Mr. HAzLEHuHsT : Mr. Norma i Norman and myself will guarantee the omission does not occur again f you will pardon us this i time. It will certainly be a most unfair thing f a town containing so many inhabitants as Runcorn has not a larger eprestntation. r. WHITLOW: I shall move an amendment against such a course being pursued. I must say that the Runcorn Guar- dians are always in some scrape. (Laughter.) Mr. NORMAN: Runcorn would pay the expense; you would not have to pay for it. Mr. WHITLOW: I think not. Mr. ik onmAx : I beg your pardon. Mr. LOWE : I think the inhabitants of Runcorn must have thought it unnecessary to look after the business. The Rev. J. Locßwoork : Probably the ratepayers of Run- corn must have thought it unnecessary to intarfere, as they were N well satisfied with the gentlemen who represented '

them last year. Had there been no nomination at all, the old Guardians would have been elected. Mr. RIGBY : I think the conduct of the Runcorn rate- payers is a gross direlection of duty, and they ought to suffer—they should be made to smart under the rod. (Laughter.) No doubt this has been a case of what is every- body's business is nobody's business. It was proposed by Mr. Norman, and seconded by Mr. Hazlehurst, that an application should be made to the Local Government Board on the subject. The resolution was lost by 13 to 8 votes, amidst much laughter. Mr. KNOWLES : Now, you Runcorn Guardians will look after the matter at the next election. ACCOUNTS. The Board passed accounts amounting to .£298 for the keep of lunatics. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The quarterly report of the medical officer of health (Mr. John Grant Bride) was presented, and stated that for the period ending the 31st ult. the registrar's returns showed 154 births and 93 deaths in the rural sanitary district of the Union. Of the births 75 were males and 79 were females. The birth rate was 86 per 1000, as against 82 during the corresponding quarter of last year. Of the deaths 60 were males and 33 females. Death rate 4 8 per 1000, as against 8 6 death rate and 4.7 during the corresponding quarter of 1881. Thirty-two of the deaths were under five years, 19 under one year, and 60 were five years old and upward. VISITING COMMITTEE'S REPORT. This document was presented, and showed that an agree- ment had been entered into with the Runcorn Board of Commissioners by which the Guardians covenanted to pay ' 21s. per week for all infectious pauper cases sent to the In- fectious Diseases Hospital at that town, and ss. for their removal to Runcorn.

THE COUNTY RATE. The Clerk produced the precept for the county rate, which gave the payments as £13,805, and the receipts £4,300, leaving a probable balance of £9,505 to be provided for. A rate of three farthings in the £ would produce £8,407 14s. 2d. For geaeral police a rate of a farthing in the £ would be required, producing £2,172 Bs. 3d. The Runcorn police rate for the quarter ending 30th June nest would be three- eighths of a penny, and would realise £248 19s. 9d. This terminated the business.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The first meeting of the new members of this Authority was held on Tuesday afternoon, at Dutton workhouse. There were present the Revs. Canon Barclay, J. W. N. Tan- ner, and John Lockwood, Messrs. T. Mclntyre, Peter Hall, W. Whitlow, C. Rigby, T. Andrews, J. Weir, J. Darbyshire, J. Cha!loner, J. Highfield, R. Ashton, E. A. Wallington, H. Lowe, J. Knowles, W. Pickering, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: ELEC- now OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELEC- now OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. MCINTYRE moved that the Rev. Canon Barclay be appointed chairman of the Board for the ensuing year. It was unnecessary for him to say oue word about the canon's qualifications for the office. Their late chairman was thoroughly conversant with his duties, and a tried public servant.

The motion was seconded by Mr. ROBERT AsmoN, who said he could fully endorse what had been said by the pro- poser, and it 'as carried unanimously. The CiteinmeN. in responding, remarked that he was exceedingly obliged for the compliment which the proposer and seconder had paid him, and which had been so hand- somely endorsed by the Board. It was, however, an office which he should, for some reasons, be glad to shirk, as two things in connection with it troubled him. One of these was that it was very unfortunate when considerable expense had been incurred by a township in carrying out certain improvements, to find that;af ter all, the water did not come to the surface, or the sewage go out by its proper outlet. There was also another matter which troubled him at times, and that was the hardship which the Authority seemed to entail upon landowners and property owners, some of whom, lii e agricultural depression, were un- consequence of the ig able to meet such liabilities. Ai, the tame time the regulq- tions which the Authority carried out had been made by the Legislature, and it was their duty to discharge their responsibilities to the utmost of their ability, however dis- agreeable they might sometimes be. In conclusion, be hoped that the effect of their work during the coming year would be shown not only in the improved sanitary condition of the district but in the increased longevity of its inhabi- tants.

MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS AND THE AUTHORITY. A letter was read by the DEPUTY CLERK from Messrs. R. Davies and Co., Warrington. stating that the executors of the late James Dutton had had before them the resolution of the committee of the Guardians offering them £5O as suffi- cient compensation for the sewer easement through their land. The communication went on to say that it was quite understood at the time that in order to avoid putting the committee to the expense of two arbitrations, Mr. Dutton's executors should await the result of the arbitration in Mr. Wright's case, and that that arbitration should be the basis on which the executors were to be compensated. Acting on this view, the amount of the compensation which would be I payable to Mr. Dutton's executors would be £BO as stated in their claim, and not £5O, and they do not think that they I would be justified in taking less. They had, therefore, in- structed the firm te inform the Authority that unlesstheBo were paid, they would have no other course open to them than to submit the question to arbitration. Mr. LOWE was certainly inclined to think that the field belonging to the executors was an unrevaluable one than Mr Wright's, and believed that if the members of the authority decided to dispute the claim, they would be only throwing away money, as it was a reasonable one, which ultimately would have to be allowed. The CLERK was asked if he knew of any similar case in the neighbourhood, and he replied that he had to do with one at Weaverham, where it was proposed to put a settling tank in a certain field, and the sum of £BOO had to be paid for the liberty. The DEPUTY, CLERK considered the offer such that it was a great question whether it was worth whiie on behalf of the authority to go to arbitration in regard to it, when the ex• pense of doing so would have to be borne by the union. Mr. ANDREWS said they had been pushed into one corner, aad he did not see why they should not go into another. Mr. KNOWLES asked whether the expense would come upon the whole of the authority's district, or only upon Frodsham ?

The DEPUTY CLERK said an application might be made to the Local Government Board to make the expenses special, and then they would fall upon Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. Mr. LOWE was of opinion that the better course would be to leave the matter to be decided by Frodsham and Frod- sham Lordship as to whether arbitration should be proceeded with or not. Mr. CHILLONER moved, and Mr. ANDREWS seconded, a motion in favour of offering the trustees £6O. Mr. LOWE : They will only laugh at you! Mr. CHALLONER : I dare say they will. Mr. ROBERT ASHTON did not see any way out of the diffi- culty at all. Certainly they were in a trap, but conlider• ing the large amount which the last arbitration cost, he thought it would be foolishness of them to go into another. He had great pleasure in moving that the £BO be paid. He did not know whether he should get a seconder or not. Mr. ANDREWS: I hope not. Mr. WEIR moved that the matter be referred to a com- mittee to make the best terms they could. Mr. WHITLOW seconded the amendment. Mr. LOWE : I should say, let us send Mr. Andrews to make a bargain with them. (Laughter.) ' Mr. AN-DI/ENS: No, no; let it go through its proper course, though I have no objection to join the committee. The amendment was put, and nearly all the members voted for it. No hand was held up for the original proposi- tion.
The CHAIRMAN (smiling): The proposer and seconder have not been true to their convictions. (Laughter.) INFECTIOrS DISEASE IN FRODSHAM.

A communication was read from the Medical Officer re- commending that the schools in Overton and Frodsham be requested to close for one month. In reply to Mr. Andrews, Mr. Farrington, the nuisance inspector, said that a special report on this matter had been already presented to the Board. Mr. ANDREWS: We have both a Medical Officer and an Inspector, and I think the matter is of so much impottance that it ought to be most carefully inquired into. The INSPECTOR said he had disinfected 15 houses since the last meeting. A sl- ort discus3ion took place about some gentlemen in the district having, as was alleged, not exercised due care in regard to his servant, who, it was stated, was sufferirg from the disease. The Board agreed to adopt the recommendation of the Medical Officer, and the Clerk inquired whether he was to send the request to propriaors of private adventure schools? The CHAIRMAN: It is a case of hardship, but still it seems that on the general principle they ought to be put on the same footing as other schools. The Board seemed to be of the same op.nion as the Clerk, viz., that the recommendation should also be the proprie- tors of private schools, who would be responsible themselves after they bad received the notification. The cemetery his donation of £2O. of Caranda in France gave some valuable results, and illus. The committee then adjourned. trated in the variety and style of ornainentation, the existence of similarity of customs and manners, between the authors of the Saxon mounds of our own country and that people to whom the Merovingian graves in Gaulish soil belong. The excavation undertaken by M. F. Moreau on the plain of Caranda had not been brought to a close, when this savant, anxious to extend his explorations, decided, from its peculiar features, to explore a slight eminence, which stands a short distance from the town of Terre en Tardenois, and is known as Sabloniere. It comprises about three hectares, or five acres of sandy land, barren, and devoid of cultivation, inclining gently to the n-eriver Ourcq, in the direction of a Calvary, which tradition said stands on an ancient Tumulus. Accordingly, two years after commencing the Caranda ex- ploration, arrangements were made for cutting through the Sabloniere elevation, and the result had been the opening of over 2,000 tombs, the contents of which preeminently prove that the cemetery of Sabloniere, like that of Caranda, had served during a long series of years as the last resting place of the Gaulish nation, of the Romans, and of the Franks who had succeeded them. Amongst the principal objects, this second discovery in the Department of the Airne had enabled the scientific world to discuss, might be noted torques, various weapons of defence, personal ornaments, as jewellery and trinkets, pottery and glassware, the latter forming beautiful examples of the art- of glass working, while some of the Gaullsh earthenware vases (of which there are many) follow in shape and contour those dis- covered some years back at the Morne; others in size and ornamentation recalled to mind the beautiful pottery of Chasseury. Numerous flint flakes, nuclei, and arrow heads had likewise been gathered from the cemetery, many of the arrow heads assuming such a perfect shape as to lead to the supposition, and with the utmost possibility, of a rather late date for their production. The circumstances of the deposi- tion of these articles were as peculiar and as interesting as was the deposition of the Caranda flakes, which engendered so lively and determined a controversy amongst several. eminent French arclueologlsts. The sandy eminence of Sabloniere of itself was, in the languaage of geology, devoid 9f flint, yet of the 2,000 graves, those of Gaulish and Merovingian date yield smaller flints in every stage of manufacture. These were scattered promiscuously around the body. The native idea con- veyed in this act was clear, and without doubt bad its origin at a time much anterior to the laying and formation of the cemetery, while it strengthened our conception of the ex- istence of a superstition, under the influences of which these bodies were consigned to their tombs. The Danish antiquary, V. Boye, examining, in the year 1863, the gallery tomb of Haumer, situate in the south-eastern part of the island of Zeeland, discovered a quantity of bones, from the appearance of which, he was led to assert that the flesh had been re- moved previous to placing them in tbegallery • and scattered in close prnximity to the debris lay several pieces of the rudest flint accompanied by others of the finest workman- ship. While M. Boye was thus engaged, Professor Hilde- brand, Baron G. Von Diiben, and Dr. Retzius were diligently opening out two gallery tombs in West Gothland, which gave similar results: thus supporting the hypothesis that a direct votive offering was recognised and accounted for these acts. That the bones were firstly fleed he (Mr. Smith) thought was scarcely worthy of credit, for that spectre of a religion, as primitive as themselves, namely superstition, would scarcely countenance what would be deemed a desecra- tion of the dead, while votive feeling would ineuce friends to place an offering rather by the side of the entire corpse, than with the bony remains. Having pointed out the differences between the flint heads found at Caranda and Sabloniere, and those discovered at Ohio, in the United States, Mr. Smith went on to show the similailty between the cemetery of Sabloniere and the Necropolis of Caranda. One of the most valuable results of the ex- cavation at the Sabloniere was that it bad opened out to the archmlogical science, a knowledge into the manners adopted by the Gaulish popu- lation, in the interment of their great men and chieftains. On the 27th January, 1876, an isolated sepulture inclining to the east, was revealed at the extreme east of the cemetery. It was the tomb of a Gaulish warrior, interred on his war chariot, and with all the insignia of his position. Mr. Smith sketched in an interesting manner, the appearance and cus- toms of the Gauls, and said, passing over isolated cases of sepulture, the pictures of Gaulish funeral customs, we found ourselves face to face with sepulchrul evidences, essentially Roman.- The peculiar style andluxuriousness of the pottery, the method of calcining and depositing the osseous frag- ments, the glass ware of indubitable type, the jewellery and trinkets, all pointed to a period when luxury was prevalent, and the country had submitted to the influence of foreign government. The custom also prevailed of placing the en- tire body in the ground, in which instances, the head was invariably raised and in a southerly direction, while the feet lay in the corresponding cardinal point. In some sepul- tures, greater care had been exhibited, and not unfrequently had graves been opened, the occupants of which had the feet. raised and resting on a fl ig or stone support; undoubtedly brought some distance with this purpose in view, since the surrounding features were such as to ' show these materials to be foreign to the neighbourhood. In a nurnber of cases the ceremonial of burying the dead had been more carefully attended to, a wooden coffin having been supplied. Those sepultures which both in the cemetery of Caranda and Sah- loniere, show signs of wooden stalls or other wooden protections intioduced a subject at once curious and in- teresting. On the first evidence it would appear striking that in these sepulchral areas such methods of burial should have been so early adopted, and indeed the explana- tions which had been hazarded tended to nothing concle- sive. It was indubitably the fact that the majority of these instances date to the Roman period and belonged to those who took part in, or immediately followed the Reeman in- vasion. The migratory inclinations of the Hebrew increased the probability of there being many of the race settling where- ever the Roman power offered protection and it was there- fore not improbable that in the vicinity of these cemeteries small Hebrew colonies were established mingling with the Populace when living, and claiming burial when dead. But it might be advanced that the national prejudices for sequestrated burial would be against the probability of find- ing their tombs amongst those of another race. That had this nation been in numbers, a separate section would have revealed itself in the burial site. But even had a separate allotment been originally made the preponderance of Romans would in time cause this isolated fragment to be encroached upon, and what was once separate, weuld then form, without outward distinction one great whole, servieg the purpose of the last and solitary tribute to mankind. A strong Jewish prejudice existed against burning the dead; it was a custom with this race to place the bodies entire ia the earth protected by a coffin _or casement. It may not be improbable, then, that some of these tombs in these cemeteries from which remains had been taken, and which plainly demonstrate the original use of a wooden shell, were those cf Hebrews who had annexed their fortunes to, or - followed in the wake of their conquerors. Not unfrequently remains, judged to be those of children, were found many in one tomb, as in one bed. In such instances they might with propriety be considered as members of one family, dying shortly after each other in infancy. If so, oould we imagine how much of the cruelty of ancient sorrow was concealed under those spaces? They formed one of the most sorrowful pages in the history of early funerals, which could not reveal to us the tears maternal sorrow had shed over remains so dear, and which were now viewed with so great indifference and curiosity. Au idea of the tender and pious affection generally surrounding tombs was not unfrequently conveyed to us by the numerous objects it had caused to be carefully laid with the body in the tomb—the lychramatories. the vases for perfumes, the plates for food, the vases for drink, the small coin—sometimes in the mouth, sometimes in the hand—to satisfy the avaricious ferryman Charon, all tended ' to point to a system of revered superstition known not to be, foreign to the Roman population. Often from the rude rot ' simple surroundings it was difficult to decipher the religion preferred Mille alive, although we were cognisant of the ancient belief in the existence of a Charon, a Lahon, and the Manes, and of the necessity of earthly materials to those passing to their elysium. Tombs had been opened, and by the side of the dead had been displayed, there placed, some, if not the whole, of the domestic earthenware crockery. The vase placed at the feet as a preventitive against diabolical visitation, or, rather, against the visitation of the evil gods, in which so great a belief existed, but little modified, ,even ,to Medimval times. Nevertheless an idea of religion and Christianity must have existed, and have prompted the symbolical use in the decoration and ornamentation of the various pieces of per- sonal adornments, so much admired by the feminine element of the luxurious mistress of the world. To the existence of this religious feeling only, however, can be attributed the custom of otnamenting fubuloe, rings, belt, plaques, buckles, and even the writing styles and vases, with the cross. Not only must religious feeling,have exercised influence on the decorative propensity, but also to it must be attributed the sanctity of the tomb ; for even in early classic times this sacred character, hallowing the rites for the dead, exerted

itself, and called into existance laws for the special protec- tion of the gods' acres. These laws protected grave yards the enforcing of heavy penaltieg rromulgatorl •" • - in several imperial edicts. After quoting several inscriptions to show the sacredness of the tombs, the lecturer exhibited a number of drawings of the vessels in earthenware and glass found in the tombs, and described their respective peculiarities. There had also been discovered at Sabloniere numerous pieces of metal which, although of the mere com- mon types than elsewhere exhumed, were nevertheless in- teresting as being illustrative of the knowledge possessed by the artificers in those early times in the art of tinning, and may be regarded as being the earliest examples of this art extant. Sabloniere had yielded but few engraved stones. In conclusion, the lecturer said the observer would not fail to see the analogy which existed between this cemetery and that at Carar.da in their general aspects and the style of objects unearthed. To decipher the customs, the usages, manners, arts, and religion of our forefathers we must have no fear, but boldly enter the tomb with the torch of truth in our hand. The spirit of profanation was foreign to the excavator as he opened out those receptacles of long-buried treasures, and the legitimate desire to speak of our forefathers as they were, impelled him onwards. Civilisation taught man to enlarge his thoughts; reason gave him understanding, enabled him to enjoy com- parison, and so follow in that course of truth which increased the scientific value of an undertaking, and so rewarded those energetic excavators who in endeavouring to cause the flame of•early history to burn the brighter had sacrificed on its altar time, means, and convenience. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Smith, on the pro- position of Mr. CHARLES WHITE, seconded by Mr. Dux. Alderman CHANDLEY then proposed a vote of thanks to the president for his services during the session. In doing so he regretted that there was not more matter in town to be obtained by the presidents of the society. He was afraid he must think the youth of the present day were rather sluggish intellectually. He asked whether it would be consistant to apply the funds of the society for a prize to the junior members of the society to read a paper on any given subject. Whether that would/stimulate the growth of intellect he did not know, but the suggestion might possibly be worth the consideration of the council. The Rev CANON DODD seconded the vote of thanks. He remarked that reference had been made to the intellectual vigour, the superior intellectual vigour of the past genera- tion, to the rising generation. (Hear, hear.) In the case of the president they had a proof of the superior physical vigour as well, for during a considerable portion of his pre- sidency, he had been at a considerable distance from War- rington, and yet he had at almost every meeting of the society found sufficient physical strength to carry him to the president's chair. He therefore hear:My seconded the vote of thanks.

The proposition having been carried with applause, The CHAIRMAN expressed his thanks to them for the vote. Adverting to the remarks of Alderman Chandley as to the intellectual capacity of the rising generation, he said he did not know whether it was true or not as regarded the males, but he thought it was not true as regarded the ladies of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) They had been very much pleased to see at the meetings of the society so many of the gentler, but not less intellectual sex. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the society would go on and prosper, and that they would be able to continue the succession of good papers. He thought the attractive element had not been so prominent as it might be, and he thought it would be well for them to have occasionally some more popular and attractive papers read than they had been able hitherto to obtain. Their meetings were often largely attended by the young and he thought it was due to them, if possible' to have attractive and intresting papers even though they might not be so deep and abstruse as they sometimes obtained. He concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to the retiring secretary, Mr. J. Paul Rylands. (Hear, hear.) They all regretted that be had to leave them, and the book would show in what an admirable and artistic manner the minutes of the meeting had been kept by him. He thought he might say without any disrespect to former secretaries, that no secretary had given se artistic and beautiful an appearance to the minute book as Mr. Rylands had done. (Hear, hear.) They all rejoiced in the fact that the gentleman who seemed likely to remain a bachelor had at last taken to himself a wife; and they all wished him very much happiness, which he was sure Mr. Rylands would have, although they were sorry that circumstances had deprived the society of his services. (Applause.) Mr. DUN had much pleasure in seconding the vote of thanks to Mr. Rylands, and congratulating him upon his marriage. There was no man, from his extensive knowledge. and study of the literary and scientific subjects in our own district, better calculated to perform tjie duties of caterer of papers to be read before the society, and in that respect Mr. Rylands' departure from amongst them would be a direct loss. (Hear, hear.) The vote of thanks was heartily _carried. - -

The Rev. R. PILCHER moved that the following gentle- men be requested to act on their behalf for the good of the society :—President, Mr. C. Broadbent • treasurer, Mr. John Dun; Rev. Canon Dodd, Mr t Robert Davies, and Mr. Henry Bleckley, council; Mr. Charles White and Mr. J. B.Young, hon. secretaries. He felt personally obliged to the officers because in the face of the discouraging attendancps which he had noticed on several occasions it really requireti a great deal of self-sacrifice and interest in the affairs of the society for gentlemen to step forward to take the management. He felt quite ashamed that there were so few present that night and especially he felt ashamed when he remembered the poor attendance on the occasion of the very admirable paper on Mrs. Browning's poetry. He must say the society did not support its officars.by their attendance in such a way a 3 they ought to do. Councillor MONKS, in seconding the proposition, said he was very glad indeed to see that the lecturer was a young man. He thought the society had done very little by way of encouraging young men, but he hoped in future they would give that encouragement that young men needed. He did not believe there was that intellectual decay described. If they would give the necessary encouragement there were young men of ability willing to do what they could to make the society a success. The proposition was carried. A conversation ensued, and Mr. Dux remarked that the members should make a point of attending, to keep up the interest in the society, if they wished to maintain it.. He thought their duty to the society ought to lead them to come and support it by their presence at the meetings. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
Mommv.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman),
and Mr. R. M.Broske.

" kucll ADO ABOUT NOTHING."—John Morris and Ellen Morris, his wife, fish dealers, High-street, were summoned for using language to Sarah Ann Bolton, Bridge-street, which was calculated to cause a breach of thg peace.—Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake) appeared for the defence.—Com- plainant said that on the 11th instant she was going from the market, where she has a stall, when she met the defen- dants, who used defamatory and very irritating language to her. Several witnesses were called on both sides.—Amongst those for the defence was Mr. Charles Dutton, market inspector, who said the defendants had occupied a stall at the market for some eighteen months, and he had had no complaints about their behaviour, though he had received several concerning Mrs. Bolton, who, he believed, from what he knew of her character, to have been the aggressor in this particalar case.—Mr. Lake also addressed the Bench, who dismissed the summons, remarking they believed one party in the case to have been as bad as the other.—Complainant's , expenses were us. 6d. Mn. GUEST, QUARRY OWNER, IN COURT.—Mr. William Guest, quarry owner, was summoned for having, on the 12th instant, assaulted George Purslow, labourer.—Mr. Burton represented complainant, who lives at Weston, and the defendant resides at Higher Runcorn. Mr. Burton said Purslow was in the employment of Mrs. Farrell, a widow, who has a quarry adjoining Mr. Guest's, but to it there was a separate enhance. On the 12th instant, Purslow had occa- sion to complain of the way in which the rubbish from the defendant's quarry was being tipped into the cart road which formed the only way of getting to Mrs. Farrell's quarry. He remonstrated with the men employed by defendant, and asked them to remove the rails on which the rubbish was carried, but they would not, and defendant flew into a pas- sion, pushed complainant partly down the bank, and when he got up, hit him three or four times with a crowbar.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defence, and said he had to take an objection to the jurisdiction of the court to settle the matter. The defendant on this occasion was only exer- cising those rights which he believed, and was advised he possessed, as lessee of the quarry and land from the Marquis of Cholmondley. From the opening statement of Mr. Burton, it appeared that the assault took place during a quarrel occasioned in respect to who had a right to the possession of certain rails. Under these circumstances, he submitted that the Bench had no jurisdiction which would enable them to try the case.—ln reply to Mr. Ashton, magistrates' clerk, Mr. Linaker said he could, if thought necessary, put in the lease executed with the Mar- quis of Cholmondley*as the result of which his client said he had a right to be upon the ground where he (defendant) stood at the time of the quarrel.—Mr. Burton read a section of the Act of Parliament relating to the legal point at issue, which stated that the justices were to be careful that they were not led away by a mere statement of a defendant, or a simple pretence to a title.—Mr. Ashton asked defendant's solicitor if he could point out on the plan, fastened to the lease produced in court, the spot where the alleged assault occurred.—Mr. Burton objected to the plan, on the ground that it was not what it purported to be, but only a tracing. —Mr. Linaker: I can prove his Lordship's signature if you wish it.—Mr. Burton : Well, then, prove it.—Mr. Beswick, agent to the Marquis, was put into the witness box, and said the lease produced was executed in the presence of his lord- ship, and the plan was at that time attached to the lease.— The Chairman: As a question of title arises in this case, we are of opinion that we cannot go on with it. The summons will be aismissed.—The complainant, who had been told exactly the same thing when he applied for the summons in c;pen court, had now to pay the expenses, in addition to the charge which would be made by his own solicitor. A WEAK AND CURIOUS CASH. A respectable-looking old man named John Aston was summoned by a peculiar- looking person, whose face appeared as if it had not seen a barber for some years, named John Darlington, for stealing a dog from him, on the Bth inst.—The complainant, who said he lived at Rock Savage, stated that the defendant brought the animal, which was worth 10s., to him on the 14th March, and "pressed him very heavily" to have it: He agreed to do so, and Aston said that if he decided not to keep it, he had better give it some one, or take it away from the district, as be dare not go home with it again. About a month after, defendant came to the house whilst he was ..at his work, and took the dog away. He had taken a license out for it.—Edwin Goodall said

he saw the animal at a certain house where defendant was, and asked him whose it was, on which he said he had given it to Darlington.—The defendant elicited from the com- plainant, during cross-examination, that he had paid Is. on account for the dog, but it appeared he had not discharged the remainder of the debt.—The Bench dismissed the case.— Complainant was afterward&charged by Mr. Riley, officer to the Runcorn School Attendance Committee, with not send- ing his child to school. On his name being called he caused some-laughter by professing to be deaf, though he apparently heard everything which had been said, for he at once began a pitiful tale about his circumstances.—The Chairman (humonronsly): You will have ss. to pay, and perhaps the same person who found you the dog licence will find you some money with which to enable you to send your children to 9chool ! (Loud laughter.) CARELESS PARENTS.—James Forster, Thomas Antrobus, and John Clarke were summoned by the Runcorn School Attendance Committee for not sending their children to school. ,Mr. Thomas Riley, attendance officer, proved tbe cases, which were from the neighbourhood of Clifton, and each defendant had 55., including costs, to pay. A DISORDERLY WOMAN. Martha Worthington was ordered to enter into her own recognisance to keep the peace six months, and pay 10.3. 6d. costs, for fighting in Church street, on the previous Monday night.—P.C. Devouport proved the case. A SAD CASE OF ROBBERY.—AIice Hall, formerly of Weston, and her daughter, Theresa Hall, were charged, the first with stealing and the latter with receiving six shirts and a pair of drawers, the property of Unsworth Brothers,High- street, on the 11th inst.—Mr. Jabez Unsworth said he was manager and partner in the firm of Unsworth Brothers. The six shirts and one pair of drawers produced were their pro- perty, and he last saw them safe on Tuesday afternoon, about four o'clock, on the pillar outside the shop eoor. The prisoners lived on the opposite side of the street, and they had frequently been in the shop.—Mr. John Arthur Smith, pawnbroker, said that on the previous Tuesday afternoon the prisoner Theresa Hall pledged the shirts with him for is. 61 He asked her to whom they belonged, and she said they were her father's.—Mr. Edwin Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street, stated that on the 12th inst. the younger prisoner pledged a shirt and pair of drawers with him for 2s. 3d., giving her own name. She said the articles belonged to Mrs. Bibby, of Weston.—lnspector Hollingworth said that on the previous Friday he received the articles which had been pledged from the pawnbrokers, and apprehended the prisoner Theresa in Church-street. He took her to the police station, and there showed her the four shirts, and charged her with stealing them. She replied, "My mother sent me with them, and I gave her the tickets." He then went to the elder prisoner's house, in Vicar-street, and told her what her daughter had said. The mother replied that a stratage woman brought the goads to the door, and asked her to let her daughter take them to the pawnshop.—Superin- tendent Williamson remarked that tie was exceedingly sorry to see the girl Theresa placed in the dock on such a charge, as he was convinced that if the mother had done her duty by her offspring she would never have been found there. He had not the slightest doubt about the other pri- soner being a thoroughly bad hearted woman, as she had enceuraged her daughter to pledge the stolen property, and this sort of conduct was one of the chief reasons why there were so many thieves. A great number of felonies had been committed in the neighbourhood where the woman lived iri a cellar, and be was very much inclined to think she had been concerned in most of them.—The Chairman said the Bench entirely approved of the remarks made by Superin- tendent Williamson. The mother in this case was placed in a most disgraceful position, as it was quite clear she had never even taught her daughter what common honesty was, much less what it was to be truthful. She would be com- mitted to gaud one month with hard labour, and her daughter would be set at liberty.—The prisoner, who preserved a very firm expressian of countenance, did not utter a word of reply.
THURSDAY.—Before Mr2S. B. Chadwick.

BEGGING IN CIIURCH-STIZEET.—An old man, who was some short time ago proved to have grossly deceived the magistrates and the police AS to his condition, was sent to gaol for 14 days for begging in Church-street on the previ- ous night.

WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 7 children, 9; total, 16. ST. PAUL'S AND ST. BARNABA.S' MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The session of this society was closed on Satur- day evening with a tea party, at which between 50 and 60 sat :lown, in the girls' schoolroom, Heathside. Afterwards the president (the Rev. S. Wilkinson) took the chair, and a presentation was made to Mr. John Gibson, the late secre- tary. The President briefly reviewed the services of Mr. Gibson, who as a secretary had proved invaluable. He then called upon Mr. John Peers, as senior member, to make the presentation of an easy chair, given by the members, in grateful recognition of Mr. Gibson's services as secretary during the past five years, and also an address given by Mr. Calvert. Mr. Peers said Mr. Gibson's whole conduct, during the seven years he bad been connected with the society, had been of the most exemplary character, such as to entitle him to their most sincere love and esteem •, and he believed he expressed the sentiments of every member when he said that they parted with him with very great reluctance and regret. He had great pleasure in presenting to Mr. Gibson the easy chair and illuminated address as a token of the members' esteem and appreciation of his valuable services as their late sccretary, and added the wish that he might live long to enjoy this. Mr. Gibson briefly responded, and expressed his indebtedness to the members for the kind way be had been received amongst them. A concert followed, which was given by the members, and a very good pro- gramme was gone through. A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, and the proceedings terminated with the sing- ing of the National Anthem.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

_ The first meeting of the newly constituted Board was held on Tuesday, at the Board's offices, Alforde-street. Ther, were present Messrs. Carey, Pankhurst, Gossage, Kershaw Handley, Dr. O'Keeffe, Shuttleworth, Forster, Sadler, Wright, Dr. Bolth, Midwood, Webster, Martley, Johnson, and Allen (clerk). Mr. Kershaw, as returning officer, took the chair, and said the business was to appoint a chairman and committees. He remarked that Mr. Gossage was the oldest member of the Board, and he had very great pleasure in proposing that he be appointed chairman of the Board.
Mr. C.REY had pleasure in seconding the proposition, which wits unanimously agreed to: _

Mr. Kershaw then vacated the chair, which was taken by Mr. Gossage. The CHAIRMAN thanked the Board for their confidence. He said they had appointed a raw hand; he had had no experience as chairman of any Board, and if he made mistakes they would bear with him. If the members accorded him the same good feeling and zupport that was given to the late chairman, Major Cross, he thought the business of the Board would be conducted in a quiet and also an efficient way. Mr. MIDWOOD mentioned the name of Mr. Kershaw as vice-chairman. It had not been customary to make the ap- pointment, but it was quite right that they should have a vice-chairman. The business was very important, and, as they might not always have the chairman present, he thought it would be wise to have a vice-chairman. He therefore proposed that Mr. Kershaw be vice-chairman. Dr. O'KEEFFE pointed out that it had not been the rule to appoint a vice-chairman. The rule was simply this: In the absence of the chairman the members appointed a chairman for the time b?.ing ; and he thought they had better confirm the old rule. Mr. MIDWOOD : That I unders_tand to be the rule, but it is quite competent for 118 to have a vice-chairman, and I think it would be well in case we should not have the chair- man present. The CHAIRMAN said they could not go beyond the Public Health Act, 1875, which stated that if the chairman was absent from any meeting at the time appointed for holding the same, the members present should appoint one of their number to act. Mr. MmwooD : I should like to have the opinion of the Board. The CHAIRMAN: Excuse me interrupting. You cannot act illegally. Mr. HANDLEY : I think Mr. Midwood is confounding the Local Board and the Board of Guardians. Mr. MIDWOOD subsequently withdrew his proposition. The appointment of committees was then proceeded with, it being agreed, on the proposition of Mr. CAREY seconded by Mr. PANKHORST, that the number and designation of the committees remain as before.

_ The appointments were as follow : Finance : Messrs. Handley (chairman), Shuttleworth, Midwood, Wright, and O'Keeffe. Gas and Water : Messrs. Pankhurst (chairman), Forster, Handley, Booth, and Webster. Highway: Messrs. Kershaw (chairman), Booth, Shuttle- worth, Midwood, and Sadler. Health: Messrs. Carey (chairman), O'Keeffe, Pankhurst, Manley, and Wright. • Hospital: Messrs. Sadler (chairman), Johnson, Carey, Manley, and Webster. General Purposes: Messrs. Carey (chairman), Handley, Pankhurst, Kershaw, Sadler, O'Keeffe, Booth, Forster, and Wright. It was decided that the meeting of the Board should be held on the second Tuesday in the month as heretofore.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT, MoNn&y.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT, MoNn&y.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun.

SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A HUSBAND.—LOVE AND JEALOUSY —James Fitzpatrick and Mary Griffiths were charged, in custody, with unlawfully wounding Michael Griffiths.—The complainant said he was husband of the last-named prisoner, and a labourer, living at 11, Bridge-street, Widnes. Fitz- patrick had lodged with him during the last six months; and on Saturday, after leaving work, he went with him to the Anchor Hotel, West Bank. He had one pint of beer, and paid for the prisoner one. During the time he was there his wife entered, and the two afterwards went out together. He (witness) followed them, and struck his wife, in a pas- sage near the public-house. The male prisoner then imme- diately knocked him down and kicked him on the head, so that he became unconscious, and afterwards lost a great quantity of blood. In cross-examination the witness said that whilst in the public-house he told 'Fitzpatrick that he would have to look out for fresh lodgings. A fortnight ago he asked the prisoner to go, and he had been on some occa- sions begged the police to eject him.—Sarah Bartley, 52, Bridge-street, said that on hearing some one cry "Don't kill me," she ran out and saw the male prisorer kick Griffiths several times, and blood was flowing from his head. Fitz- patrick was wearing clogs at the time. The wife stood by an unmoved spectator of the scene. Several men ran up on hearing the alarm she (witness) gave •, and the complainant was afterwards carried. into his own house.—Wm. Beasley, labourer, King-street, also said that he saw Fitzpatrick strike the complainant, and the wife also hit him violently on the head with a basin, which was broken in a number of pieces. Dr. McLennan said he examined Griffiths, who was suffer- ing from two incised wounds and three bruises on the head. He must have lost a great quantity of blood.—ln reply to Mr. Gaskell, the witness said that when he saw the prosecu- tor he was sober, and answered questions intelligently. It , was impossible to say what course the wounds might take. —P.C. Rogers said he apdrehended the prisoners. Fitz- patrick, in reply to the charge, said, "Who saw me do it ?" and the wife admitted that she had struck her husband on the head with the basin.—The prisoners were both commit- ted to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. A PUBLIC-HOUSE ROBBER CAUGHT.—John Haves was charged with having stolen 6d. from the till of the Royal Oak public-house, kept by Mr. Wm. B. Cross, Catherine- street.—The prosecutor said that on Saturday night the prisoner came into the bar for about half an hour, during which time there was no one else in. At last the prisoner jumped on the counter and pulled out the till. He ran to the spot, seized the man, and asked him what he was doing there. Prisoner, who was drunk, had 6d. in Lis had, and there were about 15s. in the till.—On being apprehended by P.C. McDonald, Hayes admitted his guilt, and was now sent for trial at Liverpool Sessions, there being a list of convic- tions against him. THunsuATT-Before Mr._Holbrook Gaskell, jun.

RACECOURSE GAAlBLlNG.—Elizabeth Garratty was sen- tenced to 14 days' imprisonment, on the evidence of P.C. Skinner, for gambling on Talbock racecourse on Wed- nesday. .YESTERDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. _

ALLEGED SKYAGE ASSAULT BY A MARINE STORE DEALER. ,—Paul Kerley, marine store dealer, Victoria-street, was brought up in custody charged with unlawfully wounding Luke Kelly, rag gatherer, Midweod-street.—lt appears that the prisoner only came out of gaol on Monday last, and whilst in prison the prisoner has assisted Kerley's wife to conduct the business. On Monday complainant went to.the shop with some rags, and a war of words followed; during which the prisoner ,knocked him down, and kicked him, breaking his left leg.—Sergeant Strickland was put in the box, and stated that on the previous night, at a quarter to ten o'clock, he apprehended the prisoner et Kelly's house, and charged him with unlawfully wounding complainant, with intent to do grievous bodily harm. He found that the prisoner had been making an attempt to settle the case.—Dr. O'Keeffe said complainant's right eye was black, and his left leg was broken, so that he was in considerable pain, and unable to appear.—The prisoner was remanded for a week.

SUDDEN DEATH Or •A CHILD AT ST. HELENS.—On Tuesday, an inquest was held at the Nag's Head, Eccleston- , street, on the body of Martha Roberts, a child, three weeks 1 old, danghter of William and Ellen Roberts, Cyril-street. On Saturday night the father and mother of the child went to the " fair," taking the deceased and two other children with them. Finding the ground was in a dirty state, they returned after staying a very short- time. After going to bed the child took the breast all right, and went to sleep on its mother's arm. When she awoke at a quarter-past seven next morning, she found the child was dead. The child had suffered from an impediment in the nose, or from a cold, 'which caused it to breathe with difficulty. The Coroner thought that this would cause death, especially if the clothes ' had been over its face. It was not, however, distinctly proved that the child was suffocated, though the jury would be inclined to think so.—Verdict of accidental death was returned.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

BURGLARY.—An extraordinary burglary has taken place at Lymm. John Nugent, William Buckley, and Alfred Proudfoot, warehousemen, of Manchester, early on Satur- day morning, at the instigation of Proudfoot, entered the house of Proudfoot's father, a retired gentleman, at Lymm, and stole a quantity of silver, some oil paintings, a quantity of clothing, and other articles. The prisoners were appre- hended on a boat on the canal when returning to Manchester with the plunder. When before the magistrates, Nugent and Buckley said the robbery had been planned in a beer- house in Manchester at prosecutor's son's instigation. They were all committed for trial at the assizes. LYMM LOCAL BOARD.—The annual .meeting ef this Board was held on Thursday, when there were present Messrs. Cameron, Rogers, Bailey. Taylor, Callender, Forster, Ridg- way (clerk), and Mullard (deputy clerk).—The business, which was the election of chairman and committees was quickly disposed of. Mr. Cameron was again elected chair- man, on the proposition of Mr. Rogers. The various com- mittees were also formed.
LYMNI PETTY SESSIONS.

FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. T. P. Norris and R. A. Joynson. INEBRIATES.—John Platt, of Booth's Hill, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Booth's Hill-lane, on the 27th ult., and he was fined 103. and costs.—Sarah Ann Dawnward, a married woman who was dressed in mourning, was charged with being drunk and disorderly.—P S. Har- rington said on Sunday night, the 19th ult., the defendant was very drunk at Eagle Brow. She bad two lads by her side, and they were imitating the Salvation Army, making some ridiculous antics. She was incorrigible.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs.--For drunkenness and disorderly conduct on the 19th March, R. Ra.wlinson, who did not appear, was fined ss. and costs.—Mary Crowan, a bad character, for a similar offence committed on the sth March, 1881, was committed to gaol for a month with hard labour. William Brazerrdale, fustian cutter, Broom Edge, was mulcted in the penalty of 2s. 6d. and Bs. .61 costs for being drunk in the village, on the 13th instant. MAINTFNANCE OF CHILDREN.—Thomas Bird, of Platt's- yard, Warrington, was summoned to show cause why an order should not lap made upon him to maintain his grand- children, Samuel (4) and Ellen (3), who were chargeable to the common fund of the Altrincham Union.—Mr. Toft, on behalf of the Guardians, asked for an order of is. 6d. per week, 9d. each child. Defendant was stated to be in receipt of from 235. to 295. per week.—Order made for the amount asked.--James Moore, tailor, Lymm, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his daughter who was chargeable to the Union. —Mr. Toft asked for an order Gf 2s. per week.—P.S. Har- rington: There is not a more disreputable character in Lymm, your worships. When his wife was lying dead in the house, he was drunk in other people's houses, letting his children lie about anywhere. —An order of 21. and costs was made. Assauur.—Fletcber Hol t and Henry Atherton were charged with having, on the 16th inst , unlawfully assaulted John Hart, an old man. It was proved that the defendants struck the complainant on the head twice.—Defendants alleged that they had been grossly provoked, and that if complainant was struck it was unintentionally.—They were each fined is. and 14s. 6d. costs. THREATENING LANGUAGE.—Frederick Harvey, manager of the Fleece Inn, summoned John Lea, wheelwright, Lymm, for threatening to assault him on the 28th March.— Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of £lO. BEGGING —Margaret Rooney, a tramp, was charged with begging in Church Green on the previous day.—P7S.Foden baying given evidence, the prisoner was committed to gaol for seven days.

Bold-street Chambers, Warrington, April 17th, 1882. NOTICE.—I beg most respectfully to inform the public of Warrington and the surrounding neighbourhood that since the recent dissolution with my son, T. 0 Pierpoint, I have concluded arrangements to take in as partner Mr. James Adams, who for a period of eight years has been engaged as managing assistant with W. Owen, Esq., Architect, ttc., of Cairo- street Chambers, Warrington. Our firm witl therefore from Ihis date be carried on at the above address as Architects, Sur- veyors, Estate Agents. and Valuers, under thy style or title of PIERPOINT & ADAMS. JOHN" PIERPOINT.

JTHOMAS CHILDS, hereby acknowledge that the 19 Claim made by me against Mr. Edward Badley, of Horse- market-street, Warrington, Licensed Victualler, for the sum of 108., and for which sum I sued him in the Warrington County Court ancbdbtained a judgment on the 25th August, 1881, was a fictitions claim, and that such sum was never owing by him to me. And I hereby APOLOGIZE to the said Edward Badley for having sued him for a sum of money which was never owing.—Dated the 17th April, 1882. (signed) THOMAS CHILDS. Witness RICHARD TUCKER, Solicitor, Warrington. 8, Percy-street, Lovely-lane, Warrington.

P A RLIAMENT.--SESSION 1882. ANGLO-AMERICAN BRUSH ELECTRIC LIGHT COR- PoRATION (LIMITED). BRITISH EL izOTRIC LIGET COMPANY (LIMITED). .EDDISON'S ELECTRIC LIGHTING. ELECTRIC LIGHT AND POWER GENERATOR COM- PANY (LIMITED). BIEMtNs BROTHERS AND CO., LIMITED (ELEC- T it IC LIGHTING); REF OLI7TION of Owners and Ratepayers passed at a meet- ing held at the Town Hall, on the 6th day cf April, 1882, ap- proving of a Resolution pa,sscl by the Council of the Borough of Warrington, on the 14th day of March, 1882, to oppose the rve-mentioned Bills in the present Session of Parliament. That this meeting having considered the said les lution It is unanimously resolved Th4t the Council do oppose in Parliament in the present Ses- sion thereof the following Bills A Bill to facilitate the carrying into ,effect the objects of the Anglo - American Brush Electric Light Corporation (Limited). A Bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the objects of the British Elect, ie Light Company (Limited). A Bill for conferring certain Powers on Local Authorities and Companies in England who may be entitled to use Edison's system of Electric Lighting, Heating, or Motive Power, and for o her purposes. A Bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the ajects of the Electric Light and Power Generator Company (Limited). A Bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the objects of the Siemens Brothers and Co. (Limited), and t hat the costssharges. and expenses incurred and to be incurred in opposi-g the said Bills, be charged upon the Borough Fund, Borough Rate, or other fund or rate or account of ths said Ccuccil ap- plicable thereto. Dated this lith day of April, 1882. JOHN RIOBARD PICK MERE, Mayor. W M. HY, BROoll,'Town Clerk.

LANCASHIRE INDEPENDENT COLLEGE. THE GRAND ABTISTIC COUNTY BAZAAR will be held in ST. JAMES'S HALL, MANCHESTER, on TUESDAY, MAY 2ND, 1882, and TEN FOLLOWING DAYS. The Hall will be transformed so as to represent a GERMAN MEDI2EVAL TOWN. From the Designs and under the Direction of MR. ALFRED DARBYSHIRE, The Painting of the Bcenery being in the hands of MR. ROBERT POLLITT. The Building of the Town by Mr. JAMES REILLY, of the New Globe Works, Cornbrook. There will be TWENTY-FIVE STALLS, representing the various contributing Churches and Congregations, Ac Full particulars of the OPENING OF THE BAZAAR, on TUESDAY, MAY 2, will be duly announced. Tickets may be had from Me,srs. Roberts and Son, 1,, Bridge-street; or at the offices of John Nunnerley and Co. Arpley Station, Warrington. CONTRIBUTIONS, Either in money or articles, will be thankfully received by the Secretaries, by the Members of the Local Committees, or at the Bazaar Offices, 80, Howarth's Buildings, 5, Cro3s-street, Manchester.
